nodes.title: Summary/Abstract
nodes.body:
To further enhance the information needed to support Essential Fish Habitat (EFH) and the Fisheries Ecosystem Plan (FEP), the SAFMC contracted the Florida Fish and Wildlife Research Institute (FWC-FWRI) in 2012 to create a database called Ecospecies (2948, 2940). Ecospecies builds on an earlier database created by the FWC-FWRI called the Florida Estuarine Living Marine Resources (FLELMR) system (2947). FLELMR was created in collaboration with the NOAA/NOS Strategic Environmental Assessments Division as a statewide application of NOAA’s Estuarine Living Marine Resources (ELMR) system. FLELMR has comprehensive species life history (SLH) profiles that summarize information from both primary and secondary (gray) literature. In addition to fish-habitat information, it includes information about population status and stock assessments for species that were not part of the ELMR SLH profiles (2946). FWC-FWRI has created a web-enabled Ecospecies database that includes SLH profiles organized by the FLELMR SLH outline.

Major components of the Red Snapper (Lutjanus campechanus) species life history (SLH) include the following: Taxonomy, Geographic Range, Benthic Habitat, Water Column Habitat, Artificial Reefs, Shrimp Trawl Bycatch, Food Habits, Reproduction, Growth, Value and Status, Stock Enhancement, Population, Management Regulations, Ecological Interactions, and Human Impacts. Citations and references are available for each entry in the Ecospecies database. Almost everything published concerning red snapper is reviewed in the present SLH profile.

Fishermen will be interested in sections that indicate where fish might be located, both for fishing and for nursery areas. Scientists can use the basic information and the citations to locate more in-depth data in a particular area. Managers can have rapid access to concise summaries, as well as the ability to correlate proposed actions with species likely to be affected by those actions. Short summary and overview information is provided for more casual readers.

nodes.title: TAXONOMY
nodes.body:
Scientific Name: Lutjanus campechanus (2794)
Subspecific names: None
Synonyms: Mesoprion campechanus (2794), Lutjanus campechianus (2796), Lutjanus blackfordii (2668), Lutianus blackfordii (2688).
 Common Name: Red Snapper
Other Common Names: Sow snapper, rat snapper, (northwest coast of Florida), mule snapper, chicken snapper (northeast coast of Florida), gulf red snapper, American red snapper, northern red snapper, caribbean red snapper, pensacola red snapper, mexican redsnapper, mutton snapper, and bream. Other common names are acara aya (Spanish), boca negra (Papiamento), chillo (Spanish), cora (Papiamento), huachinango del golfo (Spanish), luciano-do-golfo (Portuguese), pargre fine (French), pargo (Papiamento), pargo colorado (Spanish), pargo del golfo (Spanish), pargo guachinango (Spanish), parge real (Spanish), roodvis (Dutch), sarde rouge (French), vermelho (Portuguese), vivaneau campeche (French), vivanot jolle-bleu (French).

nodes.title: Family- Lutjanidae
nodes.body:
Taxonomic Characteristics:	 The following descriptions are taken from Rivas (2818), Anderson (2552), and Vergara (2896, 2897). Anderson‘s description includes fish that are Caribbean red snapper, L. purpureus which he considered to be conspecific with L. campechanus. He suggested the name Lutjanus aya for the composite species. However, Rivas (2818) noted that the species name aya (2567) does not apply to a snapper, and that campechanus (2794) is the oldest species name available for the Gulf red snapper. Reviews by Hildebrand and Ginsburg (2688) and Ginsburg (2654) applied the species name campechanus to the Caribbean red snapper. The information presented by Rivas (2818), however, indicates that the name campechanus refers to the Gulf red snapper and that the frequently accepted name blackfordii is synonymous with it. While there are some differences in scale counts above and below the lateral line (2818), it is not clear whether or not the Caribbean red snapper, L. purpureus (2795) is synonymous with the Gulf red snapper (Lutjanus campechanus). Rivas (2818) recognized the Caribbean red snapper as a distinct species (Lutjanus purpureus). Allen (2547) likewise treated L. purpureus and L. campechanus as separate species.

Egg/Parturition: Red snapper eggs average 0.82 mm in diameter (range: 0.77-0.85 mm). The egg is pelagic, spherical, unpigmented, and transparent, and has a single oil globule (2809).

Larva: Newly hatched larvae in the laboratory averaged 2.2 mm in standard length (SL) (2809). Lutjanid larvae collected in the field could be identified only to family by Collins et al. (2599), who also reported that the head was proportionately large and head length was about equal to body depth for red snapper larvae and juveniles 4-22 mm SL.

Identification and description of larval red snapper, Lutjanus campechanus, were based upon the general morphology, meristic characters, head spination, and pigmentation of specimens, ranging from 4.0-7.3 mm SL (2599). These specimens were selected from a total of 226 larval and juvenile L. campechanus which were collected mainly along the Texas coast from 1975 to 1977. Lutjanids <4.0 mm lacked recognizable characters, that are diagnostic at the species level. The smallest larva had not yet developed pelvic fin soft rays but had developed the pelvic spine. The pelvic spine was smooth on the anterior margin on 4.0 and 4.7 mm specimens. Between 4.7 and 4.8 mm this spine developed 30 fine serrations along its anterior margin. All larvae and juveniles 4.8-12.4 mm had these serrations. The number of serrations generally increased with specimen size between 4.8 and 12.4mm. The key to the development of the series was a unique meristic count. A brief comparison was made between L. campechanus and other lutjanid larvae and juveniles.

Bootes (2568) and Drass et al. (2618) described the development of red snapper from hatchery-reared larvae (2568) and specimens collected from the GOM. The larvae were characterized by the following features: a deep body; moderately short gut, 24 myomeres; and elongated dorsal and pelvic fins that form early in development. Specimens (1.9 to 26.1 mm) also showed the presence of weak serrations on pelvic-fin spines, absence of serrations on preopercular or dorsal spines, early forming pigment in dorsal and pelvic fins, and notochord flexion between 3.6 and 5.5 mm. Species-specific differences in number, spacing, and size of melanophores in the posterior ventral series are evident in the youngest larvae of species from the GOM whose development has been described (Ocyurus chrysurus, L. analis, L synagris, L. griseas, L. campechanus, and Rhomboplites aurorubens). Among lutjanid larvae, body depth, pelvic-ray length and serrations on the angle spine of the preopercle can be used in combination with pigmentation to identify larvae to species. Key morphological characters used to identify red snapper larvae are given in Lindeman et al. (2708) and Lyczkowski-Shultz and Hanisko (2710).

Young of Year- Identification and description of young-of-year red snapper were based upon the general morphology, meristic characters, head spination, and pigmentation of specimens ranging in length from 9.5-22.4 mm SL (2599). The specimens were collected mainly along the Texas coast from 1975 to 1977. The 12.4 mm specimen had ~ 60 fine serrations on the anterior margin of each of its pelvic spines. Between 12.4 and 22.4 mm these serrations were lost.

Juvenile- Age-1 red snapper have not been taxonomically described. Juveniles (12.4-22.4 mm SL) described by Collins et al. (2599) were most probably young-of-year (age-0) red snapper.
Presumably, juvenile (age-1) red snapper are similar in appearance to adult red snapper.

Adult: Dorsal fin IX – X spines, usually X, 13-15 soft rays, usually 14; anal fin l11-IV, usually 111, 8-10, usually 9; pectoral fin rays 15-18, usually 17; scales on lateral 1ine usually 45-47; gill rakers on lower limb of anterior arch 9 (excluding rudiments) (2734). Head large; lower jaw projecting slightly beyond upper; snout somewhat pointed; eyes small, contained more than 6.5 times in head length; interorbital region convex in the transverse plane; anchor-shaped patch of strong teeth on roof of mouth, a posterior median extension of the patch moderately developed. Pectoral fins long, reaching to anus when pressed against body; anal fin angulate in specimens longer than 50 mm; margin of caudal fin deeply notched.

Potthoff et al. (2801) described osteological development of red snapper from 129 specimens representing larvae, juvenile, and adult life stages using cleared and stained material. Emphasis was placed upon development of the vertebral column, ribs, fins and their supports, hyoid arch, branchial skeleton, mandibular arch, and opercular series.

Similar Species; Lutjanus vivanus (silk snapper), Lutjanus analis (mutton snapper), Lutjanus purpureus (Caribbean red snapper), Pristipomoides aquilonaris (wenchman), Rhomboplites aurorubens (vermilion snapper).

There is a remarkable similarity in morphology between L. campechanus and L. purpureus, starting by their same red color pattern, and coupled with completely identical (hard and soft dorsal and anal fin rays) and overlapping (hard and soft pectoral fin rays, scale on lateral line, and gillrakers) meristic characters. Based on these characters, Cervigón (2597) raised the hypothesis of the existence of a single species of red snapper for the western Atlantic Ocean distributed as far south as Brazil.

Evolutionary Relationships-Based on morphology, Rivas (2818) and Vergara (2897) hypothesized three phenetic groups within western Atlantic Lutjanus: the griseus group (L. griseus, L. apodus, L. jocu, and L. cyanopterus); the syangris or mahogoni group (L. mahogoni and L. synagis); and the analis or vivanus group (L. analis, L. campechanus, L. purpureus, and L. vivanus). Vegara and Rivas disagreed on the placement of L. buccanella. Vegara placed it in the mahogoni group, whereas Rivas placed it in the analis group. Based on isozyme and morphological data Chow and Walsh (2596) suggested there were only two well-defined groups, griseus and analis, with a third group (syangris) that had affinities to both well-defined groups.

Sarver et al. (2837) studied phylogenetic relationships of western Atlantic red snappers (Family Lutjanidae) based on mitochondrial DNA sequences Two gene regions of the mitochondrial genome were amplified: a 359 bp region of the cyt b gene and a 450 bp region of the 12S gene. The 318 base pairs of the 12S gene contained 47 informative sites. Combined 12S and cyt b sequences resulted in 640 base pairs, 112 of which were informative phylogenetically. Parsimony analysis generated three equally parsimonious trees of 282 steps. The relationship L. griseus (L. jocu, L. apodus) was supported by both bootstrap and decay indices. Moderate support was also indicated for a sister relationship between L. vivanus and L. campechanus, and for L. cyanopterus as the sister group for all other snapper species examined. In addition to analysis of the combined 12S and cyt b sequence, they also analyzed the 12S and cyt b data separately. When analyzed separately, both the 12S and cyt b sequence data indicated the occurrence of a clade containing L. jocu, L. apodus, and L. griseus and a clade containing L. vivanus and L. campechanus. On the other hand, separate analysis of 12S and cyt b differed in the placement of L. cyanopterus and E. oculatus. The authors concluded that additional sequence data will be needed to better resolve relationships among western Atlantic snappers.

A genetics study by Gomez et al. (2667) investigated the degree of similarity and the genetic structure between L. campechanus and L. purpureus. They constructed a common database of D-loop mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) sequences obtained from four populations of L. purpureus from Brazil and L. campechanus from the Atlantic coast of the USA (Florida, Louisiana, and Mississippi). Phylogenetic and population genetic analyses depicted high similarity between L. campechanus and L. purpureus, compatible with the hypothesis of a single species of red snapper for the Western Atlantic Ocean.

Gold et al. (2665) conducted phylogenetic analyses of 20 nominal species of tropical lutjanine snappers (12 from the western Atlantic, one from the eastern Pacific, and seven from the Indo-Pacific). They noted that phylogenetic relationships among western Atlantic lutjanines are not well established, in part because of morphological and behavioral similarities with the group, and in part because of the occurrence of both interspecific and intergeneric hybrids. Unfortunately, they did not include specimens believed to be Lutjanus purpureus. Neither did Sarver et al. (2837). Gold et al. (2665) stated that Gomez et al. (2667) had presented convincing evidence that there is only a single widespread species of red snapper in the western Atlantic (i.e., that L. purpureus is synonymous with L. campechanus). However, they also noted that taxonomic revision of western Atlantic lutjanines appears warrented, and they recommended that the genera Ocyurus and Rhomboplites be subsumed within Lutjanus. Until a taxonomic revision is published, it may be premature to consider L. purpureus as being synonymous with L. campechanus.

Studies to examine genetic population structure within the species Lutjanus campechanus have shown that variation in selectively-neutral genetic markers such as mtDNA and nuclear DNA satellites is low. Thus significant differences among geographic regions in haplotype frequencies have not been found (2590, 2664, 2662, 2660, 1998, 2835, 2836, 2833, 2649, 2663). However, Pruett et al. (2808) reported evidence of evolutionarily recent isolation by distance was apparent in mtDNA haplotype frequencies and Saillant and Gold (2006) reported significant differences in red snapper effective population size among northern Gulf of Mexico (GOM) regions. Therefore, although some selection pressure may exist to maintain mover phenotypes in red snapper population (2637), competing pressures must also exist, else selection likely would have driven red snapper populations to display even greater movement than what has been observed (2778).
The mtDA control regions of red snapper from the GOM (N =140) and Atlantic coast of Florida was sequenced (2649). Intra-sample haplotype and nucleotide diversities ranged from 0.94 to 1.00 and 1.8% to 2.5%, respectively. All population analyses were consistent with the hypothesis that red snapper constitute a single, panmictic population over the sampled range. A ubiquitous, predominant haplotype , shared by 23% of the specimens, appeared to be evolutionarily recent, in contrast to previous findings based on restriction fragment length polymorphism data. Tajima’s D values were suggestive of a recent bottleneck. Mismatch distributions from Gulf samples were smooth and unimodal, characteristic of recent population expansion. However, the Atlantic sample exhibited a comparatively broader, possibly multimodal distribution, suggestive of a more stable population history. Additional control region data may clarify potentially disparate histories of Gulf and Atlantic red snapper.

Saillant et al. (2834) examined temporal and spatial variations of 18 nuclear encoded microsatellites in age-0 red snapper sampled from 2004 and 2005 cohorts in each of five regions in the northern GOM and a mixed-age group off northwest Florida. A significant, positive spatial autocorrelation of microsatellite genotypes among fish sampled within the geographic range 20-100 km was detected. The results demonstrate that spatial genetic structuring among young-of-the-year red snapper occurs at small geographic scales and is consistent with a metapopulation stock-structured model of partially connected populations. This accentuates the importance of maintaining healthy local populations of red snapper in all regions across the northern GOM.

nodes.title: GEOGRAPHIC RANGE
nodes.body:
Overall: The Gulf of Mexico including the Campeche area of Yucatan, and the Atlantic Coast as far north as Cape Hatteras, North Carolina; not reported in the Caribbean Sea (2818, 1970; 2083). SEDAR24 (2852) listed the range of L. campechanus as also extending through the Caribbean to Brazil. A similar species (L. purpureus) occurs in the Caribbean with a range as far south as Brazil (2818, 2547).

By State: North Carolina to Texas, less frequently as far north as Massachusetts (2819).
By Stock: Growth rates and size-at-age information have been used to evaluate the stock structure of GOM red snapper. Fisher et al. (2627, 2628) modeled growth of red snapper from Alabama, Louisiana, and Texas with weighted mean fork length (FL) at age and weighted mean total weight (TW) at age using the von Bertalanffy growth model. Additionally, the authors compared growth of red snapper aged 1-10 years for each state by comparing linear regressions of mean FL and mean TW at age. The von Bertalanffy models predicted significantly smaller estimates for both maximum length and maximum theoretical weight for Texas red snapper compared with those from Alabama and Louisiana. Additionally, Texas red snapper were shown to differ significantly in regressions of mean weight at age. This led the authors to conclude that Texas red snapper were significantly smaller in mass (TW) at age and reach smaller maximum sizes than red snapper from Alabama and Louisiana. Fisher et al. (2628) suggested that this demographic variation in growth rates may indicate the existence of separate management units of red snapper in the GOM.
By Estuary: While red snapper are not commonly found in estuaries, Franks et al. (2928) found red snapper associated with a small artificial reef structure in Mississippi Sound. Age estimates from some specimens (N=36, 326-713 mm TL) ranged from 2-5 years. Histological examination of the gonads of 13 fish collected during late summer and fall found sexually mature males (N=5) and females with regressed (N=5) or immature ovaries (N=2). However, one female collected during July contained oocytes in the final stage of maturation. Tag recaptures were from the tag-release site and extended from 1-373 days-at-large indicative of site fidelity.
Adult red snapper sometimes move closer to shore in summer; they were collected in trawls in the lower parts of St. Andrews Bay system, Florida, in summer and fall but not in winter and spring (2766).

nodes.title: Life Mode
nodes.body:
Egg/Parturition- Red snapper spawn mainly during June through August in the northern GOM (2812). The early life history comprises a planktonic egg stage of 18-27 h (2809; 2728).
Larva-A larval stage occurs with a duration of 25-47 d (2704). Lyczkowski-Shultz and Hanisko (2710) analyzed Southeast Area Monitoring and Assessment Program (SEAMAP) larval survey data from the U.S. GOM. Red snapper larvae were captured throughout the survey area on the middle to outer continental shelf from Florida to Texas, but were consistently observed in greatest abundance on the mid-continental shelf west of the Mississippi River, especially off western Louisiana and central Texas. Larval red snapper larvae were captured in bongo and neuston nets from May through November. The months of highest occurrence were July and September (2710).

Hanisko et al. (2681) developed indices of larval red snapper occurrence and abundance for use in stock assessments. Red snapper larval data collected during Summer Shrimp/Bottomfish (1982-2003) and Fall Plankton (1986-2003) SEAMAP surveys were examined to identify time series of ichthyoplankton data that might best reflect trends in the red snapper spawning population in the U.S. GOM. Since, bongo nets were more effective than neuston nets at capturing red snapper larvae only catches from bongo nets were used to estimate annual occurrence and abundance, i.e., the SEAMAP larval red snapper index. The summer survey was conducted during the peak of red snapper spawning in June and July, but limited and inconsistent coverage during this survey did not permit development of a reliable Gulfwide (U.S. continental shelf) index of larval abundance. In contrast, the fall survey conducted near the end of the spawning season in September yielded a 16 year time series over which to examine trends in red snapper abundance throughout the GOM. Although occurrence and abundance of red snapper larvae were lower during September than in June and July, estimates from both summer and fall surveys showed the same inter-annual patterns and were highly correlated. Larvae were eight times more abundant and occurred in five times as many samples in the western than in the eastern GOM. The standardization procedure accounted for the effects of year, time of day, depth, and subregion in the western GOM, but only for subregion in the eastern GOM. Larval indices of red snapper abundance suggest an increasing spawning stock in both the western and eastern GOM after 1995.

Young of Year- A benthic young-of-year (YOY) stage occurs after the larvae undergo metamorphosis and settle to the bottom (2885). Size at settlement is about 1.7 cm. Red snapper enter the GOM shrimp fishery as bycatch when they have grown to about 5 cm TL (2891, 2672). However, they do not appear to be fully vulnerable to the trawls used in the fishery until they are 10 cm TL or longer (2672, 2646). Benthic YOY are broadly distributed over soft bottoms (2672) and other trawlable bottoms of low relief with a vertical scale in centimeters (2891). They occupy these habitats from the time of settlement in the summer of their first year through the following summer and fall, when they have reached 18-20 cm TL. The YOY exhibit highest abundance in microhabitats of low relief that range from silted patches of rubble to individual items of trash or debris like cans, mesh webbing from lost fishing gear, and plastic bags (2933, 2885). A key feature appears to be that larger predators (like adult red snapper) are not densely aggregated in the same areas (2642).

Little information exists concerning the presence and spatial distributions of YOY (age-0) red snapper in the southeast Atlantic (2817). White et al. (2919) presented two maps depicting the presence of 32 YOY red snapper captured by MARMAP near-shore off South Carolina and off North Carolina.

Juvenile- At sizes of 18 cm and above red snapper begin to recruit to high-profile natural reefs situated primarily on the outer continental shelf and to artificial reefs like oil and gas platforms situated over the inner, middle, and outer continental shelf in the northern GOM (2647, 2864, 2812). They are fully recruited to high-relief habitat by their second January at an age of about 18 months (age-1).

Adult- Older red snapper (>age 7) tend to move to deeper water (2939). They spawn over the middle and outer continental shelf zones and probably over the slope leading to the abyss in the GOM (2710).

Older red snapper are believed to move to deeper water in the southeastern Atlantic, but more data are needed to confirm this spatial distribution (2852).

nodes.title: Areal Zones
nodes.body:
Egg/Parturition- Gallaway (2939) discussed the study by Lyczkowski-Shultz and Hanisko (2710) which found red snapper larvae over the middle to outer continental shelf from Florida to Texas. Gallaway et al. (2939) noted that larval distributions coincided with the distribution of spawning adult red snapper. So, presumably red snapper eggs occur in this area (especially west of the Mississippi).

No information is available for the spatial distribution of red snapper eggs in the U.S. south Atlantic Ocean from North Carolina to Florida.

Larva- Drass et al. (2938) provided a brief synopsis of the spatial distributions of red snapper larvae in the northern Gulf of Mexico from 1982 to 1994. Lyczkowski-Shultz and Hanisko (2710) found 11 taxa of snappers from over 14,000 bongo and neuston samples collected during SEAMAP surveys in the GOM from 1983 to 2003. A total of 639 red snapper larvae were identified in bongo samples and 1053 red snapper larvae in neuston samples. The larval distributions were mapped. Red snapper larvae first appeared in May and were present as late as November. The months of highest occurrence and abundance were July and September. Larvae were captured throughout the survey area in the northern GOM over the continental shelf, but were consistently observed in greatest abundance over the mid-continental shelf west of the Mississippi River, especially off Louisiana and Texas.
No information concerning red snapper larval distributions is available for the U.S. south Atlantic, since no larval surveys are conducted.

Young of Year- Diamond et al. (2941) analyzed NOAA/NMFS SEAMAP bottom trawl data collected in the GOM from 1987 to 2007 using geographic information systems (GIS) to determine the spatial distributions of young-of-year (age-0) and juvenile (age-1) red snapper from Mississippi to Texas in the GOM. The Southeast Area Monitoring and Assessment Program (SEAMAP) trawl surveys used shrimp trawls similar to those used in the commercial shrimp fisheries for brown, white, and pink shrimp in the U.S. GOM. Catch-per-unit-effort (CPUEs) were standardized and the locations of low to high intensity CPUEs identified by interpolation using kriging in the GIS. Annual maps were created respectively for the summer and fall SEAMAP surveys. Hot spots of higher abundance of red snapper were generally located around the 30 m isobath, with hot spots spread along the Texas coast in fall, and clustered around the Texas-Louisiana border in summer. The annual maps were combined for various yearly combinations to determine inter-annual persistence of the age-0 fish captured primarily during the fall surveys, and for age-1 fish captured primarily caught during the summer SEAMAP surveys. Maps were created respectively for age-0 (fall) and for age-1 (summer) red snapper for: a) very high intensity with 2 years persistence (maps a and e), b) high intensity with 4 years persistence (maps b and f), c) 50A intensity with 6 and 4 years persistence for fall and summer respectively, and d) 75A intensity with 9 years persistence for both seasons (maps d and h). Hot spots moved annually but generally persisted in the same locations over time, indicating that marine reserves could reduce red snapper bycatch.

 The annual hot spots (zones of higher abundance) for age-0 red snapper captured in the fall were larger and more diffuse that the annual hot spots for age-1 fish captured during the summer (2941). The primary composite hot spots of age 0 red snapper started east of the Texas-Louisiana border and extended west toward the Mexican border, covering from about the 20 m isobath to the 50 m isobath. Annual zones of higher abundance (red and yellow zones) occurred off the Mississippi Delta, Louisiana, and from Galveston to Brownsville off of Texas. A composite map with >= 5 years of persistence depicted zones of highest abundance of age-0 red snapper (shown in red) just west of the Mississippi Delta, off Corpus Christi, and another hotspot off Brownsville.

In the U.S. south Atlantic, information regarding young (age-1 or less) red snapper is practically nonexistent (2919). Unlike the GOM, where young red snapper have been intensively studied, there are no published reports of young-of-year (YOY) red snapper in the Atlantic. Although White and Palmer (2918) commented on examining five YOY (59-133 mm TL) specimens to aid in the first annulus determination, they did not include these specimens in their dataset for analysis. White et al. (2919) added these records to the White and Palmer (2918) age determination dataset used to support the SEDAR24 (2852) red snapper stock assessment.

The Marine Resources Monitoring, Assessment, and Prediction (MARMAP) program conducts fisheries-independent monitoring from Cape Lookout, North Carolina to Key West, Florida (2919). A variety of traps and trawls have been used for sampling. Red snapper were captured ranging in size from 50 to 976 mm TL. The spatial distribution where YOY red snapper <150 mm TL (N=32) were captured from 1977 to 2009 occurred at an average depth of 15 m (7-18 m) relatively close to shore off South Carolina and off North Carolina (map, Figure 1) Most of these YOY <150 mm TL (N=31) specimens were captured using trawls in 1979, 1986, 1999, and 2000 (map, Figure 2).
Juvenile- Juvenile red snapper were caught in trawls on the Texas shrimp grounds (2574). The peak abundance of juveniles is in shallower water (20-46 m) than the peak density of adults.
Quantification of bycatch levels of red snapper in shrimp trawls has been done through analyses and general linear modeling of NMFS SEAMAP trawl survey data from the GOM (2672) and from observer data gathered on shrimp trawlers (2646). The early SEAMAP bottom trawl surveys were conducted in the fall from 1972 to 1984 from Louisiana to Texas; but the majority of the effort was off Louisiana. In 1985, the fall component was expanded to survey region from Pensacola, Florida to Brownsville, Texas (2646). The summer SEAMAP bottom trawl survey originated in 1982, and sampled from Pensacola, Florida to Brownville, Texas. Summer and fall surveys using a standard shrimp trawl became directly comparable in terms of spatial coverage in 1985, and shortly thereafter (1987) in terms of detailed sampling protocol. The spatial coverage can generally be described as encompassing the inner, middle, and outer areas of the continental shelf from Pensacola to Brownsville (2710).

The observer data for red snapper bycatch was collected on commercial shrimp trawlers on irregular years from 1972 to 1982, and from 1992 to 1996. Most of the shrimp fishery has been concentrated in the western GOM from Mississippi/Alabama to Texas (2646). While the depth ranges involved were not included in the paper, it is probably safe to state that the Observer data were collected from shrimp vessels fishing on the inner and middle continental shelf from Mississippi/Alabama to Texas.

Diamond et al. (2941) analyzed the NMFS SEAMAP bottom trawl data collected during the summer and fall surveys from 1987 to 2007. Juvenile (age-1) red snapper were mostly captured during summer SEAMAP trawl surveys. The annual zones of higher abundance of age-1 red snapper (red and yellow zones) determined by kriging generally extended from the upper Texas coast (east of Galveston) to western Louisiana from about the 10 m depth contour to about the 60 m depth contour. A composite map with >=5 years of persistence depicted a zone of highest abundance for age-1 red snapper (shown in red) off Galveston Bay, Texas during the summer.
Adult-  Once red snapper grow to about 8 years old, they are large enough to be invulnerable to most predation and occur over open habitat as well as at reef habitat (2939). In the western GOM, these older fish are most abundant in longline sets at depths between 55 and 92 m (2729, 2549). In this region, the zone of highest abundance of early red snapper larvae (2710) corresponds to the distribution of 8+ year adults taken on longlines (2939). This corresponds to the middle and outer parts of the continental shelf.

In the U.S. south Atlantic, spawning females were captured in MARMAP trawls and traps mid-shelf to the shelf-break (23-72 m) from South Carolina to Melbourne, Florida (2918, 2919). The locations where spawning female red snapper were captured were mapped. Most spawning females (defined as having either hydrated oocytes or postovulatory follicles) were captured either on the middle or the outer continential shelf.

Sedberry et al. (2854) reported that red snapper spawn at mid- to outer- continental shelf depths (24-67 m). Of 778 red snapper examined for sex and reproductive state, 80 were spawning females. Spawning females were collected in January and May through October in waters off South Carolina to Florida. The major spawning period was June through September. Red snapper spawned at temperatures ranging from 18.05 to 27.59oC. A map depicting locations where spawning female red snapper were captured by fishery-independent monitoring and by fishery-dependent monitoring indicated spawning occurs from South Carolina to Florida.

nodes.title: Vertical Zones
nodes.body:
Egg/Parturition- No information found. Presumably, the eggs are present in the epipelagic (euphotic) zone because the eggs are buoyant (2809). The euphotic zone extends down to a depth of 200 m.

Larva-Red snapper larvae were captured in bongo nets using double-oblique tows (two nets pulled at oblique angle from bottom to surface) over a wide range of water depths, 9-2000 m with a mean station depth =91 m and median depth =45.5 m during SEAMAP Summer Shrimp/Bottomfish and Fall Plankton surveys in the northern GOM (2710). Since depth at capture of red snapper larvae taken in bongo samples is not known, environmental data from mid and max water column depths only define the range of conditions experienced by red snapper larvae in subsurface waters. Since there is no closure mechanism on the bongo net, all that can be stated about where red snapper larvae occur in the water column is that they are pelagic. Since neuston nets were towed near the surface (within 0.5 m), larvae caught by this gear were captured in the epipelagic zone. Other sampling off Louisiana, Mississippi, and Alabama at three discrete depths during September 1984, 1986, and 1987 captured red snapper larvae more frequently and in greater numbers at depths of 5 m and 11 m than at 1 m, indicating they are slightly more common below than at the surface. Average surface environmental conditions indicate that red snapper larvae consistently inhabit warm (mean temperature = 29oC), saline (mean salinity = 34 psu), clear (median optical transmission = 87%) waters.

Lyczkowski-Shultz and Hanisko (2710) noted that the consistent presence of red snapper larvae in plankton samples taken between the 100- and 200-m depth contours on the continental shelf in both the western and eastern GOM supports the contention that red snapper spawn over a wide depth range, i.e., from mid-shelf to the continental slope.
Young of Year- Settlement of YOY (age-0) red snapper has been reported on the outer continental shelf in the northwestern GOM from June through October (2690). Age-0 red snapper occur in SEAMAP bottom trawls from the inner to the outer continental shelf, with highest abundances noted near the 30 m isobath (2941). Hence, settlement occurs within the epipelagic zone over the continental shelf.
Juvenile- Age-1 red snapper are located over various benthic habitas on the continental shelf of the GOM (2939, 2941). Hence, they occur within the epipelagic zone.

Adult- Age-2 and above red snapper (up to age-57 in the GOM and up to age-54 in the U.S. south Atlantic) have been captured at depths ranging from 9-366 m in the GOM (2729) and 7-240 m in the U.S. south Atlantic (2854). Hence, they occur in both the epipelagic and the mesopelagic vertical depth zones. The mesopelagic zone extends at depths >200 m to 1000 m.

nodes.title: Bathyl Zones
nodes.body:
Egg/Parturition- Red snapper eggs are pelagic (not associated with the bottom). It is believed they occur over the continental shelf (0-200 m depth range) and over the shelf slope (2710). The part of the shelf slope where red snapper may spawn is associated with the archibenthic zone (>200m to 1000 m).
Larva- Not applicable, since larvae are pelagic (2710).
Young of Year- YOY (age-0) red snapper are present over the inner, middle, and outer continental shelf in the GOM on sand, mud, and submerged oyster shell bed substrates (low-relief) habitats (2939). They are most abundant over the middle continental shelf (2941).
YOY red snapper have been infrequently captured over the inner continental shelf off South Carolina and North Carolina in the U.S. south Atlantic (2919). They may occur further offshore over low-relief benthic habitats, but this needs confirmation.
Juvenile- Juvenile (age-1) red snapper are most abundant over the inner, middle, and outer continental shelf in the GOM over low-relief and higher-relief benthic habitats (2939, 2941). They occasionally occur in the lower portion of estuaries (2766, 2636).

No information was found in either the primary or grey literature concerning either the areal or bathyal distributions of age-1 red snapper in the U.S. south Atlantic. However, length-frequencies gathered on at-sea headboats (which provided data on both fish kept >= 50 cm TL, and fish discarded <50 cm TL) from North Carolina to eastern Florida indicate high recruitment of juvenile red snapper ranging in size from 23 cm to 49 cm off eastern Florida from 2005 to 2009, moderate recruitment off Georgia in 2008 and 2009, and relatively low recruitment off North Carolina in 2007 and 2008, but not in 2009 (2838). It was not stated where the at-sea headboats were fishing. It appears likely that the fish ranging in size from 23-49 cm were predominately age-1 and/or age-2.

Adult- Adult red snapper are distributed over the inner, middle, and outer continental shelf and along the abyssal slope in the GOM (2939). Older (>age 7) adults tend to be found in deeper water over the middle and outer continental shelf (2729).

Williams et al. (2923) mapped the locations and relative size (varying size circles) of the number of trips for headboats catching adult red snapper from North Carolina to Florida. Red snapper headboat catches have been predominately from vessels using inlets in northeast Florida, which include; St. John’s River Entrance, St. Augustine Inlet, Ponce Inlet, and Port Canaveral. Vessels using these inlets accounted for 78% of the estimated red snapper landings from 2004-2009, while inlets in South Carolina and Georgia represented 14% of the landings. The remaining 8% of the red snapper headboat catches were widely distributed from Cape Hatteras, North Carolina to Key West, Florida. The majority of the fishing effort mapped by year from 2004 to 2009 (moderate to large sized circles representing >50 trips) was distributed off northeast Florida and off Georgia over the inner and middle continental shelf zones.

nodes.title: Mobility/Migration
nodes.body:
Egg/Parturition- Lyczkowski-Shultz and Hanisko (2710) observed that consistent presence of red snapper larvae in bongo net and neuston net samples taken from the 100-200 m depth contours on both the western and eastern GOM supports the contention that red snapper spawn over a wide depth range, i.e., from mid-shelf to the continental slope. After spawning the eggs are pelagic and float to the surface (2809, 2939).

Larva- Several authors have invoked planktonic transport of red snapper early life stages to explain the lack of genetic divergence reported among northern GOM regions (2672, 2664, 2001, 2835). Recent studies, however, have indicated larvae may not act as passive particles in the sea and that self-recruitment mechanisms are prevalent (citations in 2778). Settlement of juvenile red snapper has been reported on the outer continental shelf in the northwestern GOM from June through October (2690).

Several authors hypothesized that oceanic transport of eggs and larvae may be sufficient to facilitate population mixing, despite the lack of hydrodynamic modeling of egg or larval transport in the northern GOM. Gold et al. (2664) reported that mtDNA haplotype frequencies were not significantly different among northern GOM regions, thus the authors failed to reject the null hypothesis of a single panmictic stock. However, they also suggested, based on intrapopulational mtDNA diversity differences, that GOM red snapper might include recently derived, but as yet not genetically distinct population subunits.

Gold et al. (2697) conducted a study to examine the advection of red snapper larvae in the northern GOM. The potential for repopulating the eastern Gulf stock through larval transport was addressed. Transport pathways across topographic features that inhibit alongshelf flow (e.g., the Mississippi River delta, DeSoto Canyon, and the Apalachicola peninsula) and interregional larval transport were considered. An advective field of currents was developed from a large database of drifter and moored currents, augmented by an operational model to fill gaps. The starting points for larval transport were the locations and day of the year of larval captures from the SEAMAP program ichthyoplankton surveys. Because the field of currents was derived from near-surface observations and the depth distribution was uncertain, findings were expressed in terms of maximal transport pathways. Transport pathways were principally vectored toward the west during September, October, and May under the influence of relatively strong climatological westward wind stress. Eastward pathways occurred in June, July, and August under the influence of weaker shoreward wind stress. Westward transport pathways past the Mississippi delta were found near the delta, away from typical juvenile settlement habitat. Water movement from east to west across the Apalachicola peninsula occurred in the fall, suggesting the potential for genetic exchange from the eastern to the western Gulf. Eastward water movement across the Apalachicola peninsula occurred in July, but only along the outer shelf.

It has been hypothesized that there are pathways of larval connectivity and transport from the Gulf of Mexico to the Atlantic (2805), but oceanographic surface conditions on the west coast of Florida do not favor transport of eggs and larvae in this direction during the spawning peak of red snapper in the GOM (Jun - Aug). A two-dimensional model that utilizes wind stress data shows that the summer (Apr - Sep) months are characterized by continuous flow to the northwest with Ekman surface transport toward the northwest Florida coast. To evaluate transport below the surface, a three-dimensional model is necessary (2850).

Young of Year- Red snapper as small as 18 mm settled on relatively unstructured open shelf habitats in the GOM off Alabama in summer, but by the winter age-0 fish had recruited to artificial reefs that provided greater bottom complexity and relief (2888).

Juvenile- In Texas, juvenile red snapper moved offshore from shallow water (about 15-30 m) in summer to deeper water (35-60 m) in winter, based on depths of capture by trawl (2735, 2574). Bradley and Bryan (2574) reported ontogenetic movement of red snapper to structured habitats of increasing dimension occurred as an inshore to offshore migration throughout the juvenile stage. The movement may be a means of avoiding cooler inshore water in winter. The actual cue for movement, however was not a drop in temperature, because movement occurred before the temperature declined. Nelson and Manooch (2746) reported no size segregation between shallow (<35 m) and deep (>35 m) waters of the Carolinas.

Nieland and Wilson (2757) randomly sampled red snapper (n=300) killed using the explosive removal of an obsolete oil and gas platform off Louisiana. Otolith-based aging revealed the majority of the fish were 2 and 3 years old (53% and 37% respectively), while virtually no age-1 fish were present in their sample. Patterson et al. (2778) speculated that the lack of older fish at both platforms and artificial reefs may indicate that thigmotaxis or the threat of predation subsides with age and size, thus older fish display less site fidelity and greater movement (2784, 2779, 2876). Alternatively, high fish mortality rates at platforms and artificial reefs may remove snapper very quickly from the population once fish recruit to the commercial or recreational fishery (2757, 2778).

Adult: Adult red snapper remain in their reef habitations during cooler months. Tagging studies generally indicate little movement, particularly when the fish are released in water less than 14 m deep (2892, 2560, 2624). Adult red snapper sometimes move closer to shore in summer; they were collected in trawls in the lower parts of St. Andrews Bay system, Florida, in summer and fall but not in winter and spring (2766). Occasional tagged adults were caught 5-150 nautical miles from the point of release after 29-1,163 days of freedom (2561, 2730, 2559).

Site fidelity (SF) provides an annual estimate of reef fish immigration or emigration from a reef (2939). For red snapper, 2- to 3-year-old fish at artificial reef structures in shallow water show high fidelity to a site on temporal scales of months to a year, albeit the probability of detecting ultrasonically tagged red snapper at a site one year after release was only 50% (2842).

Mitchell et al. (2729) reported larger (median TL ranged from 545 to 815 mm among surveys), older red snapper were captured at higher rates in outer shelf habitats during experimental longline surveys in the eastern (off Alabama-Mississippi) and western (off Texas) GOM. Fisheries-dependent data confirm that larger, older fish are captured more frequently in commercial-longline sectors operating offshore (2549).

The two main approaches that have been applied to estimate red snapper site fidelity are conventional and, more recently ultrasonic tagging (2778). Szedlmayer (2880) conducted the first ultrasonic tagging experiment on red snapper on artificial reefs off Alabama. He concluded that red snapper displayed “high” site fidelity (SF) to artificial reefs, yet the mean time fish were detected was only 150 d for a species with a maximum longevity >50 years (2925). While one fish was detected in the Szedlmayer study for 597 d, several others were lost from the study area. Both “stayers” and “movers” have important implications for population and connectivity (2615). But, movers can no longer be tracked with ultrasonic receivers once they move beyond the range of the receivers. Hence, the emphasis in red snapper ultrasonic tagging has tended to be weighted toward the stayers. For example, Schroepfer and Szedlmayer (2842) concluded that ultrasonically tagged red snapper displayed high site fidelity to artificial reefs because 87% (13 out of 15) of the fish were detected within 200 m of the study sites 99% of the times they were detected. Westmeyer et al. (2917) reported even lower probability of detection at petroleum platforms off Louisiana after one year. Site fidelity provides an annual estimate of reef fish immigration or emigration from a reef (2939).
Conventional tagging studies are better suited for estimating dispersion distances and rates of movers (2778). Among various studies, fish were captured at natural reefs, artificial reefs (including petroleum platforms), or both. However, most of the existing tagging studies were conducted over artificial reefs sites in the north-central GOM (2891, 2779, 2876). An exception is data from the Schlitz Tagging Program conducted off Florida in the 1960s (2559, 2731). Fable (2624) also reported movement data for red snapper tagged over a variety of natural and artificial reefs off Texas, as did Diamond et al. (2615).

A number of tagging studies have been conducted using red snapper in the GOM (2939). Fable (2624) tagged 299 red snapper at natural reefs off Texas and 17 fish were recovered. Gallaway et al. (2640) reported very high short-term fidelity for red snapper at platforms in the Buccaneer Gas and Oil Field offshore of Galveston, Texas during the summer months. Szeldlmayer and Shipp (2891) tagged and released 1,155 small red snapper at artificial reefs offshore of Alabama. A total of 146 tagged fish were recovered, but only 37 of these had known recapture locations. A total of 28 (74%) were recaptured within 2 km of their release site. Watterson et al. (2909) tagged red snapper at 9 artificial reefs off Alabama from March 1995 to January 1997. Eighty percent of recaptured fish that were not at liberty during Hurricane Opal were recaptured from 1.7 to 2.5 km from their site of release. Fish that were at liberty during Hurricane Opal (October 1995) showed greater movement. The at-liberty fish moved on average 32.6 km, with 8 fish moving over 100 km, and 3 fish moving over 200 km.

Patterson et al. (2784) continued the tagging study of Watterson et al. (2909) through August of 1999. Hurricane George passed within 50 km of the tagging site during August 1999. Of fish recaptured at tagging sites, 199 (97%) were captured at the site where they had been released while 5 had changed location. Patterson and Cowan (2779) used the data gathered by Patterson et al. (2783) to estimate SF by modeling the rate of decline in recaptures at the tagging sites over time to obtain an annual instantaneous rate of decline (D). They used the data to estimate the total mortality (Z), the total annual instantaneous emigration (Q), and the natural mortality (M). Estimated SF values ranged from 24.8% for all recaptures to 25.3% for all recaptures of fish that were released at their original captures, to 26.5% for recaptures for fish tagged and recaptured in the intervals between hurricanes.

Strelcheck et al. (2876) tagged 4,317 red snapper at 14 experimental reefs off coastal Alabama between January 1999 and October 2002. Some 629 recaptures were reported, of which 412 (65%) were made by researchers at the original release site and 217 were reported by fishers. They concluded that observations of high site fidelity (SF) and low dispersal rates provided support for the hypothesis that artificial reefs offshore Alabama provide suitable habitat for adult red snapper. In another conventional mark-recapture study, 5,614 red snapper were tagged between July 2002 and August 2005 (2615). Tag returns provided location information for 82 fish. Of these, 54% moved an average distance of 20.4 km. In a second program, over 9,000 fish were tagged aboard charter headboats, and private boats between 1983 and 2006. In the latter case, 60 returns were analyzed. Most (72%) were recaptured at their release site, with 28% showing an average movement of 19.1 km. Diamond et al. (2615) found that the spatial scale of movements was small enough to support the idea that red snapper stocks in the northern GOM are relatively isolated and that there may be a separate demographic stock off Texas. Thus, all of these studies (2876, 2615) support the view of limited movement and relatively high SF.

The issue of confidence about positional information for tagged fish reported by fishers has prompted a number of ultrasonic telemetry studies for red snapper (2880, 2890, 2842, 2788, 2893, 2894). Szedlmayer (2880) reported residence times on artificial reefs of 17-597 days, and Szedlmayer and Schroepfer (2890) estimated red snapper were resident on an artificial reef for a mean time of 212 days, with one fish staying at one reef for up to 597 days. Using the published information along with new ultrasonic tagging studies, Schroepfer and Szedlmayer (2842) used event analysis described by Allison (2548) to provide a newer estimate of residence time on reefs. The median residence time increased to 373 days.

Topping and Szedlmayer (2894) estimated residence time, SF, and movements of red snapper at 6 sites in the northern GOM using long-term telemetry monitoring. Event analysis was used to estimate SF and residence, based on right-censoring fishing and natural mortality. Median residence time was 542 days, ranging from 1 to 1,099 d, with 72% of the fish staying at least 1 yr at the site. Some fish (N=12) showed seasonal and directed movements to other sites (up to 8 km away) and returned to original sites 7 mo later. Diel movements away from the structure tended to occur at night. Site fidelity and residence times of red snapper were greater than in any previous study and show the importance of artificial reefs for this species. In an additional study, Topping and Szedlmayer (2950) used both manual and passive telemetry to examine fine-scale movement patterns and residence time of adult red snapper (550-745 mm TL) around artificial habitats in the northeastern GOM. These fish (N=12) were manually tracked over 24-h periods; fish stayed near the artificial reefs (<100 m, with 75% of locations within 30 m of the structure), but were significantly further from the reefs at night (mean = 27.5 m, SD = 7.1) than day (mean = 19.1 m, SD = 8.2). Home range area and mean distance from the reef increased with fish size. These fish also showed long term residence of 332–958 d based on passive acoustic monitoring. The close proximity of these fish to the reef over 24-h periods and the long-term residency provides evidence that these artificial reefs are important habitat for red snapper and should be considered an effective management tool.
Two tagging studies on red snapper have been conducted in the U.S. south Atlantic: one by South Carolina Department of Natural Resources (SC DNR) and the other by the Mote Marine Laboratory (2584, 2851). SC DNR’s tagging of red snapper began in 1990 and is ongoing. Through this study, 1,568 red snapper have been tagged by recreational fishermen with 176 fish returned (11.2% return rate). Few fish tagged have been over the 20 inch size limit (1.6%). Of the fish that have been recaptured, 2.4% of the red snapper were greater than the legal size limit at the time of tagging and 25.6% of the red snapper were greater than the legal size limit at the time of recapture.

In the largest tagging study, Burns et al. (2582) of Mote Marine Laboratory tagged and released 5,272 red snapper in the GOM (from Naples, FL, to the eastern border of Texas) and Atlantic (from Cape Canaveral, FL, to Georgia) over a 13 yr period. Approximately 40% of these fish were tagged in the Atlantic. Forty-four percent of the specimens were recaptured within 1.9 km of the tagging site. Less than 10 of the 410 recapture events showed movement>100 miles and movement between the Gulf of Mexico and the Atlantic coast is not mentioned in the report.

The Mote Marine Laboratory has been tagging red snapper off Florida since 1997, and 4,124 have been tagged with 443 fish returned (10.7%) (2584). Few fish have been tagged over the 20 inch size limit (1.6%). Of the fish that have been recaptured, 3.6% of the red snapper were greater than the legal size limit at the time of tagging and 32.5% of the red snapper were greater than the legal size at the time of recapture.

Burns and Brown-Peterson (2584) tagged red snapper on both the east and west coasts of Florida. Plotting red snapper tag and recapture location showed the majority of the fish were site faithful, although some moved longer distances. The largest movement distance recorded was 362.4 km or 225 miles over a period of 48 months. Additionally, tag recaptures from the Mote Marine Laboratory database show a red snapper traveling from off Pensacola (Florida panhandle) to St. Augustine (Atlantic coast). Movement on the east coast tended to be more often from north to south and vice a versa due to the narrow shelf whereas west coast fish could expand over the much broader shelf. The general direction of movement, determined by fish tagged in the Florida Panhandle, was to the east and southeastern in the GOM. This is consistent with a clockwise direction along the Gulf coast reported for red snapper in previous studies (2813, 2694, 2783). This may indicate that re-recruitment to the southwest Florida coast may have come from the northern Gulf of Mexico.

Diamond et al. (2615) provided a list of factors that have been suggested to be important in affecting the percentage of fish that move compared to the percentage that remain at a site. These included size or age of fish (2735), depth of capture (2559, 2909), seasonal patterns due to water temperature or reproductive condition (2892, 2559, 2909), hurricanes (2909, 2783, 2787). The accuracy of positional data reported for tag returns by fishers can also be an issue regarding site fidelity (SF).

It has also been hypothesized that SF of reef-associated organisms is dependent on prey availability and the availability of suitable refuge, i.e., the resource mosaic hypothesis (2638) and density-dependent habitat selection (2707). Reef-associated fish species that rely on benthic prey as the primary component of their diet may create a gradient of prey depletion (or feeding halo) around the reefs, resulting in negative feedbacks to reef fish energetic, residence times, and local abundance, particularly when the feeding halos of adjacent reefs overlap (2707, 2939). The degree of prey depletion and negative feedback can alter the potential for sustained productivity of an artificial reef or reef complex. Bioenergetic demands increase as foraging area increases, resulting in increased emigration from resource-depleted reefs to reefs containing a greater abundance of prey.

Once red snapper grow to about 8 years old, they are large enough to be invulnerable to most predation and occur over open habitat as well as at reef habitat (2939). In the western GOM, these older fish are most abundant in longline sets at depths between 55 and 92 m. In this region, the zone of highest abundance of early red snapper larvae (2710) corresponds to the depth distribution of 8+ year adults taken on longlines (2729, 2939).

Gallaway et al. (2939) presented histograms depiciting the relative frequency of age groups of red snapper residing at offshore oil and gas platforms, artificial reefs, and over soft bottom in deeper water in the northern GOM. Explosive removals determined that the most frequent age groups (N=16,505) found to be present on oil and gas platforms were age-2 (34%) and age-3 (29%) (2656). Age-4 was the only other age group representing as much as 10% of the population. Similar data for the age structure of red snapper at oil and gas platforms were presented by Nieland and Wilson (2757). Szedlmayer (2883) determined the ages for 3,415 red snapper collected from 94 different artificial reefs off Alabama. Age-1 comprised about 14%, age-2 (36%), and age-3 comprised 25% of the total population. Red snapper on the Flower Gardens Banks (N=780) were predominantly ages 3, 4, and 5 (2936). In contrast red snapper sampled by Mitchell (2729) caught using longlines over soft bottom in deeper water were predominantly comprised of red snapper ranging from 8 to over 17 years of age (2939).

Gallaway et al. (2939) finished their review of red snapper life history in the GOM by concluding that prior to the proliferation of offshore oil and gas platforms and artificial reefs (e.g., pre-1980s), young new recruits occurred over open substrates between age 0 and age 2. In this habitat, natural mortality was high due to the lack of cover affording protection from predation, and the fish were subject to shrimp trawl bycatch as well. Age-2 red snapper were commonly taken in shrimp trawls along with age-0 and age-1 fish until about 1990, which demonstrated their abundance in open habitats (2672). After this stage, natural reefs in the northern GOM would then harbor red snapper age 3 and greater. They suggested that recruitment of the age 0-2 fish to the natural reefs was inhibited by the presence of adult or larger fish occupying the reefs. After age-8, red snapper would increase their foraging range to include soft-bottom habitat in deeper water, because they reached a size that reduced population predation.
Symbiotic: No information found.
Schooling: While red snapper do exhibit schooling behavior, not much has been published about it. As for the commercial fisherman that specifically target red snapper, their techniques have changed through the years (2852). The fisherman are now utilizing rod and reels instead of the traditionally used bandit gear. They use lighter mono-filament lines to generated more bites and be more productive. The fisherman is targeting large schools of 5 to 10 pound fish which are favored more by the fish markets. Although when a large 20 to 30 pound red snapper is hooked, the lighter tackle is less likely to land the fish.

nodes.title: Artificial Reefs
nodes.body:
Ontogenetic habitat shifts in red snapper habitat utilization is complicated due to the proliferation of artificial reefs deployed in the north-central GOM and the vast number of oil and gas platforms, which function as artificial reefs, erected in the northwestern GOM (2926, 2917, 2778).

Gallaway et al. (2647) characterized the food habits of red snapper at the Buccaneer Gas and Oil Field located offshore from Galveston, Texas, at depths of about 10 fathoms (20 m). They suggested that red snapper moved away from the platforms during the late night to early morning period to feed over soft bottoms. Hastings et al. (2683) obtained similar results for lutjanids at research platforms in the northeastern Gulf. Peabody (2787), Peabody and Wilson (2788), and McDonough (2724) also suggested that nocturnal movements of red snapper away from Louisiana platforms was related to feeding behavior.

Dufrene (2620) characterized the inner-shelf area offshore eastern Louisiana to panhandle Florida and suggested that this benthic habitat was about 15% shell (submerged oyster shell banks) and 85% soft sand, mud substrate. The vast majority of the inner shelf in this area is composed of sand, mud, and silt, with little or no vertical relief (2939).

On a larger spatial scale, Parker et al. (2772) estimated that 2,571 square kilometers of natural reef habitat (3.3% of the bottom) is present at depths between 18 and 91 m in the region between Pensacola, Florida and Pass Cavala, Texas. Of this, only 1.6% (1,285 square kilometers) was comprised of reefs having relief >1m (2772, 2939). If one adds natural reefs further offshore not assessed by Parker et al. (2772) the total area with high-relief natural reefs becomes 1, 578 square kilometers (2939). Thus, high-relief natural reefs constitute about 2% of the shelf area.

About 2,300 oil production platforms present of the Louisiana coast in 1976 enhanced red snapper fishing by providing three-dimensional habitat (2878). It had not been determined if artificial habitat primarily increases production or just redistributes adult populations.

Some 4,000 offshore oil and gas platforms are located across the shelf of the western GOM and provide on the order of 12 square kilometers of artificial reef habitat (2939). Platforms differ from natural reefs in many ways but a unique feature is that that they span the entire water column. Offshore petroleum platforms extend from the beach to the abyss, from Alabama to southern Texas. The highest platform densities occur in shallow and mid-shelf areas.

The construction of oil and gas platforms in the GOM as well as other artificial reefs has corresponded to changes in habitat distribution patterns for red snapper (2939). In 1960, there were about 351 offshore oil and gas platforms in the northern GOM, but these increased to 1,520 by 1970, and reached 2,540 by 1980. From 1990 to the present, the number of platforms has averaged about 4,000, considering both new installations as well as removals. They proposed that the increased construction of oil and gas platforms as well as other artificial reef habitats has provided protective habitat for age 2 fish that would otherwise have suffered high mortality over open habitats. Although fishing mortality can be high at these new habitats (2757), Gallaway et al. (2939) suggested that prior to their construction mortality was even higher for age 2 fish over open habitat. This being the case, they suggested that the removal of production platforms and other artificial reefs will likely result in a large reduction in red snapper available to the directed fisheries. They concluded that the existing literature is consistent with the premise of density-dependent natural mortality in red snapper for at least age 0 and age 1 fish, and likely for older fish as well. If this aspect is incorporated in the assessment models, management advice may be substantially altered.

An area of 3,108 square kilometers offshore Alabama has been designated for artificial reef placement and it is estimated that on the order of 10,000 small reefs occur in this area (2939). Collectively, these reefs equate to a total area of 0.1 square kilometers. This is the largest of the artificial reef areas. The area of artificial reef habitat in the western GOM is small compared to the area of natural reefs. However, artificial reef habitats (especially oil and gas platforms) located in near-shore and mid-shelf zones appear to be used by age-2 red snapper much more than their proportional area would suggest.

Research has been conducted to discriminate between nursery areas for age-0 red snapper in the northern GOM using otolith microchemistry (2780, 2785). More recently Sluis (2859) was able to assign juvenile (age-1 and/or age-2) red snapper to either artificial reefs or oil and gas platforms based on otolith microchemistry.

Age-2 Population Size at Platforms -1992

Stanley (2864) showed that an average of 5,304 (95% CI = 2,756) red snapper occupied each major platform during the winter 1992. Gallaway and Cole (2641) used the Stanley (2864) estimate along with platform distribution, size and count data along with red snapper age composition data to estimate 3 million (95% CI = 1.7 to 4.2 million) age-2 red snapper were present around oil platforms throughout the entire GOM at the beginning of 1992.

Goodyear’s (2672) red snapper stock assessment estimated the total age-2 red snapper population in the GOM at the beginning of 1992 was 3.7 million fish. Collectively, these data suggest 70-80% of the total age-2 red snapper population were living around offshore platforms in 1992 (2641, 2939).

Age-2 Population Size at Platforms -1995

Gitshchlag et al. (2656) provided data from explosive platform removal studies in 1995 that suggested, on average that 775 (95% CI =482-1,062) red snapper were present at each offshore platform, large and small combined. These data when multiplied times the number of platforms present in the GOM in 1995 (4,000) times the fraction of fish that were age-2 suggested that 1.1 million age-2 red snapper were present at offshore platforms in 1995. The SEDAR7 (2847) red snapper stock assessment suggested that the total age-2 red snapper population in the western GOM in 1995 was 1.6 million fish. These data suggest that approximately 70% of all age-2 red snapper were living around offshore platforms in 1995 (2939).

Thus, results from at least two independent studies (2864, 2656) suggest that a high proportion of the age-2 red snapper population in the western GOM reside at offshore oil and gas platforms (2939).

The main finding summarized by Gallaway et al. (2939) was that submerged oyster shell present in the northern GOM acts as essential habitat protecting age-0 and age-1 red snapper from predation. Without this benthic habitat, most of these “recruits” would not survive. Likewise, artificial reefs created off Alabama, and oil and gas platforms created off Mississippi, Louisiana and Texas provide high-relief benthic habitat that enhances the survival of age-2 red snapper. Prior to the creation of artificial reefs and oil and gas platforms, they suggested there was a high mortality on age-2 fish due to predation. The general absence of high-relief natural reefs inshore and on the mid-continental shelf tended to limit the survival of these early life-stages of red snapper.

Shipp (2856) and Shipp and Bortone (2857) have proposed that the creation of artificial reefs and oil and gas platforms have tended to enhance the production of red snapper. It was the transformation of the substratum from a predominantly sandy mud habitat to one having increased areas of hard bottom with high-relief that relieved the “bottleneck” that had previously prevented red snapper from increasing in abundance. Artificial reefs may attract fish but, in addition they also provide increased habitat that relieves a “bottleneck” in the life history that previously restricted population abundance. Shipp and Bortone (2857) called this concept the habitat limitation hypothesis.

Some studies have indicated attraction because red snapper were mostly feeding on prey from pelagic environments and open sand-mud habitats (2723, 2914), while others have indicated significant feeding on reef species and artificial reefs were enhancing prey resources (2767, 2888, 2810).

Further evidence of the habitat limitation hypothesis rather than purely attraction was provided by Stedlemayer and Shipp (2891). They demonstrated a marked increase in abundance of early-juvenile (age-0) red snapper within the Alabama artificial reef area following large-scale artificial reef placement. Thus, the increased population of this area was likely attributable to a habitat-related recruitment increase and not a result of migration from other areas.

Szedlmayer (2883) concluded that based on fisheries-independent studies on artificial reefs off Alabama that his group had conducted over the previous decade (2882, 2886, 2889) that red snapper populations may be in better condition compared to past assessments. Using SCUBA surveys on shell/block artificial reef habitats, mean total mortality (Z) was estimated as Z=2.3 for age-0 to age-1 red snapper, similar to previous estimates of Z=1.98 (2754) and Z=2.12 (2747) derived from SEAMAP shrimp trawl data. Natural mortality (M) was estimated by Szedlmayer (2883) based on the difference between total mortality (Z) and fishing mortality (F), with the present estimate M=1.9 for age-0, M=0.6 for age-1, and M=0.35 for ages 2 to 54. Combining ages, growth rates, mortalities, and length-weight relation, the estimated transitional spawning potential ratio (SPR) was estimated = 0.21 at F=0.19, and maximum yield was attained when F was increased to 0.3. The main difference is that the Szedlmayer (2883) stock assessment used age-specific estimates for M obtained from benthic habitat surveys rather than stock assessment models not tied to habitat-related information.

Shipp and Bortone (2857) concluded that if the habitat limitation hypothesis is correct, it will be necessary to maintain or even increase the amount of artificial reef habitat to keep pace with fishing pressure. Programs such as “rigs to reefs” efforts off Louisiana and Texas would have to be continued, as would reef construction off Alabama.

All previous GOM stock assessments have concluded that red snapper in the GOM are overfished and undergoing overfishing. However, recent published studies (2883, 2650, 2939, 2857) have shown that red snapper are density-dependent and that age 0 and age 1 fish have a much higher natural mortality rate than was used in previous stock assessments. By using a density-dependent model and a higher natural mortality for age-0 and age-1 fish, it appears that red snapper stock are neither overfished nor undergoing overfishing (2675). Also, because the natural mortality for age-0 and age-1 fish are much higher than originally assumed, shrimp trawls have less effect on red snapper reaching age 2+ than previously thought. Future stock assessments need to consider density-dependent models and higher natural mortality rates for age-0 and age-1 red snapper.

Cowan et al. (2608) disagreed with the habitat limitation hypothesis proposed by Shipp and Borton (2009) and with what they called “faith-based fisheries management” of red snapper. While there were a number of concerns outlined in the paper, Cowen et al. (2608) took exception to the idea that available habitat for age-1+ fish and older red snapper can limit population size. They claimed that the premise that year class success in red snapper is not determined until the fish are between 1.5 and 2 years old (the time that they begin to inhabit reefs as sub-adults) was inconsistent with a periodic (bet-hedging) life history strategy.

Some believe that the availability of interstices (i.e., small hiding spots) for newly settled post-larvae and juveniles can be limiting; those individuals not finding refuge suffer high predation rates (2608). In this case, mortality is thought to be density-dependent (2631, 2689, 2632, 2633). But, Cowan et al. (2608) asserted that age-0 red snapper rarely recruit directly to high-relief natural or artificial reefs; that they settle on sand/mud substrates and transition to more structured habitat with size and age. It is this transition that makes them susceptible to shrimp trawling.

Others believe that the supply of ref fish larvae is limiting, with good year classes being determined by density independent factors that occur while larvae are planktonic prior to settlement on the reefs (citations in 2608).

In neither of the above scenarios is habitat for adults limiting; many studies have shown that adult fish usually do not saturate reefs (citations in 2608). In nature, however, it is unlikely to be a simple dichotomy, as more than one factor can be limiting at different life stages (multiple causalities).

Cowan et al. (2608) argued that the amount of habitat for adult red snapper, especially artificial habitats that account for <5% (2871) of total useable habitat as compared to suitable natural habitats, probably does not limit recruitment or population size. They argued that artificial reefs may increase carrying capacity, but this may be negated because they attract predatory fish and fishermen. They inferred that red snapper life history was inconsistent with the notion that habitat limitation (2939, 2857) is a strong actor in regulating population size in this species.

A number of arguments against the habitat limitation hypothesis and against the concept that artificial reefs enhance production of red snapper were presented by Cowan et al. (2608). Perhaps all that can be concluded is that many changes have occurred concurrently, making it difficult to differentiate which factors (fishing pressure, shrimp trawling, impact of hurricanes, management measures, artificial reefs) have been most important in allowing red snapper populations to increase in the GOM. Given that offshore shrimp fishing effort (early 2010) was down by as much as 75-85% (2850) owing to recent coastal storm damage, economic woes, high fuel prices and cheap imported shrimp, bycatch has been declining for the last several years, especially since 2002, and the directed fishery (that also has been impacted by high fuel prices) has recently been constrained by the 2006 Magnuson-Stevens Reauthorization Act (MSRA) to lower total allowable catches (TACs). Simply put, the recovery formula long prescribed in the agency assessment has finally been realized, although recent estimates of natural mortality (M) for age-0 and age-1 red snapper may diminish the role that bycatch reduction can play in recovery of the stock. Even so, recent sampling off Louisiana and the Florida panhandle (2611, 2848) indicates that the increase in numbers is mostly comprised of 3-7 year old fish, but numbers are indeed increasing. Given that artificial reefs and especially oil and gas platforms have been in place for many years (2857), it seems counterintuitive to award credit to artificial structures for the beginning stages of a stock recovery that is just now becoming apparent.

Results of both the Gazey et al. (2650) study and the work presented by Brooks (2848) indicate there is a strong likelihood that natural mortality (M) for juvenile red snapper in the GOM is density-dependent and perhaps quite a bit higher than was assumed during SEDAR7 (2847). Density-dependent mortality was not incorporated into the assessment (2848) for two principal reasons. First, doing so would be a radical departure from an update versus a benchmark assessment. And secondly, there was no time to explore coding the CATCHEM model to incorporate density-dependent mortality into the assessment.

A review of several published studies, along with the above investigations indicates that natural mortality (M) may have been underestimated in SEDAR7 (2847) for age-0 and age-1 red snapper in the GOM (2848). The estimates of M from these studies ranged from 0.98 to 3.7 for age 0 and from 0.6 to 1.4 for age 1 red snapper. The lower ranges are the values used in SEDAR 7 (2847). However, none of the studies were able to distinguish natural mortality from emigration; therefore, it is possible that some of the M values reviewed were too high. Accordingly, the continuity run maintained the SEDAR7 values, whereas two alternative models utilized a value twice that of SEDAR7 (2847).

Syc (2879) compared the age of red snapper to known age of artificial reefs off Alabama. The size and age of red snapper were sampled from April through November 2010 and compared with the age of the artificial reefs at the site of capture. Artificial reefs were deployed in 2006 (N=20, 4 year old reefs), 2009 (N=10, 1 year old reefs) and 2010 (N=10, 0.5 year old reefs). Red snapper were sampled with hook-and-line and a fish trap. After sampling was completed, SCUBA divers estimated the remaining red snapper densities at sample reefs using visual surveys, photographs, and video recordings. Syc found significantly older fish on older reefs. This finding supports previous telemetry studies that showed long-term residency of red snapper on artificial reefs (2894). This relation between reef age and fish age supports previous studies that indicated red snapper production from artificial reefs (2891, 2883, 2939). The increased production is likely due to an increase in available reef habitat, which was previously found to be a controlling factor affecting the density and growth of red snapper (2891, 2885, 2650).

Red snapper are recruited to the newly deployed reefs rapidly as juveniles (approximately age-1) and then reside on these reefs for several years (2879). If these reefs were only attracting red snapper, there would be no correlation between fish age and reef age, since red snapper would simply be migrating to and from reefs. In the present case (2879), the age distribution would have been random, with no clear dominate age classes. However, dominate age classes for each reef year were found and correlated with reef age, providing evidence that artificial reefs were producing rather than simply attracting red snapper. If artificial reefs are enhancing the population and experiencing no fishing pressure, Powers et al. (2806) estimated that these reefs could increase production by 6.45 kg wet weight per 10 square meters in the first year. Since the reefs used by Syc (2879) were not known to fishermen, fishing mortality was limited and following the rational of Powers et al. (2806), had the potential to increase production.

Several studies have suggested that red snapper populations are overfished and that habitat limitation is not a controlling factor (2841, 2783, 2608a). Clearly, there is significant fishing mortality of red snapper in the northern GOM (2653). However, if fishing mortality was the limiting factor for red snapper and habitat was not important, we would not expect differences in fish age resulting from reef age (i.e. all reefs whether fished or not would show similar age distributions). Red snapper enter the fishery around age-2, (recreational size minimum = 406 mm, commercial = 330 mm), with the catch predominately consisting of 2 to 4 year old fish. If fishing mortality was effectively limiting red snapper, these ages would be harvested and drastically decreased when analyzing the age distribution. However, these ages represented
