59% (N=602) of the total catch, indicating that fishing mortality was not controlling the red snapper population (2879).

One substantial difference between the study by Syc (2879) that suggests habitat limitations, and previous studies which suggested fishing mortality limitations was Syc’s use of fishery independent data. The previous studies mainly used fisher y dependent data for red snapper caught by recreational and commercial fishers (2891, 2556, 2784, 2930). This difference may account for differing results. Syc (2879) suggested that fishing mortality probably had little influence on age distributions from artificial reefs sampled. In addition, it was possible to sample smaller red snapper that fishery dependent sampling programs cannot access due to size limitations on the fishery. The significant differences between red snapper abundances on the three reef years provide support for increased red snapper production from artificial reefs.

 Research has been conducted to discriminate between nursery areas for age-0 red snapper in the northern GOM using otolith microchemistry (2780, 2785). More recently Sluis (2859) was able to assign juvenile (age-1 and/or age-2) red snapper to either artificial reefs or oil and gas platforms based on otolith microchemistry.

nodes.title: Substrate
nodes.body:
Egg/Parturition- Not applicable-since eggs are planktonic (2809, 2728).
Larva- Not applicable-since larvae are planktonic (2809, 2728, 2710).
Young of Year- In the northwestern GOM, Szedlemeyer and Conti (2885) observed newly settled age-0 red snapper on open bottom (sand and mud) as well as low-relief shell habitat. However settlement was significantly higher on shell ridges. Rooker et al. (2841) collected newly settled red snapper on shell ridges, but observed large numbers of settlers on mud habitats away from low-relief shell ridges suggesting factors other than structure may be critical during the early post-settlement period.

A number of studies have demonstrated that age-0 and age-1 red snapper are abundant over sand, mud, and shell-rubble substrates in the U.S. GOM. Red snapper were sampled at three natural banks on the inner continental shelf of Texas (2651). Digital side-scan sonar and multibeam data were used to define inshore (mud), ridge (shell), and offshore (mud) habitats for Freeport Rocks, Heald Bank, and Sabine Bank in 2003 and Freeport Banks on 2004. Results indicate that both shell and inshore and offshore mud habitats associated with these natural banks serve as settlement habitat for red snapper, and all three habitats have the potential to function as nursery areas for this species. Settlement sizes and ages reported by Geary et al. (2651) were similar to those of previous studies off Mississippi and Alabama (2935, 2885) and off Texas (2841). Unfortunately, these benthic habitats are the same areas fished by the GOM fisheries for pink, brown, and white shrimp (2786, 2563).

Shrimp trawling in the U.S. GOM from Florida to Texas is conducted over sand, mud, and submerged beds of oyster shell (2913, 2914). Wells et al. (2913) analyzed the spatial distribution and abundance of age-0 red snapper over sand, low-relief shell rubble, high-relief shell rubble, and at high-relief habitats within a de facto non-trawl area and in similar habitats where commercial shrimp trawling occurred. Age-0 red snapper were most dense over sand and low-relief shell rubble habitats and moved to higher-relief shell rubble and natural habitats by age-1. Habitat-specific growth rates of age-0 fish were highest over sand (range 0.05-1.03 mm per day). Densities of age-0 red snapper were highest over trawled sand, but higher over non-trawled shell rubble by 6 months of age (age-0.5+). Red snapper collected over sand and low-relief shell rubble areas exposed to trawling had truncated size distributions, higher mortality estimates, and lower production potential (the latter evaluated with G-Z and P-B ratios) compared with fish over non-trawled areas of similar habitat. The results suggest that juvenile red snapper residing over non-trawled areas may have a higher probability of survival than fish in areas exposed to commercial shrimp trawling.

Research indicates that structured habitats are essential nursery areas for age-0 red snapper (2885). Laboratory experiments indicate both wild and hatchery-reared juvenile red snapper show associations with structure, (i.e., artificial reefs, 2718) and shell habitats (2887).

Sampling trawls deployed by Rooker et al. (2841) and Geary et al. (2651) contained mesh bags that retained recently settled young-of-year red snapper for which biogenic structures such as worm tubes may provide sufficient structure in soft sediments (2935). Furthermore, mud habitats were immediately adjacent to shell rubble habitats and may have served as foraging areas. Patterson et al. (2786) reported red snapper juvenile (age-0?) density in sand habitats was significantly correlated with sponge biomass. Hence, they concluded sponges provided habitat complexity at a scale sufficient for juvenile (age-0?) snapper. Similarly, Workman and Foster (2933) reported juvenile (age-0?) snapper in sand habitats typically were associated with objects such as squid egg cases, woody debris, or discarded drink cans, that fish used for either refuge or orientation (2778).

Age-0 Red Snapper In GOM Shrimp Trawls

Regulation of GOM red snapper did not start until 1984 with the implementation of the reef fish management plan by the Gulf of Mexico Fisheries Management Council (GMFMC) (2691). The first stock assessment of GOM red snapper occurred in 1988 and concluded that the stock was overfished and that overfishing was occurring (2669). The assessment also noted that the GOM shrimp fishery contributed heavily to the red snapper fishing mortality (F) by harvesting age-0 and age-1 red snapper as bycatch. Another red snapper stock assessment was conducted by Goodyear and Phares (2674). This assessment concluded that the stock condition was less than one percent of the target 20% spawning stock biomass ratio (SSBR). To rebuild the stock by 2000, a complete closure of the directed fishery would be required and there would also need to be a 60% reduction in shrimp trawl bycatch of juvenile red snapper.

It is well documented that juvenile red snapper are a significant portion of shrimp trawl bycatch in the GOM with some 20 million estimated to have been taken in shrimp trawling in 1989 (2750). Warren (2902) estimated that the capture of juvenile red snapper in shrimp trawl bycatch was 34 million fish per year. More recent estimates of juvenile snapper bycatch in the shrimp trawl fishery vary from 25 to 45 million per year (2847). Although a portion of these fish may survive capture; the vast majority do not survive and are discarded (2679). Goodyear and Phares (2674) estimated that 90% of the fishing mortality of age-0 and age-1 red snapper in the GOM resulted from shrimp trawl bycatch.

This led to the requirement that shrimp fishing vessels must install bycatch reduction devices (BRDs) to increase the escapement of juvenile red snapper from the trawls (2642). Beginning in May 1998, the National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS) required that BRDs be installed on trawls used in the commercial shrimp fishery. BRDs were mandated for use in the U.S. GOM shrimp fishery to reduce shrimp trawl mortality of juvenile red snapper. Conditional survival of juvenile red snapper from shrimp trawl bycatch had been estimated to be in the order of 12%. The BRDs were believed to be capable of reducing the bycatch mortality by more than 50%. Hence, BRDs were mandated by GMFMC to support rebuilding the red snapper stock in the GOM by the target date of 2019. Research programs were initiated to evaluate whether BRDs were capable of reducing bycatch mortality by more than 50% (2776).

Branstetter (2575) coordinated evaluations of various types of BRDs using observers on commercial shrimp trawlers in the GOM and U.S. south Atlantic. In the western GOM, red snapper occurred in 393 of 719 total fisheye tows and 201 or 403 expanded mesh tows. Their distribution tended to be offshore of the 10 fathom (20 m) contour except off south Texas where near-shore captures of red snapper were not uncommon. Reduction levels of red snapper by BRDs were strongly correlated to seasons and the associated size of the fish on the shrimp grounds. Based on the data gathered, the smallest fish (age-0) recruit to the shrimp grounds in the late summer-early fall at a size of about 50 mm FL. If smaller fish (<50 mm FL) recruit to the grounds earlier, they did not occur in the final catch. It may be that these fish pass though the meshes of the cod-end. The juveniles continue to reside in these regions through age-1 (mean size about 175 mm FL). (For stock assessment purposes all fish become age-1 at the start of the calendar year i.e., at 6 months of age, but for the purposes of this discussion, ages represent biological ages where spawning birthdates are mid-summer). Quarterly stratification of the red snapper length-frequencies taken in both the “control” and “BRD” net indicated that during the first calendar quarter the majority of individuals were small age-0 fish less than 120 mm FL, and at this size there was very little reduction. As the year progressed, and these fish increased in size to larger than 110 mm FL, reductions increased, but only for fish larger than 110 mm FL. By mid-summer, when most red snapper on the shrimp grounds were larger than 100 mm, reductions were substantial. During the fall, when the next year-class began recruiting, overall reductions were reduced again because of the limited reduction of these smaller fish, but there were still good reductions for the few larger fish.

Research studies into swimming performance and behavior of red snapper in relation to bycatch reduction have been published (2622, 2934, 2776). This size-limited reduction has a kinematic basis (2575, 2622). Fish smaller than 100 mm cannot sustain a swimming speed to overcome the speed of the trawl, thus they tire and are pushed to the back of the cod end during and extended tow time. Red snapper 60-100 mm can sustain a swimming speed of only about 0.2-0.3 meters per second, and have a burst speed of about 0.6-1.0 meters per second, whereas the trawl is being pulled forward at about 1.3 meters per second (2.5 nautical miles per hour). Once the juvenile red snapper attain a size of 110 mm, they can produce the needed sustainable swimming speed to keep a constant position with the net, and seek escape routes.

Parsons and Foster (2776) found a significant effect of fish size and season on red snapper critical swimming speeds using a Brett style swim tunnel. For fish ranging between 6 and 17 cm SL, critical swimming speeds ranged from about 35-70 cm/s, depending upon the season. However, critical swimming speeds did not differ between day and night. This was important, since most shrimp trawling in the GOM occurs at night. A Vortex Generating Bycatch Reduction Device (VGBRD) was used to evaluate red snapper behavior during day and during the night. During daylight, 79.2% of red snapper exited the VGBRD in an average of 4.1 minutes. However, during night-time tests, only 17.6% of the red snapper exited the VGBRD in an average of 5.0 minutes. Behavioral tests revealed a strong negative phototactic response in dark adapted red snapper. Furthermore, they found that when the VGBRD was illuminated with LED lights placed downstream of the exit, 96% of red snapper exited the device in 7.1 minutes. In color/contrast choice experiments, red snapper unerringly associated with the dark colored (black or dark green) panel placed on the bottom of the experimental tank. In another set of experiments, they found that red snapper displayed a strong optomotor response, i.e., the tendency to following and match speeds with a moving pattern. They concluded that illumination, color/contrast, and/or the optomotor response may improve BRD performance.
Modeling conducted by Goodyear (2672) of both NMFS SEAMAP bottom trawl data and commercial shrimp trawl data collected by on-board observers found that age-0 and age-1 red snapper predominated in the catches. Goodyear estimated that 310.7 million red snapper were captured in commercial shrimp trawls from 1982 to 1992 with 138.5 million (44%) being age-0 and 172.2 million (56%) being age-1.

A study was conducted to assess the feasibility of meeting the 60% escapement requirement using BRDs on shrimp trawls (2646). They reanalyzed the SEAMAP bottom trawl data, the commercial observer data, and shrimp fishing effort in a general linear model and estimated that 198.1 million red snapper had been captured in shrimp trawls from 1982 to 1992. They estimated that 129.4 million (65%) red snapper were age-0 and 68.8 million (35%) were age-1. The revised estimates averaged on the order of 30 to 47% lower than the NMFS estimates by Goodyear (2672). Nevertheless, the estimated bycatch levels were high (26 to 32 million per year). The age structure of the bycatch consisted of a much larger fraction of age-0 fish and fewer age-1 fish than had been estimated by Goodyear (2672). Gallaway et al. (2646) concluded that BRDs did not effectively exclude age-0 red snapper, and that existing stock recovery policy based on the NMFS model bycatch estimates derived from using BRDs to reduce shrimp trawl mortality of juvenile red snapper may be ineffective.

Gallaway and Cole (2642) estimated that the maximum potential exclusion of juvenile (age-0 and age-1) red snapper with the use of BRDs was only about 25-27%, not the 59% that had been previously estimated (2907, 2908). If rebuilding required a 50% reduction in bycatch mortality of age-0 and age-1 red snapper, Gallaway and Cole (2642) concluded that the use of BRDs by itself would not produce the mortality reductions necessary to meet this objective. Bycatch reduction of juvenile red snapper from BRDs is currently estimated to be below 15% (2634, 2691).

Beginning in May 1998, NMFS required that BRDs be installed in penaeid shrimp trawl gear in the GOM (2650). Changes in observer protocols were introduced, one of which was that all red snapper collected in shrimp trawls would be enumerated and measured when possible. This yielded a time series of catch data and length frequency data from the GOM commercial shrimp fishery.

Bycatch estimates (2751, 2752) were improved by both the new red snapper observer data and by the development of an improved bycatch model. The red snapper length data gathered by observers in the GOM were used to make subjective estimates of the age-0 and age-1 fractions in the bycatch (2753). Nichols et al. (2005) also used seasonal SEAMAP trawl survey data to estimate the instantaneous natural mortality (M) was 0.6 for age-1 red snapper. This value was used in conjunction with the ratio of age-0 to age-1 mortality used by Goodyear (2672) to infer that M for age-0 red snapper was 1.0 (2847). These values were used in the SEDAR7 (2847) stock assessment as the best estimates of the M for age-0 and age-1 red snapper in the GOM. Cordue (2005) recommended that future red snapper stock assessments should model post-recruitment density-dependent mortality “as this is critical for determining the impact of penaeid shrimp bycatch on red snapper rebuilding.”

Gazey et al. (2650) analyzed NMFS’s post-1998 Observer file and constructed a length-based, age-structured model (2653) to objectively estimate the growth and mortality parameters and age composition of the commercial shrimp trawl bycatch of red snapper in the western GOM using 81 length frequency datasets (a total of 239,521 fish were measured) collected from July 1999 to February 2007. Important findings of the modeling include: (1) the shrimp trawl bycatch during the first and the third trimesters is dominated (86-87%) by age-0 fish, (2) the growth pattern of age-0 and age-1 fish suggest the fish form an annulus during the winter months, (3) the natural mortality of age-0 fish appears to be double (a minimum 70% increase) the value used in the last stock assessment (done in 2005), and (4) the evidence of density-dependent juvenile mortality derived from the length-based, age-structured model was overwhelming (i.e., density-dependent mortality indices derived from the model supported the concept that survival of age-0 and age-1 red snapper were related to the availability of benthic habitat). Inclusion of these findings in the red snapper stock assessment has the potential of substantially alter management practices.

Age-0 Red Snapper In Trawls South Atlantic

Very little data has been collected concerning the spatial distributions and relative abundance of age-0 red snapper in the U.S. south Atlantic (2817). While BRDs were installed on shrimp trawls associated with the shrimp fisheries from North Carolina to Florida in the southeast Atlantic, no young-of-year (age-0) or juvenile (age-1) red snapper have been reported as bycatch (2844, 2575, 2737, 2823, 2906, R. Pugliese pers. comm. SAFMC, 2012). Red snapper were either absent or rare in the shrimp trawl catches monitored by observers. Trawl catches by weight were dominated by estuarine and/or near-shore species such as Cannonball Jellyfish, White Shrimp, Spot, Atlantic Menhaden, Other jellyfish, Brown Shrimp, Atlantic Croaker, Southern Kingfish, Blue Crab, and Star Drum (2829).

Branstetter (2575) presented maps depicting the locations where commercial shrimp trawling using BRDs was conducted in the GOM and U.S. south Atlantic from 1993 to 1996. Most of the trawling depicted using BRDs in the GOM was conducted over the middle continental shelf over sand, and mud substrates. Most of the trawling depicted in the U.S. south Atlantic was located near shore. Red snapper were common in shrimp trawls monitored by observers in the GOM, but not in the southeastern Atlantic. The most likely explanation for the absence of age-0 and age-1 red snapper in commercial shrimp trawl catches in the U.S. south Atlantic is that the shrimp fisheries are conducted near shore; while post-larval settlement of red snapper occurs farther offshore, similar to patterns mapped in the GOM (2941).
The absence of age-0 and age-1 red snapper associated with fisheries-independent trawling conducted by MARMAP further offshore in the U.S. south Atlantic may be related to the mesh sizes used in the trawls (2919). The Yankee Trawl used has a mesh of 5.1 cm in the cod end, and 1.3 cm in the cod end liner. Age-0 and age-1 red snapper may be able to escape through this mesh size.

Juvenile- Several studies have indicated that juvenile red snapper use inshore low-relief habitats during early life and migrate to high relief habitat in deeper waters as they grow (2574, 2887, 2885, 2935, 2786). Field studies have found that juvenile red snapper (>60 mm SL) recruit to artificial reef structures in the GOM (2935, 2888).

Wells (2005) and Wells and Cowan (2912) studied the abundance and spatial distributions of red snapper off the north-central GOM on the Alabama and Mississippi inner continental shelf. Seabed characterization was performed with digital side-scan sonar and with sediment box-cores. They found that juvenile red snapper were predominantely collected over low-relief sand habitats, which is similar to the findings by Rooker et al. (2841) and Patterson et al. (2786).

Wells et al. (2914) described habitat-specific differences in community structure, highlighting the differences between trawled and non-trawled areas of the northern GOM continental shelf. They characterized fish and invertebrate community structure over sand, shell-rubble, and natural reef substrata, and assessed the effects of trawling on sand and shell-rubble habitats and their associated communities during quarterly trawl surveys over a 2-year period. Fish and invertebrate communities differed significantly among habitat types, and with respect to trawling exposure. Habitat characteristics were quantified with video transects sampled with a remotely operated vehicle, and included percentage coverage of tubeworms, bryozoans, anemones, corals, and algae, significantly affecting fish community structure. Diversity indices differed among habitats, with the highest Shannon diversity (H’) and Pielou’s evenness (J’) over shell-rubble, specifically non-trawled shell-rubble. In addition, higher values of H’ and J’ were found over trawled sand relative to non-trawled sand habitats. Length frequency distributions of several abundant fish species showed truncated size distributions over trawled and non-trawled habitats and were both habitat- and species-specific. Median lengths of juvenile (age-1) red snapper were significantly lower over trawled sand (97.4 mm TL) in comparison to non- trawled sand (123.8 mm TL), and significantly lower over trawled shell (125.2 mm TL) in comparison to non-trawled shell (143.8 mm TL) habitat. Numerically, red snapper displayed an affinity for reef habitats both outside and within non-trawled habitats, providing further support for the view that red snapper have an affinity for structured habitats over the sizes found in this study (mean TL 155 mm ± 2mm SE).
Juvenile snapper display a strong thigmotaxis, seeking structured environments (2933, 2887, 2554, 2636). Szedlmayer and Howe (2887) reported juvenile red snapper selected oyster shell versus sand habitat in tank trials, while Patterson et al. (2786) reported highest juvenile densities in trawl samples off Alabama and Mississippi came from high-relief (2-3 m) shell rubble ridge habitats. Seemingly contrary results were presented by Rooker et al. (2841) and Geary et al. (2651) that demonstrated that juvenile red snapper were in high densities in relatively unstructured mud habitats, and Patterson et al. (2786) reported moderately high juvenile densities occurred in sand habitats off Alabama and Mississippi. It is not clear whether these were young-of-year (age-0) red snapper or juvenile (age-1 and age-2) red snapper.

Adult- Adult red snapper are common in submarine gullies and depressions where food may accumulate and over coral reefs, rock outcrops, and gravel bottoms in the Gulf of Mexico (2872, 2699). Usually fewer fish are supported by smooth bottom without high relief than by bottom with three-dimensional structures, such as offshore oil and gas rigs, artificial reefs, and wrecks (2698, 2863).

The ability to make accurate estimates of fish abundance over a particular habitat is contingent upon the use of appropriate sampling methods (2911). They compared the catch per unit area (A), the relative catchability (q-ratio), and the length-specific bias of four different gear types on sampling red snapper over natural low-relief habitats on the inner continental shelf of the northern GOM. The goal was to assess the overall performance of using a standard otter trawl, a crab trap, a chevron trap, and a stationary 4-camera underwater video array during six quarterly smapling cruises performed in 2004 and 2005. Results indicated that trawls collected the most red snapper per unit areas and had catchability estimates for red snapper that were three to five times greater than the crab traps. Additionally, trawls were the most selective gear for collecting juvenile and sub-adult red snapper from 30 to 250 mm TL (ages 0 and 1). The chevron trap collected the second highest number of red snapper and proved the most useful at collecting red snapper from 150 to 440 mm TL (ages 1-5). The catchability of the chevron trap was three times greater than the underwater video array, which was size selective for both 100 to 150 mm TL (age-0) and 300 to 350 mm TL (ages 2-3) red snapper. The ultimate goal of the project was to provide the most appropriate survey methods for future studies that aim to collect red snapper over natural low-relief reef habitats. The comparison demonstrated that the chevron trap is most effective in sampling adults, while trawls appear to be the most effective gear for sampling age-0 fish.

Wells and Cowan (2912) found that sub-adult and adult red snapper were found over higher relief habitats such as the shell-rubble and natural hard bottom reef habitats. They showed both significantly higher abundance and larger size over the reef habitat. No seasonal effects were observed. Red snapper accounted for 59% of the overall similarity within reef fish assemblages and 20% of the total dissimilarity between shell and reef fish assemblages. It has been suggested that red snapper recruit to these high-relief habitats at about 18 months of age or 20 cm TL (2642).

While a considerable amount of information is available concerning benthic habitats in the U.S. south Atlantic, there is almost nothing published concerning how red snapper use various benthic habitats in the region (SAFMC FEP 2008).

nodes.title: Depth Distribution
nodes.body:
Wilson and Nieland (2926) noted that the western GOM off Louisiana and Texas currently produced significant portions of the commercial and recreational harvests of red snapper, however, this was not always the case. Annual commercial landings in the five states bordering the GOM indicate a shift in the fishery from the eastern to the more western GOM since 1970 concomitant with the placement of several thousand oil and gas platforms into the area. Quantitative estimates of red snapper have been derived both from assessments of the effects of platform removal via explosives and from hydroacoustic surveys of selected platforms. Based both on these estimates and on the number of platforms, they estimated from 1.2 to 7.2 million red snapper live around platforms placed at depths of 20-100 m. Many of these are relatively young individuals of ages 2-4 years.

Petroleum platforms differ from traditional artificial reefs in that their vertical profile extends throughout the water column and provides habitat from the photic zone to the substrate (2926, 2929). Historically, a major obstacle in deriving scientific data about the effect of deep water artificial reefs (and platforms) on fishes and other nekton was the difficulty in quantifying abundance and species composition associated with these reef communities. Wilson et al. (2929) successfully used two complementary techniques, hydroacoustics and point count visual surveys, to estimate the abundance (biomass) and species composition of fishes at several of these structures (2865, 2866, 2867, 2868, 2869, 2870, 2871) and natural reefs (2928). In these studies dual-beam hydroacoustics provided estimates of acoustic biomass, density, size distribution, and the near field area of influence. A remotely operated underwater vehicle was used to determine species composition. They found from 10,000 to 30,000 fishes associated with individual platforms; the lowest numbers were found at the largest and deepest structures, leading them to question the value of deep water structures as artificial reefs. They reported that the density of fishes around platforms was ten times greater than open water and from two to three times greater than fish density associated with the upper portion of the West Flower Garden Bank off eastern Texas; species composition also differed between these two habitat types (2928).

It is of interest that some oil and gas platforms in the eastern, central, and western portions of the GOM had substantial populations of red snapper, while others did not have any red snapper (2929). The depths where reef fish species were observed at the platforms varied depending on the depths where the platforms were situated. The composition of the platform fish community has been shown to change with location and water depth. Previous researchers have noted a zonation of the assemblage of fishes associated with platforms and have divided the shelf waters of the northern GOM into three zones: coastal (water depth < 27 m), offshore (water depth 27 to 64 m) and bluewater (water depth > 64 m) (2640, 2647, 2645). This was more recently confirmed by Stanley and Wilson (2870), who reported that, at a platform in 219 m of water, pelagic bluewater fishes were found principally in the upper 100 m of the water column and fish density was essentially zero below 100 m depth. At a platform situated at a water depth of 60 m, they found fishes throughout the water column, but fish density was highest near the surface and adjacent to the bottom; the fish community was characterized as reef-associated shelf species. At a nearshore platform at 20 m depth, fishes were found throughout the water column and the population was characterized as estuarine.

Platforms situated closer to shore at depths <27m, generally had red snapper (2929). Platforms at intermediate depth range (27-64 m) were observed to have higher densities of red snapper, while those situated in deeper water (>64 m) tended not to have red snapper associated with them (with one exception). Generally, speaking red snapper tended to be found near the bottom depth ranges of the platforms. Smaller red snapper were stacked higher-up with larger snapper tending to aggregate around the platforms in deeper water (2812, 2929).

Red snapper are an important species for both commercial and recreational interests in the northern GOM and as such warrant some special discussion (2929). Of all the habitats included in this study, red snapper were proportionally most dominant at the deeper low-relief feature in comparison to the more shallow high relief feature at Sonnier Bank. This finding is similar to that reported by Wilson et al. (2928) for toppled and partially removed artificial reef structures. Red snappers were proportionally abundant at several platforms in all three regions of the study area; most of these platforms were at the shallowest depths included in the survey design. Few red snappers were observed at those platforms in deeper water at the edge of the outer continental shelf. The movements of red snapper over their potential 50 year lifespan can help to explain some of the observed distribution. After spending the best part of their first two years in shallow, inshore waters, red snapper begin an offshore migration in search of more suitable, deepwater habitats that might include reefs, lumps, depressions, and wrecks (2757). In the northern GOM, these suitable habitats include the many oil and gas platforms that have been sited at moderate depths in the nearshore waters. After a residence at the platforms of perhaps 5-8 years, the red snapper migrate away from the platforms and spend the rest of their lives in a relatively solitary existence at natural or anthropogenic, non-platform structures in deeper waters toward the edge of the outer continental shelf (2656, 2757, 2939).

Allman and Fitzhugh (2549) also provided length at age data to support the contention that older red snapper are found in deeper water associated with commercial longline catches. Their observations about age differences among gears are consistent with other studies that show red snapper undergo a general ontogenetic shift in habitat and depth. Nieland and Wilson (2756) reported that age-1 and younger fish dominated benthic habitats sampled by survey trawls, whereas age-2 and age-3 fish dominated the samples obtained by explosive removal of an oil platform. Nieland and Wilson (2756) further indicated that commercial hook and line collections of red snapper in Louisiana waters revealed few age-2 fish, and in a follow-up paper they speculated that fish older than about age-6 become rare in the hook and line catches due to mortality and emigration from the platforms (2925). Mitchell et al. (2729) also suggested older red snapper are less reef-obligate, based on research longline catches.

A comparison of the age, length, and species composition of the NMFS longline survey was conducted to explore the potential of a deepwater (>150 m) reservoir of large, older red snapper in the GOM (2900). There is concern that there may be a large biomass that is relatively less vulnerable to the fishery and ‘not seen’ by the assessment model because these fish are not taken by the fishery. The age composition of red snapper and depths fished by the NMFS longline survey in the GOM were compared with age composition and depths of the commercial fisheries from logbook reported depths. There was little evidence from the NMFS longline survey of a large biomass in GOM waters beyond 150 meters. A peak distribution of red snapper catches occurred between 50-100 m. The percent of positive sets where red snapper were caught were 0% (0-25 m), 5.61% (25-50 m), 24.78% (50-100 m), 8.57% (100-150 m), and 0% (150-450 m). However, the age composition of the survey differed from that of the various fisheries, even though the fisheries span the depths where the NMFS longline survey encounters older fish. There were more older fish caught by NMFS longline surveys and by commercial longline vessels in the western GOM in comparison to the eastern GOM. It appears that older red snapper may be only partially selected for by the fisheries, particularly the handline fishery and to a lesser extent by the longline fishery. While the commercial longline fishery in the GOM does capture older fish, it is in a lower proportion in comparison to the NMFS longline survey, indicating that some biomass may be less selected for by these fisheries. Some caution should be taken in these conclusions as the age composition for the commercial fisheries only represents landed fish and not discards, which could be high if fishers do not possess red snapper quota. The results suggest that there could be additional older biomass relatively less vulnerable to the fisheries but that this reduction in vulnerability is likely a spatial rather than a depth-related process and it likely occurs in waters shallower than 150 m. This lends support to the dome-shaped selectivities estimated by the CATCHEM model for the commercial handline and eastern GOM longline fisheries (2848).

Scott-Denton et al. (2846) used observer data to describe the commercial bottom longline and commercial vertical-line fisheries in the GOM. From July 2006 through December 2009, data were collected from 9,468 sets collected during 308 trips aboard 2005 reef fish vessels. Of 30,125 red snapper observed being caught, 2456 were taken on longlines and 27,669 were caught on vertical lines. Approximately 77% of the red snapper taken on vertical lines were caught in the western GOM, with the remaining taken in the eastern GOM. Hotspot analyses of the vertical line fishery for red snapper using GIS indicated that the highest CPUEs occurred from the Florida Panhandle to the Mississippi Delta, off the Louisiana-Texas border area, and off Corpus Christi. Low CPUEs occurred on the West Florida Shelf. The majority (65%) were kept. Based on visual observations, 24% were released alive, 10% were discarded dead, and 1% discarded in an unknown condition. Depths of red snapper capture ranged from 6.0 to 558 m. Most (29%) of red snapper were caught in waters <37 m, followed by 37-46 m (26%), 47-56 m (13%), 57-64 m (13%). The remaining depth zones comprised 19%. The immediate minimum assumed mortality of red snapper was 27% in the longline fishery and 28% in the vertical line fishery.

Recently, red snapper fishermen have claimed that a cryptic portion of the red snapper population in the South Atlantic is not being fully exploited or largely missed by the fishery (Southeast Fisheries Science Center 2010). The fishermen have suggested that the biggest and oldest red snapper exist in the deepest depths and are not accessible by hook and line gear. They note that currents in the deeper depths prevent effective fishing with vertical hook and line gear and that the distance vessels must travel offshore to get to the deeper depths can be cost prohibitive.

Cuellar et al. (2610) analyzed MARMAP data in the U.S. south Atlantic. Mean catch rates (CPUEs) were examined in relation to depth (range 10-110 m) for various gears (Yankee trawl, Hook-and-line, Florida Trap, and Chevron trap). Mean CPUEs for red snapper were somewhat higher at 20 m and at 70 m with the Yankee trawl (Fig. 7 in 2610). Mean CPUEs for red snapper were highest at 30 m respectively for the Hook-and-line data and for the Florida trap data. The highest mean CPUE occurred at 40 m with the Chevron trap. Plots of mean fork length (FL) versus depth were also created for each gear type (Fig 8). No increasing trend in mean FL with depth was apparent with the Hook-and-line, Florida trap, or Chevron depth data. Mean FL increased with increasing depth (20 to 70 m) with the Yankee trawl data. Hence, bigger (longer) red snapper were captured in deeper water with the Yankee trawl.

In the U.S. south Atlantic, Hester and Nelson (2685) analyzed landings data obtained from Dr. Jennifer Potts (leader of the Life History Working Group for the SEDAR 24 red snapper stock assessment) collected from recreational Charter boats (CB), Head Boat (HB), Private Recreational (PR) boats, and commercial boats (CM) from North Carolina to Florida. There were 759 data records with depth recorded by minimum and maximum depths fished, along with the sex, fork length (FL) in mm, total length (TL) in mm, and the calendar age of each fish. Where a depth fished was not provided by fishing location (most of data for each fisheries), a depth was computed by averaging the minimum and maximum depths fished provided per trip. While there was a lot of scatter in the data, a positive regression was derived indicating that the total length increased with increasing depth. Plots of mean age and median age by depth for all sectors demonstrated that older fish (up to about age 9) tended to occur in deeper water. Similarly, longer fish tended to occur in deeper water.

The median depth fished in the U.S. south Atlantic by HB was 89 ft (27 m), CB 127.5 ft (39 m), and CM 135 ft (41 m) (2685). The median size of red snapper in the catch for each fishery was found to be 561.5 mm TL for HB, 558.0 mm TL for CB, and 607.0 mm TL for CM. Fishing effort frequency distributions also indicated the approximate depth ranges fished. For HB the range was 1-175 ft (1-53 m), CB 1-280 ft (1-85 m), CM 1-336 ft (1-102 m). While CM tended to fish in somewhat deeper water than the recreational boats combined and catch slightly longer red snapper, the mean differences were not large. The analyses supported assertions by the commercial fishermen that they fish closer to shore, than what had been assumed during the SEDAR15 (2850) stock assessment. There were not many older fish being caught and landed by these fisheries.

The Date Workshop report produced by the SEDAR24 Life History Working Group (2851) presented two graphs (Figure 2.9.1a and 2.9.1b) that depicted the depth distribution of U.S. South Atlantic red snapper for fishing fleets combined. Figure 2.9.1a depicted the size (TL mm) versus depth. There is no increasing relationship of length with depth apparent from the graph. The second graph (Figure 2.9.1b) depicted the age of red snapper versus depth. Approximately 30 fish ranging in age from age-30 to age-50 are included in the graph. Most of these older fish were found at depths ranging from 150 to 300 ft (50-100m). The proportion of older fish in the plot declined at depths ranging from 300 to 400 feet (100-133 m).

Landings for red snapper using longline gear in the U.S. south Atlantic have never been large (2853). The SAFMC prohibited the use of longline gear inside 91 m (300 ft) in 1992. In 1999, the council also prohibited vessels with longline gear aboard to possess red snapper (Snapper Grouper Amendment 9). Hence, there presently is no longline fishery directed at red snapper in the U.S. south Atlantic, which could catch older red snapper in deeper water.

Logbook data from commercial vessels and recreational headboats were analyzed by NOAA/NMFS staff (2853). Also limited depth data were collected for some headboat trips by observers. They noted that ideally one would have detailed depth of capture information for red snapper caught in all fishery sectors. Unfortunately, this was not the case. Plots were created that examined snapper fishing effort by depth and the relative proportion selected by age groups up to age 20. However, it was not stated at what depths the older fish were captured.

Accounts by fishermen have suggested that red snapper exhibit a seasonal migration from offshore to inshore to form spawning aggregations (2853). These aggregations have been termed “snapper bonanzas,” owing to the large daily catches produced during these events. Like other snapper-grouper species that form spawning aggregations, they are likely more vulnerable during this time. If the largest (and oldest) red snapper are moving inshore to form spawning aggregations and their vulnerability is increased during that time period, then the results suggesting a constantly increasing selectivity, peaking at the oldest ages, may be more accurate. The general conclusion drawn from the analysis was that dome-shaped selectivity likely was not appropriate for the commercial handline sector and might not be appropriate for the recreational sectors (2853). These conclusions were largely driven by the age at depth data, which suggested no significant trend in age 5+ fish with depth.

A peer review of the red snapper research and management in the GOM recommended the need to monitor the number and length frequencies of red snapper discards (2942). Onboard observers were suggested as the best way to estimate discard mortality rates. This led to research and monitoring programs on both recreational and commercial fishing vessels (2943). Several studies have focused on depth as an important factor in determining discard mortality of red snapper due to the visible impact of barotraumas (2598). Studies conducted in shallow water (<35m or <115 feet) estimated discard mortality rates of 20% or less (2771, 2814, 2782, 2583). Studies conducted in deeper waters generally estimated higher discard mortality rates ranging from 17% to 93% (2655, 2814, 2616, 2582, 2755, 2579, 2614, 2873). The increase in discard mortality with increasing depth is an expected result and has been described for red snapper and other snapper grouper species (2784, 2581, 2782, 2824, 2873).

To estimate discard mortality rates, a “sink or swim” approach was suggested in which onboard observers would note the short-term fate of discarded red snapper: whether or not the fish swam down out of site (2616, 2682, 2873). Another suggested method to determine mortality rate involved releasing red snapper in cages, then lowering them to depth. This method was used by Gitschlag and Renaud (2655) and by Render and Wilson (2814).

Dorf (2616) put observers on recreational headboats off Texas and collected data during 54 trips fishing at a mean depth of 40.2 m (range 13.4-95.4 m). Red snapper less than the 1999 federal minimum size in the GOM of 450 mm (18-in) TL made up 93.4% of the 3,863 snapper collected. Those less than the Texas state minimum size of 375 mm (15-in) made up 64.0% of the catch. When brought on board, 70.2% of snapper appeared normal and 26.1% had protruding stomachs. Of the discarded red snapper, 60.6% were released alive and swam down, 22.8% swam erratically, 15.2% floated, and 1.4% were discarded dead. Galveston had the highest discard: landing ration (211:1) and smallest mean fish sixe (0.7 kg, 343 mm). Port Aransas had the lowest discard: landing ratio (5.2:1) and the largest mean fish size (0.9 kg, 387 mm).

Venting fish to reduce the effects of barotraumas and reduce discard mortality of red snapper has been researched. Red snapper caught in shallow water experience little benefit from venting (2814, 2815, 2581, 2584). In fact, venting fish may cause increased mortality for a variety of species (2920, 2011). However, vented red snapper caught in waters deeper than 42 m increased survival compared to non-vented red snapper (2584). Smaller red snapper, which survive barotraumas better than larger fish, are normally found in shallower water while larger fish are typically found in deeper water (2584).

Hook type has been discussed as a potential mechanism to reduce discard mortality. However, Burns et al. (2584) found that there was not a significant decrease in discard mortality for red snapper caught on circle hooks compared to J hooks. SEDAR7 (2847) stated red snapper discard mortality decreased by 50% for fish caught with circle hooks compared to those caught with J hooks. A decrease in mortality of red snapper with circle hooks was also noted by Koenig (2581, 2700) and by Rummer (2825).

Nieland et al. (2755) sampled red snapper from commercial landings from the GOM off Louisiana from October 2001 to May 2004. Red snapper ages (N=2,867) estimated from counts of annuli on otoliths ranged from 1 to 14 years; however, the vast majority (97.7%) of these were ages 2 to 6 years and the modal age was 3 years. Total lengths of all specimens were less than 600 mm TL. They also investigated the fate of red snapper regulatory discards (individuals <382 mm [15-in] TL) during 16 trips on working commercial vessels; over two-thirds of 4,839 red snapper assigned among four discard fate categories (ranging from alive and vigorous to dead) were returned to the water either in moribund or dead condition. Mortality among regulatory discards was very high and related to depth of capture. Among the discards, 778 (16%) swam down vigorously, 714 (15%) swam down slowly or erratically, 1,765 (36%) were alive but could not swim down, and 1,582 (33%) were dead. There was a significant positive relationship between the percent mortality (proportion of discards in categories 3 and 4) and capture depth (across depth range 10-90 m) for all fishing opportunities where five of more discards were assessed.

Among 399 potential discards retained for age and length analyses, 86% were between 12 and 15 inches (305-381 mm) TL and 85% were 2 years of age (2755). They concluded that the minimum size regulation appears to do little to protect juvenile red snapper from commercial fishing mortality. Heavy red snapper mortality, which begins as bycatch mortality in shrimp trawls, continues as discard mortality at sublegal lengths when they first recruit to the offshore fishing grounds, and persists as harvest mortality among the youngest legal year- and size-classes. If the minimum size limit is intended to provide a respite from such mortality, a reconsideration of the utility of the minimum length regulation of the commercial harvest of red snapper in the GOM may be warranted.

In addition to the direct mortality monitored, “sink or swim” indicators suggest that red snapper experience a delayed mortality associated with injuries and stress obtained from capture (2614). The ability of a fish to submerge after discarding is often used as a proxy for survival, but this practice underestimates total discard mortality because delayed mortality is overlooked. Fishery managers need a way to link “sink or swim” indicators, or variables observed during capture and release, with delayed mortality rates. Diamond and Campbell (2614) conducted a cage study of red snapper off the coast of Texas to estimate delayed mortality rates and to find factors that could link immediate and delayed mortality, between surface and bottom waters. Immediate mortality (17%) was predicted by the interaction of depth and the differences in temperature between surface and bottom waters. Lactate levels were also significant predictors of immediate mortality in fish whose blood was tested. Delayed mortality (64%) was predicted primarily by a condition index consisting of the presence or absence or injuries, symptoms of barotraumas, and fish behaviors immediately after capture. Specific categories included bleeding, protruding intestines, everted stomach, exopthalmia, the presence or absence of flapping or gilling behaviors, and problems with cage submergence. The majority of fatalities occurred within 24 h after fish were placed in the cages. Their mortality estimates indicated that red snapper discard mortality was significantly underestimated in the 2005 stock assessment for red snapper (2847). Diamond and Campbell (2614) concluded that the use of indices that relate the condition of an individual fish at capture to its probability of delayed mortality is an excellent method for linking immediate and delayed mortality and will likely be applicable to many species that are subject to catch-and-release fishing.

Campbell et al. (2588) and Campbell (2587) analyzed the sublethal effects of simulated capture of red snapper using physiological responses, condition indexing, and performance variables. Simulated catch-and-release (CAR) fishing included combinations of depth of capture and thermocline exposure reflective of environmental conditions experienced in the GOM. Frequency of occurrence of barotrauma and lack of reflex response exhibited considerable individual variation. When combined into a single condition or impairment index, individual variation was reduced, and impairment showed significant increases as depth increased and with the addition of thermocline exposure. Performance variables, such as burst swimming speed (BSS) and simulated predator approach distance (AD), were also significantly different by depth. BSSs and predator ADs decreased with increasing depth, were lowest immediately after release, and were affected for up to 15 min, with longer recovery times required as depth increased. The impairment score developed was positively correlated with cortisol concentration and negatively correlated with both BSS and simulated predator AD. The impairment index proved to be an efficient method to estimate overall impairment of red snapper in the laboratory simulations of capture and shows promise for field conditions, to estimate release mortality and vulnerability to predation.

Campbell et al (2589) related angling-dependent fish impairment to immediate release mortality of red snapper. They made use of a condition index (BtR score) to evaluate the relationship between CAR-related impairment and immediate release mortality in the recreational red snapper fishery. Symptoms of barotrauma and impairment showed positive relationships with capture depth and occurred more frequently during the summer sampling than in the fall. Impairment, as measured by the BtR score, showed significant logistic relationships with immediate release mortality proxies such as floating and erratic swimming at release. Logistic curves had inflection points at BtR scores of 0.3-0.4 (on a scale of 0-1), above which fish experienced high immediate release mortality regardless of season (60-100%). Mean BtR scores were lower than the inflection point of the logistic curve, resulting in immediate release mortality estimates ranging from 20% to 28%. Recaptured fish showed significantly lower impairment than non-recaptured fish. The BtR score is a proficient method to estimate both impairment and immediate release mortality of red snapper in field settings.

The key to a successful CAR program is that fish actually survive the CAR experience (2825). Management strategies are typically designed assuming CAR is below 20%. Recent field studies suggest this may be possible for red snapper retrieved from depths ranging from 20-40 m (2784, 2582) but rates may be greater than 70% if red snapper are retrieved from deeper depths (2581). Logbook records from commercial vessels suggest rates may range upwards of 72-78% (2797). CAR mortality depends on a multitude of factors. However, the main underlying cause of CAR mortality is directly related to depth of capture.

The most effective way to manage a fishery that succumbs so seriously to CAR mortality is not via size limits, seasonal closures, and bag limits (2826, 2825). All combinations seem problematic; either the socioeconomics of the red snapper fishery or the potential for population growth and recovery are negatively impacted. Rummer (2825) proposed that it would seem logical to impose fishery restrictions to discrete areas such that fish populations can be safeguarded from all fishing and CAR activity, therefore protecting age, size, sex classes and ratios simultaneously. For fish like red snapper, where overfishing is widespread and CAR mortality is high, marine protected areas (MPAs) and/or no take reserves (NTRs) were proposed as having the greatest potential for overall conservation and sustainability of red snapper fisheries.

Estimated Discards SEDAR24

Observers working for the Gulf and South Atlantic Fisheries Foundation Inc (GSAFFI) gathered data on the amount of discarding and discard mortality on snapper-grouper species caught on commercial hook-and-line (HH) vessels in the U.S. south Atlantic (2677,2678). The data were collected on HH vessels fishing in Latitude zones 30 to 33 stretching from northern Florida to southern North Carolina. A relatively high proportion of the red snapper catch taken in 2007 was below the 50 cm minimum size. In terms of numbers, 97.7% of the catch of red snapper taken in 2007 was considered to be discarded bycatch (2677). Detailed information concerning CPUEs for red snapper kept and discarded was presented by statistical zones for Latitudes 30-33 for 2008 and for 2009 (2678). During 2008, the percentages discarded ranged from 57.7-77.9% during the first trimester, 58.4-73.3% in the second trimester, and 21.0-42.0% in the third trimester. During, 2009, there was a decrease in the proportion of red snapper discarded which appears to be related to a decline in abundance of red snapper below the 50 cm minimum size limit. The proportion discarded across zones 30-33 ranged from 15.5-27.5% during the first trimester, 15.9-28.5% during the second trimester, and 3.8-10.2% during the third trimester. Overall, the percent discarded during 2008 and 2009 averaged 34.8% (2678). These data were provided to NMFS for use with the SEDAR24 stock assessment.

The GSAFFI reports demonstrate that discarding rates of red snapper can be very high when there are high numbers of undersized red snapper due to periodic recruitment. The length frequency for red snapper during 2007 demonstrates high recruitment of undersized fish ranging from 30-50 cm TL (2677). Tabulated mean catch rates (CPUEs) for both kept and discarded red snapper indicate that most of this recruitment occurred off northeast Florida and off Georgia with lower mean CPUEs off South Carolina and North Carolina (2678). A decrease in mean CPUEs of discarded fish occurred, while mean CPUEs of kept fish increased by the third quarter of 2008. This trend continued into 2009 with mean CPUEs of kept fish increasing, while mean CPUES of discarded fish decreased. The simplest explanation for this is that growth of the recruits during 2008 allowed more fish to be kept and fewer fish to be discarded as they increased in size to exceed the minimum size limit of 50 cm (20 in) TL. This pattern is also apparent with length frequencies for red snapper measured from 2007 to 2009 by at-sea observers on headboats off Florida and to a lesser extent off Georgia (2838). With the At-Sea Headboat Observer Program off northeast Florida, they found that out of 1176 red snapper measured for length frequencies during 2005-2006, 1028 (87.41%) were discarded because they were below the minimum (50 cm) size limit (2850).

nodes.title: Discard Moralities South Atlantic
nodes.body:
The estimates of discard mortality used in SEDAR15 (2849) were 90% for the commercial fishery and 40% for the recreational fishery in the U.S. south Atlantic (2851). The recreational estimate (40%) matched the discard mortality estimate for red snapper from the GOM for fish caught in waters deeper than 20 m (2847). A working paper was developed for SEDAR24 which includes a comprehensive discussion of discard mortality (2598). To account for an increasing discard mortality rate with depth, three models were investigated to describe these depth effects. Two of the models (2581, Diamond et al. unpublished) used a logistic regression function to model the mortality rate and one used a linear trend (2755). The plenary decided to use the depth model presented in Burns et al. (2581) to estimate discard mortality (2851). The discard mortality estimate for the commercial fishery was 48%. The mortality rate chosen for both the recreational headboat fishery and the recreational charterboat fishery was 41.3%. The private boat mortality rate estimate used in SEDAR24 was 38.8%.

The plenary decided to develop discard mortality estimates based on the relationship of discard mortality with depth (2581). This method, used observer data having depth information for released fish (2677, 2010). These observer data were collected during 2007-2009 between latitudes 30 and 33. Estimates of mortality were obtained by calculating a weighted average mortality from the Burns et al. (2581) equation, weighted by the depth profile. The profiles were computed in 25 ft intervals while the mortality estimates from Burns et al. (2581) were computed at the mid-points of these intervals. These estimates were relatively insensitive to interval width since approximately the same result (same whole percent) was obtained with 1 ft intervals from the observer data. To represent discard mortality of red snapper discarded from 1992-2009, the working group recommended the commercial mortality estimate based on discarded fish (48%).

In August 2001, the Southeast Fisheries Science Center (SEFSC) initiated a program to collect discard data from commercial fishing vessels landing federally managed species in the GOM and U.S. South Atlantic (2720). A reporting form was developed as a supplement to the mandatory coastal logbook forms. Discard data from the SEFSC coastal fisheries logbook program were used to calculate the number of red snapper that were discarded in the U.S. South Atlantic during the period January 1, 2001 through December 31, 2009. Fishing gear strata included handline, electric reel (bandit rig) trolling, longline, trap, gillnet and diving. Selected fishers were required to complete a supplemental discard form for every trip they made. To calculate species specific discard rates, discard data were matched to the effort data reported to the coastal logbook program.

A delta lognormal model was used to calculate the yearly least square means of the red snapper discard rate (2720). This method combined separate general linear model (GLM) analyses of the proportion of trips that discarded red snapper and the discard rates of trips that discarded red snapper to construct a single standardized discard rate. Total discards for each year were then calculated using a ratio estimator: yearly least square means (discard rate)*reported yearly total effort.

Discard mortalities (in units of 1000 fish) were modeled with the Baranov catch equation, which required estimates of discard selectivities and release mortality probabilities (2852). Discards were assumed to have fleet-specific mortality probabilities, as suggested by the data workshop (commercial lines, 0.48; for-hire, 0.41; private, 0.39). Annual discard mortalities, as fit by the model, were computed by multiplying total discards (tabulated in the DW report) by the fleet-specific release mortality probability. For for-hire and private fleets, discard time series were assumed to begin in 1983, with the start of the 12-inch size limit; for the commercial lines fleet, discards were modeled starting in 1992 with the 20-in size limit. Discards from the commercial dive fleet were assumed negligible and not modeled. Using these methods the numbers discarded per year were added to the reported fisheries landings data that were used to compute fishing mortalities.

Actual red snapper discards may be higher than the calculated totals presented by McCarthy (2720). In the limited observer data available discarded red snapper were more common than
retained red snapper (60% to 40% of 644 fish) (2851). Self-reported discards obtained from logbooks were reported in numbers of fish and lack length information making a similar comparison with landings data difficult. Discards and landings of red snapper from the commercial fishery, however, appear to be relatively low, particularly when compared to the recreational fishery. The total commercial discards from McCarthy (2720) may represent a minimum estimate of the number of red snapper discarded from the commercial fishery. The conclusion of the Commercial Work Group was that the SEDAR 24-DW01 report by McCarthy (2720) represents the best available information on commercial red snapper discards.
  Egg/Parturition- Collins et al. (2604) captured sexually mature female red snapper in spawning condition (hydrated oocytes) during 1999 off Alabama and the west coast of Florida at depths ranging from 23.8 -122.0 m.
Sedberry et al. (2854) captured adult female red snapper in spawning condition in the southeastern Atlantic over a depth range of 24-67 m in MARMAP trawls from South Carolina to Melbourne off eastern Florida. A spawning aggregation of red snapper was observed at Scamp Ridge off South Carolina at a depth of 53 m (2845). Presumably, eggs occur within the epipelagic (euphotic) zone extending from 0-200 m (2710).

Larva-The consistent presence of larval red snapper collected in SEAMAP plankton samples during summer and fall surveys between the 100 m and 200 m contour in both the western and eastern GOM supports the contention of Collins et al. (2604) that red snapper spawn over a wide depth range, i.e., from the mid-shelf to the continental slope (2710). Hence, larval red snapper occur in the epipelagic zone extending down to 200 m.

Young of Year - Diamond et al. (2941) analyzed NMFS SEAMAP trawl survey data collected during summer and fall surveys in the GOM from 1987 to 2007. The primary composite hot spots of age 0 red snapper captured during summer surveys started east of the Texas-Louisiana border and extended west toward the Mexican border, ranging from about the 20 m depth contour (isobath) to the 50 m depth contour Diamond et al. (2941).

Juvenile- Juvenile (age-1) red snapper were mostly captured during summer SEAMAP trawl surveys in the GOM (2941). Annual zones of higher abundance of age-1 red snapper (red and yellow zones) extended from the upper Texas coast (east of Galveston) to western Louisiana ranging from about the 10 m depth contour to the 60 m depth contour.

Adult- Red snapper are abundant at depths of about 4-110 m (2592) and have been caught at 7-146 m in the GOM (2735, 2526). Red snapper were the second most abundant lutjanid captured in MARMAP surveys in the U.S. south Atlantic (2610). Although not as abundant as vermillion snapper, red snappers occurred 124 times (322 individuals) from depths ranging from 7-68 m. In the Carolinas, they are usually found at depths of 46 to 91 m over both low and high relief areas (2676). Red snappers captured in MARMAP surveys ranged in length from 2 to 85 cm. The maximum size of red snapper is approximately 91 cm (2819).

nodes.title: Temperature
nodes.body:
Egg/Parturition- Collins et al. (2604) captured sexually mature (mature ovaries with hydrated oocytes) female red snapper off Alabama and the west coast of Florida in the GOM at locations with bottom temperatures of 20.6oC and ranging from 26.8-29oC.

A spawning aggregation of red snapper was observed at Scamp Ridge off South Carolina in the U.S. south Atlantic at a bottom temperature of 20.9oC (2845).

Larva-Lyczkowski-Schultz and Hanisko (2710) tabulated the range of temperatures where red snapper were caught in surface neuston nets in the GOM during the Summer Groundfish (SG) surveys and the Fall Plankton (FP) surveys from 2000 to 2003. Surface water temperatures ranged from 27.1-31.0oC (mean=29.4oC) for SG, and ranged from 25.4-30.3oC (mean=29.2oC) for FP.

Young of Year- Dorf and Fisher (2617) analyzed trawl survey data collected by Texas Parks and Wildlife Department in the Texas Territorial Sea (TTS) near five passes in the GOM off Texas. A total of 7,688 red snapper were captured that were believed to be age-0 with mean TL of 90 mm, and a coast-wide mean CPUE of 2.1 per hr. Catches were low along the northern coast with 0.4% collected near Sabine Pass and Bolivar Pass combined. Matagorda Pass, Aransas Pass, and Brazos Santiago Pass along the southwest coast accounted for 16%, 43.8%, and 39.8% of the total catch respectively. The smallest YOY began to appear in July at all three passes. Time series analyses revealed the catch is strongly seasonal, repeating from year to year, and positively related to water temperature. Statistical analyses found that temperature was significant, while salinity and dissolved oxygen were not significant in the autoregressive time series model. The TTS is not uniform YOY habitat, and distinctly different regions are evident due to bathymetry and oceanography. Egg and larval advection from Mexico may play an important role in recruitment to the southern TTS. A long-term increase in the abundance of YOY red snapper from 2000 to 2007 was found, which is coincident with decreased commercial shrimp fishing effort and the use of bycatch reduction devices (BRDs).

Juvenile- High value habitat for juvenile red snapper in the western GOM determined from a habitat suitability index (HSI) model was characterized as temperatures ranging from 24-26oC (2644).

Adult- Red snapper have been taken at 13-32oC (2526, 2820). One of a sample of seven red snapper died at 12.5o C-near the lower tolerance limit in a laboratory test (2732). The upper tolerance limit is about 33.5oC (2526). A spawning aggregation of red snapper was observed at Scamp Ridge off South Carolina at a bottom temperature of 20.9oC (2845). In the laboratory, red snapper under simulated natural conditions spawned in water of 23-25oC and salinity of 31-34 g/L (2553).

nodes.title: Salinity
nodes.body:
Egg/Parturition- A spawning aggregation of red snapper was observed at Scamp Ridge off South Carolina at a bottom salinity of 36.5 g/L (2845). Presumably, eggs occur near the surface over the same salinity range documented for larvae caught with neuston nets (2710)

Larva- Lyczkowski-Schultz and Hanisko (2710) tabulated the range of salinities where red snapper were caught in surface neuston nets in the GOM during the Summer Groundfish (SG) surveys and the Fall Plankton (FP) surveys from 2000 to 2003. Surface water salinities ranged from 24.2-35.7 psu (mean=32.5 psu for SG, and ranged from 27.2-36.6 psu (mean=34.7 psu) for FP.

Young of Year- No information found.

Juvenile- High value habitat for juvenile red snapper in the western GOM determined from a habitat suitability index model occurred at salinities around 35 g/L (ppt) (2642).

Adult-  A salinity of 60 mg/L was lethal to all red snapper in a laboratory test, but they survived exposure to about 45 mg/L without serious effects (2692). They are marine fish and have been taken in waters of 33-37 mg/L (2735). A spawning aggregation of red snapper was observed at Scamp Ridge off South Carolina at depth of 53 m and a bottom salinity of 36.5 g/L (2845).

nodes.title: Dissolved Oxygen
nodes.body:
Egg/Parturition- No information found.

Larva- Lyczkowski-Schultz and Hanisko (2710) tabulated the range of dissolved oxygen levels where red snapper larvae were caught in surface neuston nets in the GOM during the Summer Groundfish (SG) surveys and the Fall Plankton (FP) surveys from 2000 to 2003. Surface water dissolved oxygen levels ranged from 4.7-6.7 mg/L (mean=5.7 mg/L) for SG, and ranged from 5.5-6.6 mg/L (mean=6.1 mg/L) for FP.

Young of Year- No information found.

Juvenile- Seasonal habitat suitability index (HSI) models were developed for juvenile red snapper (age-0 and age-1) in the western GOM (2644). Habitat factors considered in the analysis included water temperature, salinity, and dissolved oxygen at the bottom; depth and density of offshore petroleum platforms; and low-relief bottom structures. High value habitat for juvenile snapper was characterized by depths between 18 and 64 m, water temperatures of 24-26oC, salinities around 35 g/L, and dissolved oxygen levels of at least 5 mg/L. Density of low-relief structures was not a significant habitat element, and an inverse relationship was found between juvenile red snapper abundance and the density of offshore platforms. Results of the model analysis suggest that the step-like expansion of the hypoxic area (dissolved oxygen <= 2 mg/L) offshore of the mouth of the Mississippi River and west to the Texas border, which first occurred in 1993, reduced the habitat carrying capacity for juvenile red snapper in this region by up to 25%, averaging 19%. Gallaway et al. (2644) suggested that this environmental change may limit the level to which overfished GOM red snapper can be rebuilt to historical levels.

Adult- No information found.

nodes.title: Turbidity
nodes.body:
Egg/Parturition- No information found.

Larva- Lyczkowski-Schultz and Hanisko (2710) tabulated the range of optical transmission levels where red snapper larvae were caught in surface neuston nets in the GOM during the Summer Groundfish (SG) surveys and the Fall Plankton (FP) surveys from 2000 to 2003. Surface water optical transmission levels ranged from 24.7-93.3% (mean=81.8%) for SG, and ranged from 74.7-88.7% (mean=86.4%) for FP.

Young of Year- No information found.

Juvenile- No information found.

Adult- No information found.

Floating Habitat: No information found.

pH: No information found.

Light: No information found.

Ammonia: No information found.

Currents/Tides: Dorf and Fisher (2617) suggested that water current patterns explained the advection of eggs and larvae from Mexico to hot spots of abundance for age-0 red snapper captured in bottom trawls off the southwest coast of Texas.

Other Habitat: No information found.

nodes.title: FOOD HABITS
nodes.body: Trophic Mode: Juvenile and adult red snapper are carnivorous (2722).

nodes.title: Feeding
nodes.body:
Larvae-Newly hatched larvae in the laboratory began actively feeding on a culture of algae and rotifers 3 days after hatching and were 2.5 mm SL 4 days after hatching (2809). Snapper larvae demand sufficient quantities of small prey organisms at the onset of first-feeding (2702, 2762, 2706, 2816). Copepod nauplii have proved to be an appropriate prey for red snapper larvae being cultured (2764, 2705, 2763). Little information exists concerning what larval red snapper feed on in the ocean.

Young of Year- No information found.

Juvenile- Small zooplankters were common prey of juveniles up to 150 mm FL, but the fish probably start to prefer larger prey when they are about 100 mm FL (2574). Stomachs of juveniles most frequently contained shrimp throughout the year in the Gulf of Mexico (2585, 2574). Other crustaceans (including crabs), fish and squid were found in 2-10% of the sampled fish. The types of prey that contributed the greatest percentage by volume to the diet of juveniles were squid, octopuses, and shrimp. Juveniles and adults eat a large variety of species of mollusks, crustaceans, and fishes.

Adult- Camber (2585) reported that adult red snapper in the GOM took the following prey (in decreasing order of frequency of occurrence); shrimp, small reef fish, crabs, and gastropods. He stated that tunicates may be taken in the spring.

Futch and Bruger (2639) stated that red snapper may feed over sand, shell, or mud bottoms next to reefs or other rocky bottoms. Many of the prey of red snapper are found over level bottoms adjacent to the reefs, rather than on the reefs themselves (2612).

nodes.title: Food Items
nodes.body:
Larva- No information found.

Young of Year- No information found.

Juvenile One of the most comprehensive early red snapper diet studies was conducted by Bradley and Bryan (2574). They described the diets by season, of trawl-collected (open sand-mud habitat) and hook-and-line reef “rough bottom areas” red snapper from off the Texas coast. They described the diets of 258 open-habitat and 190 reef habitat red snapper (25-325 mm FL) and found that juvenile red snapper were dependent on shrimp, crabs, and crustaceans. They described a change in juvenile red snapper diet as fish size increased. Young red snapper depended almost exclusively on invertebrates, and showed a gradual increase in vertebrate prey with growth. However, they did not separate out the proportions of juveniles sampled over reef versus open habitats.

Lee (2703) and Szedlmayer and Lee (2888) examined the diets and habitat shift of juvenile red snapper from open sand-mud habitat (little or no relief) to artificial reef habitat (1 cubic meter concrete or PVC blocks), from June 1993 through December 1994. In 1994, fish settled over open habitat from June to September, then began shifting to reef habitats. The shift was almost complete by December (visual surveys using SCUBA). Stomachs were examined from 1639 fish ranging from 18-280 mm SL. Of these, 850 had empty stomachs, and 346 from open habitat and 443 from reef habitat contained prey. Small red snapper (<60 mm SL) fed mostly on chaetognaths, copepods, shrimp, and squid. Larger red snapper (60-280 mm SL) shifted feeding to fish prey, greater amounts of squid and crabs, and continued feeding on shrimp. Red snapper diets separated by habitat types rather than fish size for the size ranges that over-lapped habitats. These diet shifts were attributed to feeding more on reef prey than on open-water prey. Thus, the shift in habitat shown by juvenile red snapper was reflected in their diet and suggested differential habitat values based not just on predation refuge but on food resources as well.

Wells et al. (2915) used stable isotopes and stomach content analyses to describe the diet of red snapper in the northern GOM. Approximately 1000 fish were collected over two years to test the possible effects of ontogeny, habitat, and a non-trawl reef permit area on red snapper diets. Stable isotopes of carbon, nitrogen, and sulfur were measured in both red snapper and potential primary producers. Ontogenetic shifts in diet occurred with increasing red snapper size-at-age, resulting in higher carbon13 and higher nitrogen15 isotope values and lower sulfur34 isotope values in larger fish. Stomach content results supported ontogenetic shifts in diet by showing a change in diet from zooplankton, mysid shrimp, and squid for juvenile (ages 0 to 1) to diets dominated by benthic crustaceans and fishes for adults (ages 2+). Habitat-specific differences in isotopes and stomach contents of similarly sized fish were identified; however, feeding differences, both in carbon13 and in prey identified in stomach contents, were detected, but were minimal. Red snapper from outside a single non-trawl reef permit area had higher nitrogen15 isotope values and lower sulfur34 values than for conspecifics inside the non-trawl reef permit area. The analyses of stable isotopes demonstrated that red snapper (ages 0 to 2) rely on sand and mud-associated prey regardless of the habitat from which they were collected, suggesting that the importance of shell and natural reef habitats was more important for red snapper survival than for additional prey resources. Juvenile red snapper occupying sand and mud recruit to structured habitats, such as shell-rubble to obtain refuge from predators, while obtaining prey items such as fish, from adjacent sand and mud areas.

Adult-  Most red snapper diet studies have found that as individuals grow, there is a shift in their diet from invertebrates and zooplankton to a dependency on fish (2735, 2574, 2888). A few studies (e.g., 2585) have reported that large red snapper continue to eat demersal crustaceans. Pelagic zooplankton contributed to the diet of all size classes of red snapper examined by McCawley and Cowan (2722), decreasing only for snapper larger than 500 mm FL. Moseley concluded that it was inefficient for red snapper larger than 110 mm SL to exist on zooplankton. However, Siegel (2858) found that adult red snapper up to 550 mm SL off Alabama continued to consume significant amounts of pelagic zooplankton, especially larval decapods and stomatopods.

Gallaway et al. (2647, 2939) reported the gut contents of red snapper at oil and gas platforms in winter contained mainly fish (small carangids, mainly platform associated rough scad). In spring, the diet was dominated by fish (unidentified fish 23.5%, Atlantic cutlass fish 19.3%, and carangids-probably scad 18.6%, and mantis shrimp 29.5%. In fall, crustaceans (shrimp, 53.2% and crabs 17.2%f or a total of 70.4%) and fish (26.6%) dominated the diets. Clearly, soft-bottom prey were a major component of the diet, but reef associated fish were taken when abundant.

Siegel (2858) described red snapper food habits from habitats sampled offshore Alabama and some samples from Louisiana and Florida. For adults, fish and crabs constituted the main part of the diet. Of interest, all sizes of adults were noted to consume crabs, rock shrimp, penaeid shrimp, larval decapods, and larval mantis shrimp.

Ouzts and Szedlmayer (2767) examined the diets of red snapper collected from the artificial reef area offshore Alabama among four diel feeding periods (dawn, day, dusk, and night) and among three standard size classes small (200-299 mm SL), medium (300-399 mm SL), and large (400-499 mm SL). A total of 432 stomachs were examined, of which 164 contained prey. Prey items were assigned a habitat association based on the literature, authors’ observations, and expert opinion. Small red snapper fed mostly on reef and sand prey types, medium red snapper fed on similar portions of reef, sand and mixed habitat prey types; and large red snapper fed mainly on prey observed to use a variety of habitats. Red snapper were found to feed throughout the 24-hr cycle, with mean gut fullness being significantly lower at dusk than for the day period. Fish were the dominant prey throughout the 24-hr cycle. The second-most important prey group changed with period: shrimp were codominant for dawn, tunicates for day, and crabs were codominant for dusk and night periods.

As previously described, the study by Szedlmayer and Lee (2888) focused on food habits of juvenile (< 200 mm SL) red snapper from open bottom and artificial reefs offshore of Alabama. However, 61 specimens were collected from reefs that ranged from 200-250 mm SL. For these fish, the principal prey categories on a volumetric basis were fish (59.7%), shrimp (27.8%), and crabs (12.5%). For the fish-prey category approximately 65% were reef associated taxa. Reef associated shrimp species constituted 54.2% as compared with 42.4% from open-bottom habitats. The Szedlmeyer and Lee (2888) findings indicate that adult red snapper (200-250 mm SL) fed on both reef and open habitat prey types. Even if, all crabs and all the shrimp but pistol and cleaner shrimp are treated as soft-bottom species, reef prey still constituted about 46% of the diet based on this data set (2939).

McCawley et al. (2723) collected diel food habitat data for red snapper in the Alabama reef areas during July and August 2000. A total of 109 red snapper stomachs were collected from fish 295-560 mm FL. Of these 46 contained prey. When examined on a diel basis red snapper appeared to feed throughout the day and night, with no obvious pattern in feeding periodicity. McCawley et al.
