(2723) concluded that less than 2% of the red snapper diet organisms came from reef-associated organisms, based upon the defined habitat associations of the identified prey organisms.

McCawley (2721) and McCawley and Cowan (2722) examined the stomach contents of 656 red snapper ranging from 207 to 913 mm FL. Of these, 268 (40.9%) contained identifiable prey, 262 (39.9%) were empty, 63 (9.6%) contained only bait, and 63 (9.6%) contained only unidentified material. All the fish examined were considered to be adults. The unidentified material category contributed the largest proportion of red snapper diet by % weight (35.9%), followed by crab (20.2%), fish (19.5%), adult mantis shrimp Squilla empusa (12.6%), and pelagic zooplankton (8%).

On a seasonal basis, McCawley and Cowan (2722) found that fish was present in red snapper diets in all seasons (comprising between 34.5% and 31.8% by weight after the unidentified material was excluded), but they did not contribute the greatest amount by % weight in any season. The diets in summer and winter by % weight was composed of adult mantis shrimp (33.0% and 33.4% respectively), in fall of crabs (35.1%), and spring of pelagic zooplankton (45.6%). Demersal crustaceans (crabs and adult mantis shrimp) were present in all seasons comprising between 41.9% and 54.4% by weight of the diet in summer, fall and winter. During the spring, red snapper fed on high numbers of pelagic zooplankton. Statistical analyses indicated that red snapper were feeding on nearly the same kinds of organisms year around. Appendices 1 to 3 in the paper by McCawley and Cowan (2722) summarize the findings of the various red snapper diet studies.

McCawley and Cowan (2722) estimated that only 1.3% of the red snapper diet (excluding unidentifiable material) consisted of reef associated organisms. In contrast, the dominant components of the diets were species associated with sand and mud habitats (41.2%) and the water column (31%, mainly mantis shrimp and larval fish). Their interpretation of these data was that adult red snapper were almost, if not entirely trophically independent of the reefs on which they lived. In contrast, Gallaway et al. (2939) concluded that many red snapper food habit studies show substantial feeding on reef prey types, which supports the contention that red snapper are obtaining significant food resources from reef habitats.

The recruitment of age-0 red snapper to high-relief habitats such as artificial reefs or natural reefs may also be limited by predation from larger, older red snapper or by predation from other reef-associated species (2554, 2793, 2736). Age-0 red snapper were excluded from complex habitat (concrete blocks) when older red snapper were added to a tank (2554). In caging experiments conducted in the field, higher abundance of red snapper occurred on reefs when predators were excluded; in captivity, age-0 red snapper spent more time associated with complex habitat when a predator (Gulf flounder Paralichthys albigutta) was present (2793).

Chapin et al. (2594) assessed the survival and movement of hatchery-reared red snapper on artificial habitats in the northern GOM. Hatchery-reared red snapper were released onto artificial reef habitats. The fish showed 12.7% survival after 7 months on small habitats (0.86 cubic meters) and 3.1% survival after 8 months on large habitats (3.9 cubic meters). Emigration was estimated by the movement of fish to unstocked habitats and accounted for 76.8% of the decline in abundance at release sites after 26 days. Age-0 fish showed higher survival and growth rates on small habitats (27.6% at 26 days; 0.33 mm per day) compared with large habitats (13.2% at 34 days; 0.26 mm per day) which may be due to increased predation and competition on the large habitats. Fish became evenly distributed among adjacent habitats 26 days after release, indicating that stocking densities at release habitats were above carrying capacities. These observations suggested that providing additional habitat around red snapper release sites would increase survival.

Shipley and Cowan (2855) developed a bioenergetics model for red snapper in the GOM off the coast of Alabama where significant numbers of artificial reefs exist. The model was used as a decision tool for optimal spacing of artificial reefs during deployment. The bioenergetics and consumption rates of red snapper by age class foraging on artificial reefs provided input to the fuzzy rule-based model. After conducting multiple simulations, highest certainty in optimal reef spacing was achieved at reef distances between 0.50 and 0.95 km such that no more than two fit within a 1-square kilometer area. The results inform fisheries managers about placement of artificial reefs to affect the health and survival of reef-associated species.

Based on the life history of red snapper and the potential effects of predators on reef fish recruitment, the proximity of larger artificial reefs and their associated reef fish communities may affect new recruitment of juvenile red snapper (2736). Small artificial reefs were placed near to (15 m) and farther away (500 m distant) from larger artificial reefs at a site off Alabama. Divers used visual surveys to identify and count all fish present on the small reefs and estimated fish lengths. Significantly higher abundances of age-0 red snapper were detected on the small distant reefs (500 m) than on the small nearby (15 m) reefs. Significantly higher densities of rock seabass and pygmy filefish were observed on the small distant reefs compared with the small nearby reefs. Mean species richness was significantly higher on the small distant reefs than on the small nearby reefs. The study indicated that if artificial reefs are built to provide habitat for juvenile red snapper, they should not be placed in areas immediately adjacent to existing adult habitat, conversely habitats intended for adult fish should not be placed near important red snapper nursery areas.

Nowling et al. (2759) used otolith microchemistry to successfully discriminate between red snapper collected from artificial reefs and those collected from oil and gas platforms. A total of 98 otoliths were analyzed by inductively coupled plasma-mass spectrometry (ICPMS) from collections made from both artificial reefs and oil and gas platforms in Alabama and Louisiana over a two-year period from 2002 to 2003. A suite of 15 selected stable isotopes were analyzed, because they were most likely to be present at oil and gas platforms and in the metals and other materials used in artificial reefs, and in the circulating heavy “muds” used while drilling wells. Linear and stepwise discriminate analyses were performed to show that by using subsets of all the elements measured, it was possible to discriminate among artificial reefs and oil and gas platforms at average misclassification rates in the order of 10%.

Sluis (2859) conducted a similar otolith microchemistry study using 17 elements to determine habitats of origin for red snapper collected off Texas, Louisiana, and Florida. Specimens collected off Destin, Florida, off Louisiana, and off Texas exhibited elemental signatures indicating they had come from regions with oil and gas platforms. Specimens collected off Tampa, Florida did not have an oil and gas platform elemental signature. Maximum likelihood estimates (MLE) based on region-specific baseline data indicate that red snapper collected from Destin, Florida were estimated to predominately originate from Louisiana (82.1%) and secondarily from Alabama (16.1%). Red snapper collected from Tampa, Florida were also estimated as originating from Louisiana (53.6%) with more influence from Alabama (37.8%).

nodes.title: REPRODUCTION
nodes.body:
Gender: White and Palmer (2918) found that red snapper sampled off North Carolina to Key West had a sex ratio that did not differ significantly from 1:1. They are gonochoristic. The sex ratio had not changed since 1986. White et al. (2919) presented computations that did not differ from the expected 1:1 ratio of male to female red snapper.

Mode: Red snapper are batch spawners periodically releasing eggs into the water column (2809).

nodes.title: Domain
nodes.body:
Fertilization: External fertilization of eggs by male sperm.

Spawning Strategy: The f ish spawn primarily away from reefs (2574). Spawning was reported at depths of 18-37 m over a firm sand bottom with 1ittle relief in the GOM (2560).

Sedberry et al. (2854) captured adult red snapper in spawning condition in the southeastern Atlantic over a depth range of 24-67 m and a temperature range of 18.05-27.59oC in MARMAP bottom trawls from South Carolina to eastern Florida off Melbourne. Examination of sexually mature ovaries of female red snapper collected by MARMAP found that spawning occurred at depths 23-27 m and latitudes 27o-33oLatitude in the southeastern Atlantic from South Carolina to Florida (2919). Maps were presented depicting the spatial distributions of spawning females clustered off South Carolina, Georgia, and northeastern Florida. Two maps show capture locations for young-of-year (age-0) red snapper situated on the inner continental shelf off of South Carolina and North Carolina. The total number of age-0 red snapper collected with MARMAP trawls from 1979 to 2000 was 31 fish.

Schobernd and Sedberry (2845) reported observing a large school of at least 20-30 red snapper, which appeared to be a spawning aggregation, situated at Scamp Ridge off South Carolina, at 19:29 Eastern Daylight Time (EDT) on August 2, 2002. The school was seen from a submersible at a depth of 53 m, with a bottom temperature of 20.9oC and salinity of 36.5 g/L.

Phelps et al. (2791) noted that brood behavior in hatchery tanks can give some indication of anticipated spawning. A few hours before sunset, male red snapper were observed to follow a female with a swollen abdomen, swimming close to her vent area. Spawning behavior included fish schooling and slow swimming, interrupted by sudden group swimming and rushing toward the water surface. This pattern was repeated several times. Spawning occurred mainly in the late afternoon/evening hours. Several fertilized spawns with egg development in the blastula stage were collected in the late afternoon to early evening hours, before lights started dimming off (at approximately 1900 hrs). Fertilized eggs were found in the egg collector 30 min to 2 hr after the spawning behavior was observed. Floating eggs were carried by the water current from the spawning tank to the egg collector. Jackson et al. (2696) examined the abundance of hydrated eggs in ovaries of wild-caught red snapper along the northern GOM and concluded that spawning peaks around 1600 hours.

Reproductive Periodicity: In general, red snapper spawn in summer and fal1 in the GOM. They have one peak spawning period in Florida waters and two peaks in Texas. Individual fish probably spawn several times during the spawning season (several egg stages occur simultaneously in the ovaries); the protracted spawning season and variation in gonadosomatic indices in fish of similar size during the season are consistent with this hypothesis (2600).

Information on spawning seasonality as well as size and age at maturity are available for the northern GOM (2574, 2927, 2601, 2931, 2932), the southern GOM (2577), and the U.S. south Atlantic (2918). Prior to 2008, the only information on reproduction for the southeast GOM was 30 years old (2639). More recently, a detailed study of the east and west coasts of Florida was conducted by Brown-Peterson et al. (2576).

Geary et al. (2651) reported that spawning occurred from April through late August at three banks off Texas. Peaks were generally unimodal with the majority of recruits from June and July hatch dates. This is roughly two weeks later than the peak in the hatch date reported by Rooker et al. (2841). Szedlmayer and Conti (2885) reported that peaks in hatch date distributions of red snapper in the northwestern gulf vary by several weeks between consecutive years. Gonadal analysis suggests that red snapper spawning occurs in the northwest GOM from April through October, suggesting that a second pulse of recruits may enter the fishery in the late fall (2604).

Despite the lack of significant genetic differences, Jackson et al. (2695) reported maturity schedules and size-specific fecundity were significantly different between red snapper populations east and west of the mouth of the Mississippi River. They suggested early maturity at smaller size in the eastern GOM may be a genotypic response to high fishing mortality having selectively removed later maturing genotypes, a response that would not be apparent in selectively neutral genetic markers such as mitochondrial DNA (MtDNA) or nuclear DNA microsatellites (2808, 2835). Regardless of the causative factor, the fact that regional differences exist implies some degree of isolation between the eastern and western GOM. Patterson et al. (2778) asserted that regional differences in size at age reported by Fisher et al. (2628) further support that population structure exists in GOM red snapper, which has not been revealed by traditional fisheries genetics applications (2808, 2663).

White and Palmer (2918) collected otoliths and gonadal tissues from red snapper sampled between Cape Lookout, North Carolina and Key West, Florida during 1979-2000. The mean size of red snapper from fishery-dependent samples, were 594 mm TL and ranged from 70-976 mm TL. Fish sampled from fisheries-independent gear had a significantly smaller mean TL (426 mm, range = 121-866 mm) than fishery dependent samples. The mean size of red snapper was significantly smaller in the 1980s when compared to the 1990s, regardless of gear type. The overall sex ratio was not significantly different from the expected 1:1, regardless of gear type. The smallest mature female was 287 mm TL and the largest immature female was 435 mm TL, with an estimate of length at 50% maturity of 378 mm TL. Histological examination of the gonads indicated that female red snapper were in spawning condition from May through October, with a peak between June and September. The gonadosomatic index (GSI) for females ranged from a low of 0.35 in November and December to a high of 2.67 in June. Males were found to be in spawning condition thoughout the year.

Brown-Peterson et al. (2576) collected red snapper from recreational-for-hire boats at two distinct areas of Florida to examine potential differences in their reproductive biology. Samples were obtained from the Florida East Coast (St. Augustine to Melbourne N=66) from June to November of 2004 and 2005, and from the Dry Tortugas (N=81) during May, June, and August 2004-2005. There was a significant relationship between length and batch fecundity of red snapper from the East Coast but not from the Dry Tortugas. Relative frequency estimates were low in Dry Tortugas fish (27 ± 11 eggs/g) relative to 235 ± 56 eggs/g in East Coast fish, but similar to those reported from Alabama. Spawning frequency estimates varied from every 2.2 days on the East Coast to every 4.3 days in the Dry Tortugas. The apparent regional differences in reproductive biology among Florida red snapper may require region-specific management plans for this species.

  Parental Care: None reported.

Seasonal Energetics: Wakeman et al. (2899) studied oxygen consumption, energy consumption, and growth of red snapper.

nodes.title: Maturation
nodes.body:
Juvenile- Information included under Adult.

Adult-  Authors of early studies of GOM red snapper reproductive biology concluded that fish began reaching sexual maturity at a small size (<300 mm TL) and had protracted spawning seasons extending through the summer months (2574, 2639, 2735). Collins et al. (2601) were the first to estimate batch fecundity in red snapper and to establish that the spawning season extended from April through October in both the eastern and western GOM. Red snapper usually show partial sexual maturity when 1 year old and show full maturity when about 2 years old and 375 mm in fork length (FL) (2734).

Length at maturity has been reported to be 320 mm FL (2585), and between 190 and 300 mm SL (2735). Wilson et al. (2927) presented preliminary estimates of maturation at 290 mm FL. Age-at-maturity has been reported as greater than 2 years old in the GOM (2639).

Ovary analysis has also varied among studies. While authors prior to 1976 (2585, 2735, 2574) used macro-assessment of gonad maturation, later authors (2639, 2924, 2601) used histological techniques to determine stages of oocyte maturation. Histology is a more effective method for staging oocytes because it allows a detailed view of cross-sectioned and stained oocytes (2695).

Jackson et al. (2695) used red snapper collected during the spawning season off Alabama and
Louisiana, to describe maturation schedules of red snapper. Progression of oocyte maturation to vitellogenesis was used to define and identify sexually mature females. Combined data showed that smallest mature red snapper was 267 mm FL and was two years old. The smallest with hydrated oocytes, indicative of imminent spawning, or postovulatory follicles, indicative of recent spawning, were 285 and 297 mm FL respectively, and both were two years old. Red snapper off Alabama reached maturation at smaller sizes and younger ages than those sampled off Louisiana. Growth rates did not differ between the two regions. Such differences in maturation schedules may document an important stock response to reductions in populations size.

A comparison of maturity schedules indicated that red snapper captured off Alabama reached 50% maturity before 275 mm FL and before they were 2.5 years old, and raw data showed 100% maturity by 575 mm FL (2695). Females captured off Louisiana reached 50% maturity before 325 mm FL and before they were 2.5 years old, and raw data showed 100% maturity by 625 mm FL and 6.5 years old. Compared to Alabama, Louisiana female red snapper progressed more slowly to reach 100% maturity over size- and age-classes.

In the U.S. south Atlantic, White and Palmer (2918) noted that male red snapper reach maturity as early as age-1 or 200 mm TL, with all males mature by age-3 or 378 mm TL. Females can be mature by age-2 or 287 mm TL, with all females mature after age-4 or 435 mm TL. The gonadosomatic index (GSI) of female red snapper peaked in June and remained high until September.

White et al. (2919) used data obtained from the NOAA/NMFS Marine Resources Monitoring, Assessment and Prediction (MARMAP) program to assess reproductive condition in red snapper in the southeastern Atlantic for the SEDAR24 stock assessment. The youngest sexually mature female red snapper was age-2 and the oldest was age-4. The smallest mature female was 265 mm TL, and the largest immature female was 435 mm TL. Age at 50% maturity was 1.87 yr and length at 50% maturity was 370 mm. Mature females were present in 0% of the age-1 class, 54% of age-2, 86% of age-3, 93% of age-4, and 100% of females age-5 or older. Mature males were present in 50% of age-1 class, 93% of age-2, 97% of age-3, 100% of age-4, 97% of age-5, and 100% of males age-6 or older. All male red snapper were mature at 451 mm TL and larger.

Fecundity: Fecundity of fish sampled in northwest Florida ranged from 0.2 million eggs for a female about 3 years old and 386 mm FL to 9.3 million for a fish about 12 years old and 754 mm FL (2600).

Only limited fecundity information is available for red snapper along the Atlantic coast of the U.S. (2851). The relationship between batch fecundity (BF) and TL (BF = 9548*TL – 5,224,104; r2 = 0.67) was estimated for 12 specimens, 560-937 mm (Brown-Peterson et al. 2009). The small sample size and the lack of specimens < 560 mm made this equation of minimal use for the SEDAR24 assessment. An estimate of fecundity at age was available from the GOM, but was not as predictive as an estimate of fecundity at length (see 2931; 2629) because batch fecundity reaches an asymptote at an age of approximately 10-12 yr.

Given the lack of a usable fecundity estimate from the Atlantic region, three proxies to estimate fecundity were considered: 1) gonad weight versus age, 2) gonad weight versus whole fish weight, and 3) gonad weight versus total length (2851). The first proxy (gonad weight versus age; was not considered adequate because of a large gap in the age data, and, secondly, the linear nature of the relationship was inconsistent with the non-linear relationship evident between gonad weight and fish size (whole weight or TL) as fish grow. The second proxy is probably a better option, given the need to relate gonad weight to spawning biomass. The gonad weight (Wg) - whole fish weight (Wf) relationship is expressed as a power function:

Wg = 3.1416x10-5 Wf 1.743; SEa = 3.1836x10-5, SEb = 0.1107.

The gonad weight (Wg) - total length (Lt) relationship, third proxy, is expressed as a power function:

Wg = 1.207x10-11 Lt 4.524; SEa = 3.16x10-11, SEb = 0.3923.

The Life History Working Group for SEDAR24 recommended the use of the second proxy, gonad weight – fish weight, as an estimate of fecundity in the assessment (2852). The recommendation was accepted at the plenary session of the Data Workshop.

nodes.title: Development
nodes.body:
Egg/Parturition- In the laboratory, initial hatching began 20 hr after fertilization (2728), and about 50% of the eggs hatched within 25 hr of fertilization (2809).

Larva-	Newly hatched larvae in the laboratory averaged 2.2 mm SL (2809). The larvae began actively feeding on a culture of algae and rotifers 3 days after hatching and were 2.5 mm SL 4 days after hatching.

Young of Year- No information found.

Juvenile- No information found.

Adult- Porch et al. (2799) modeled batch fecundity (BF) on size and age of red snapper for use in stock assessments in GOM waters. Batch fecundity is a principal determinant of the reproductive potential of indeterminate spawners. BF appears to increase geometrically with length and asymptotically with age based upon combined data from reproductive sampling programs by NMFS in the GOM and MARFIN in the southeastern Atlantic. As the life history pattern of red snapper sets up a potential disconnection between size and age, Porchet al. (2799) modeled their interaction as explanatory variables of BF. Visual analysis suggested a dome-shaped relationship between BF and age within a given size-class. To test this, a log-linear model and a new “standardized” age model (where the effect of age depends explicitly on the size of fish) were fitted to the data. These analyses suggest that the effect of age, while statistically significant, was relatively small (the models with age and length terms explaining only slightly more of the variation in BF than a simple power function of length). The age effect seems to be most pronounced for fish that are exceptionally small or exceptionally large given their age, which constitute a small fraction of the sample and presumably also a small fraction of the population at large. Hence, it seems unlikely that including this interaction would have any important ramifications for stock assessments of red snapper. Nevertheless, the effect of age on BF remains open to the degree that old fish (i.e., greater than age 13) were rare in the combined data set and tended to exhibit lower BF values than predicted. Age effects of other reproductive determinants remain to be evaluated but the authors found hydrated females to be of greater size-at-age than non-hydrated red snapper suggesting an age-length interaction on batch fecundity.

Mating/Spawning Duration: Only limited information is available for red snapper along the U.S. south Atlantic coast. Brown-Peterson et al. (2576) reported that spawning occurs every 2.2 days based on a sample of 66 specimens collected during June through November. Estimates from the GOM revealed that spawning frequency increases until about Age 6; little information is available for older ages (2931, 2629).

Sex Ratio: Red snapper are gonochoristic with an equal sex ratio of 1:1 (2576, 2919)

nodes.title: Length Range
nodes.body:
Egg/Parturition- Red snapper eggs averaged 0.82 mm in diameter (range: 0.77-0.85 mm) (2809).

Larva- Newly hatched larvae in the laboratory averaged 2.2 mm SL (2809). The larvae began actively feeding on a culture of algae and rotifers 3 days after hatching and were 2.5 mm SL 4 days after hatching. Body length (BL) is equivalent to notochord length or standard length (SL) depending on the stage of development of the larvae (2704). A total of 96 hatchery-reared red snapper larvae ranged in body length (BL) from 1.9 to 26.1 mm BL, and a total of 118 wild caught-larvae ranged from 2.6 to 20 mm BL (2618).

Daily growth rates observed by Geary et al. (2651) of 1.09 mm per day at Freeport Rocks, 1.01 mm per day at Heald Bank, 1.01 mm per day at Sabine Bank) off Texas overlap the upper end of red snapper observed by Rooker at al. (2821) of 0.78-0.88 mm per day, and 0.54-0.86 mm per day found by Szedlmayer and Conti (2885).

Young of Year- The age-0 larvae undergo metamorphosis and settle to the bottom when they are 16-19 mm TL and 26 to 30 days of age in the GOM (2809, 2885, 2841, 2939). Settlement was observed in July and the newly settled fish (most <40 mm TL) were found over open or low relief habitat off Alabama (2888). Age 0 red snapper enter the GOM penaeid shrimp trawl fishery at about 67 days of age and 50 mm TL (2939). Age-0 fish began moving onto reefs as they reached sizes approaching 100 mm TL and by December were found on the reefs from which age-1 fish had abruptly disappeared (2888).

Juvenile- Wells (2910), also working offshore Alabama, observed an increase in mean size of age-1 red snapper corresponding to a shift from sand (96.1 mm TL) to low-relief shell (127.0 mm TL) to high relief habitat (172.3 mm TL).

Nieland and Wilson (2757) analyzed size frequency distributions of red snapper killed by explosives at an oil and gas platform off Louisiana. A peak in the size frequency distribution indicated that age-2 red snapper ranged from 250-380 mm TL. Because of the 15 inch minimum size limit imposed by the GMFMC age-2 red snapper were not observed in size frequencies representing catches of red snapper taken from either the commercial or recreational fisheries.

Adults- Nieland and Wilson (2757) found a second peak in the size frequency of red snapper killed by explosives at an oil and gas platform off Louisiana. Age-3 red snapper ranged in size from 381-480 mm TL. Adult red snapper in the GOM range in length up to 104 cm TL (2846).

Red snapper initially grow quickly and then growth slows steadily as larger size associated with long life span is reached (2574). In the GOM, under-yearling fish grew 25 mm/month in August and September.

Length Conversions: The relations of SL to FL and FL to TL (lengths in mm) and N (sample size) were reported by Futch and Bruger (2639) as follows:

FL = 1.1585 SL + 13.3 (N = 21)
TL = l.0678 FL + 3.5 (N = 100)

Nelson and Manooch (2746) reported the following relation:
TL = 1.0712 FL + 1.7 (N = 180).

Additional length-length relations are given in Parrack (2774). Length- length relations show a high linear correlation (2774).

Weight-Length Conversions: Length-weight relations calculated for severa1 areas in the GOM were similar (2774). The length-weight relation changed at 190-300 mm SL (2735).

nodes.title: Wet-Dry Weight Conversions
nodes.body:
Length at Age:
  Male-No information found.

  Female-No information found.

Sexes Combined-Age-length keys for red snapper in the southeast Atlantic have been presented by Manooch et al. (2712, 2713), White and Palmer (2918), and McInerny (2725). Mean total lengths at age in the southeast Atlantic were presented by Manooch et al. (2712) and McInerny (2725). McInerny presented a comparison of mean total lengths (TL) at age for the commercial fishery between 2003 and 2006 for Florida, and for North Carolina, South Carolina, and Georgia combined (Table 5). Table 6 presented a comparison of mean total lengths at age for the commercial fishery and for the recreational fishery off Florida between 2001 and 2006. In Table 7, McInerny (2725) presented a comparison of mean total lengths at age during the period of: a) no regulation, b) the fishery management plan (FMP), and c) after passage of Amendment 4. Mean back-calculated total lengths at age for red snapper in the southeast Atlantic were presented up to age-11 by Manooch et al. (2712), up to age-20 by McInerny (2725), and up to age 15 for various locations in the GOM (Louisiana, West Florida) and southeast Atlantic (Carolinas, East Florida) by Nelson and Manooch (2746). All of these studies cited presented mean lengths at age for the sexes combined.

nodes.title: Longevity
nodes.body:
Egg/Parturition- The early life history includes a planktonic egg stage for 18-27 hours (2809, 2728).

Larva- The larval stage has duration of 25-47 days (2704).

Young-of-Year- A benthic young-of-year stage occurs after the larvae undergo metamorphosis and settle to the bottom (2885). Size at settlement is about 1.7 cm. Age-0 fish initially occur over sand, mud bottoms, then migrate to submerged banks of oyster shell (2709, 2793). Red snapper as small as 18 mm settled on relatively unstructured open shelf habitats in summer, but by the winter age-0 fish had recruited to artificial reefs that provided greater complexity and relief (2888).

Juvenile- A comparison of maturity schedules indicated that red snapper captured off Alabama reached 50% maturity before 275 mm FL and before they were 2.5 years old (2695). Females captured off Louisiana reached 50% maturity before 325 mm FL and before they were 2.5 years old. Based on the age at which 50% of the fish are sexually mature, age-1 and age-2 red snapper can be classified as juveniles.

Adult-  Maximum ages for red snapper derived from reading scales were age-4 in the northern GOM (2735), age-13 off Louisiana (2746), age-9 off Alabama (2898), and age-11 off western Florida (2746). In the U.S. south Atlantic, Nelson and Manooch (2746) aged red snapper from east Florida and the Carolinas and found fish as old as 16 years using scales and otoliths. Research by Beamish and McFarlane (2562) called into question the reliability of ages derived from scales and proposed the need for age validation studies.

Recent advances in otolith preparation methodology have allowed red snapper to be aged reliably in the GOM up to the following ages: 42 yr (2891), 53 yr (2812), 31 yr (2777), 52 yr (2925), 47 yr (2551), 53 yr (2729), 55 yr (2556), and 57 yr (2549). Patterson et al. (2784) found that the oldest female sampled was 34 years, and the oldest male was 33 years old.

Manooch and Potts (2711) aged red snapper from the U.S. south Atlantic up to 25 years old using sectioned otoliths. White and Palmer (2918) found that the age range determined from otoliths for fishery independent samples in the south Atlantic was 1-22 years with a mean age of 3.1 years, and 1-45 years for fishery dependent samples with a mean age of 4.2 years. The oldest red snapper aged using sectioned otoliths in the south Atlantic was 54 years old (2725).

Potts et al. (2802) gathered otoliths to determine the age structure of red snapper collected from North Carolina to the east coast of Florida during the summer months of 2009. All fish were collected with hook and line gear by recreational and commercial fishermen. The oldest red snapper caught off North Carolina was 12 yr, off South Carolina 20 yr, off Georgia 22 yr, and off northeast Florida 37 yr. Further studies are needed to determine whether older red snapper occur in deeper water offshore.

Aging Structures/Methods: Using scales, several studies found rapid growth in young fish. Scale annulus formation off the U.S. GOM coast is complete by early summer for fish ages 2 and older (2773).

A 35% decrease in the production in red snapper in the commercial GOM fishery from 1965 to 1975 prompted Futch and Bruger (2639) to further examine the age and growth of red snapper (2626). Among 240 red snapper taken off the west coast of Florida, they estimated red snapper ages of 1 to 5 yr from 200 readable whole otoliths; however, they postulated ages up to 20 yr for larger individuals whose otoliths were unreadable.

Bortone and Hollingsworth (2569) determined ages of red snapper using scale, otoliths, and vertebrae. They found that all three body parts had a statistically similar level of readability (between 75% and 80%). However, they only examined 46 red snapper.

Nelson and Manooch (2746) were used scales and also sectioned some otoliths to examine the age structure of red snapper in the northern GOM as well as the west-central Atlantic. They examined 2,151 scales (from both the GOM and U.S. south Atlantic) and142 sectioned otoliths (Atlantic only) to examine the growth and mortality of red snapper along the U.S. south Atlantic and the northern GOM. They attempted to validate their ages using monthly mean marginal growth increments performed on scales (2626). This technique indicated that red snapper in the GOM form annuli during June and July. They were unable to perform marginal increment analyses on otoliths, because they did not have otoliths sampled throughout all 12 months of the year. However, 18 one-year-old red snapper sampled in the Carolinas during June all exhibited the beginning of new growth (translucence) at the otolith section edge, leading them to suggest that scale and otolith annuli form simultaneously.

A number of studies using sectioned otoliths have found greater longevity of red snapper than what was originally reported from age determinations using scales (2626). Szedlmayer and Shipp (2891) used counts of annuli on sectioned otoliths for 409 red snapper sampled with hook and line off Alabama. They reported a maximum age of 42 years, a substantial increase over the previously reported maximum age of 13 years determined from scales (2746).

Render (2812) estimated ages from sectioned otoliths for red snapper sampled from both the recreational and commercial fisheries off Louisiana. Render observed a maximum longevity of 53 years. He validated his age estimates through marginal increment analysis. The increased longevity estimates reported by Szedlmayer and Shipp (2891) and Render (2812) were available for the stock assessment conducted by Goodyear (2672).

A number of laboratories in the GOM region began routine annual aging programs of red snapper in an effort to track age structure trends over time for stock assessment purposes (2607, 2925, 2551). Wilson and Nieland (2925) tracked the age structure off Louisiana during eight years of variable collection effort from 1989 to 1998. Allman et al. (2551) sampled commercial and recreational fisheries from Texas to the west coast of Florida in 1998 and 1999. A total of 8,169 otoliths were sectioned. Validation work was conducted using marginal increment analysis.

The consequences of incorrect age determinations of red snapper was first pointed out by Rothschild et al. (2822) in their review of the red snapper GOM management plan. In particular some life history aspects of red snapper appeared to differ from typical long-lived marine species, such as their rapid growth and early maturity that were more consistent with short-lived species. Red snapper in the GOM mature as early as age two and show rapid growth within the first 10 years of life and fecundity increases with age (2891, 2604, 2932). The inconsistency between red snapper life history and that of other long-lived species, and the lack of direct mark recapture studies, showed a need for further validation of annual increment formation in otoliths of red snapper, especially for older larger fish.

Szedlmayer (2881) studied the formation of daily otolith increments in age-0 red snapper after marking them with oxytetracycline dehydrate (OTC). For wild red snapper, the mean otolith increment deposition rate was daily (0.97 increments per day) when growth rates were fast (0.63 mm FL, length of fish per day), but not daily (0.82 increments per day) when somatic growth was slow (0.2 mm length of fish per day). For reared larvae (N=8), increment deposition rates were daily (0.99 -1.03 increments per day), and growth rates ranged from 0.6 to 0.9 mm per day. Growth rate affected increment deposition rate as a threshold function, i.e., when growth rate was <0.3 mm length of fish per day, deposition was less than daily, but above this level increment deposition did not exceed a daily rate. As growth rates increased increment widths increased. Examination of a sub-sample (N=8) of the otoliths from the slowest growing wild fish by electron microscopy did not increase increment counts. Because red snapper are late spring-early summer spawners, young fish can expect maximum growth due to warm summer temperatures. Thus, daily ageing methods should be well suited for this species.

The use of bomb-radiocarbon was applied to validate otolith section ages in the GOM (2555, 2556). Ages of red snapper ranged from 2 to 55 years with back-calculated years at birth ranging from 1943 to 1996. Baker and Wilson (2556) stated that their radiocarbon chronologies based on accelerator mass spectrometry (AMS) provided evidence that otolith section-based age estimates for red snapper were valid.

A second age validation method applied to red snapper was radiometric testing, which measured the chemical disequilibria of 210Pb (lead) to 226Ra (radium) (2930). Radiometric ageing of fish otoliths relies on the principal assumptions that (1) 226Ra is naturally incorporated into the otolith either at a constant rate or at a rate that is proportional to the mass increase of the otolith, (2) that the otolith remains a chemically closed system and there are no losses or gains of radionucleids (e.g., radon 222Rn), and (3) the initial activity ratio of 210Pb to 226Ra is close to zero. Baker et al. (2557) showed that some of these assumptions were violated in red snapper otoliths. In whole otoliths of both red snapper and red drum (Sciaenops ocellatus) 226Ra activity was inversely correlated with the otolith mass increase with age, validating the assumption that 226Ra accumulation in otoliths occurs at a rate proportional to that of calcium (Ca). 222Rn emanation from otoliths decreased as otolith mass increased. 222Rn loss occurred in all red snapper otolith samples (<=4.1%), and decreased with increasing size (age) of the otolith.

Although a validated aging method may have proved successful for a given study there is no guarantee that those structures will be interpreted the same by other readers (2586). Allman et al. (2005) noted that while validation of aging methods is an important criterion in estimating growth and longevity, age interpretation remains largely subjective. This subjectivity can pose a significant problem in aging red snapper otoliths due to challenges in interpreting the first annulus and in discerning annuli in older individual fish.

A measure of precision is a valuable means of assessing the reproducibility of age determinations beween individuals or laboratories (2586, 2626). A number of the laboratories conducing red snapper age-growth studies have determined the average percent error (APE) to evaluate aging precision of red snapper (2812, 2784, 2925, 2551, 2550).

Wilson and Nieland (2925) noted that training and experience are critical to achieving accuracy and high between reader concensus on red snapper annulus counts due to the high level of difficulty of interpretation.

The Gulf States Marine Fisheries Commission (GSMFC) began to conduct yearly aging workshops in 2003 in an effort to bring together all aging laboratories in the GOM to discuss and standardize processing and aging techniques (2714, 2626). The GSMFC compiled a red snapper reference collection of otoliths to support ongoing aging programs to monitor the consistency of aging between individuals and laboratories (2626). The Panama City red snapper reference collection consisted of 300 adult red snapper otolith sections. The collection was distributed to seven external laboratories for aging. Average percent error (APE) was then used to compare age determinations between the seven laboratories and the Panama City Laboratory. Initial comparisons of Panama City ages to external laboratories indicated that laboratories 1-4 had APEs below the 5% target and laboratories 5 and 6 had APEs slightly above (2550). Comparison with laboratory 7 generated an APE of 11.6%. This APE was attributed to a new employee at laboratory 7 as well as a slightly different method in otolith preparation. This effort demonstrated the source of aging errors and highlighted the importance of a reference collection.

Similar studies are being conducted in the U.S. south Atlantic (2919). A red snapper aging workshop was held during August 2009 in Charleston, South Carolina (2802). Red snapper otoliths (N=196) in a ‘reference’ set from fishery-independent and fishery-dependent were aged during the inter-laboratory workshop. The average percent error (APE) for readers from South Carolina Department of Natural Resources (SC DENR) was 9.13%. Additonal red snapper otoliths (N=447) were aged with an initial agreement of 67% and agreement within two annuli of 93% between two readers. Ages determined for red snapper otoliths ranged from 0 to 35 years.

The current ageing technique of counting annual growth increments on sectioned otoliths is often difficult and subjective in young red snapper (2565). In particular, identification of the first annulus is subject to reader identification and is a source of considerable error in aging young fish (2690, 2925, 2841, 2550). Interpretation of the putative first annulus in sectioned otoliths of red snapper has been a source of debate among otolith readers throughout the GOM (2937). The chemical marker alazarine complexone was used to validate the periodicity of first opaque annulus formation in red snapper otolith sections. Juvenile red snapper were immersed in 100 mg alizarin complexone per liter of seawater solution in November 2005 and then reared in 6000 liter circular tanks until July 2006. Otoliths were then removed from the fish and thin sectioned. All experimental otolith sections displayed a distinct fluorescent mark ranging from 0.62 to 0.96 mm from the core when viewed under a microscope with a rhodamine filter. The diffuse opaque annulus was located distally to the alizarine mark in all specimens (ranging from 0.88 to 1.51 mm). The distal position of the presumptive first annulus relative to the alizarin mark in all specimens indicates that this diffuse opaque annulus in red snapper sectioned otoliths forms during the first winter after hatching. Translucent marginal edges of all otolith sections indicate that first annulus formation is completed by mid-July.

A new method for determining the age of red snapper was developed involving shape analysis of otiliths (2564, 2565). Multidimensional scaling and non-parametric analysis showed significant shape differences of age-0, age-1, and age-2 fish. Discriminant function analysis and cross-validation classification showed 65.6% correct age classification based on shape variables alone, and 86.7% correct age classifications with inclusion of otolith weight in the discriminant function. Otolith shape can provide an objective method for ageing young red snapper.

The periodicity of otolith growth increments (opaque and translucent zones) from adult red snapper was examined through a mark and recapture study conducted (2005-2010) and laboratory holding of hatchery-reared red snapper over a two year period (2002-2004) (2884). Wild red snapper (N=295) were caught on hook-and-line, marked with anchor tags, injected with oxytetracycline dihidrate (OTC), and released in the GOM off Alabama. Marked fish were recaptured up to 2.8 years after release (n=35) and sagittal otoliths were dissected, sectioned and examined under white and blue-violet light. The number of opaque growth zones past the OTC mark was compared to time at liberty for each fish and supported an annual periodicity of growth increment formation. Also, most (87%) of the hatchery reared fish showed two opaque zones that supported an annual increment formation rate. However, an unusual timing of opaque zone formation was shown for mark-recaptured fish. Based on known timing of OTC marking, otoliths from mark-recapture fish showed opaque zone formation from late summer (August) to early winter (December). This fall formation of opaque zones is in contrast to previous studies and its timing may relate to the end of spawning for this species.

Research has been conducted to determine chemical signatures of red snapper otoliths associated with studies to determine differences in population demographics in the GOM (2780, 2785, 2781, 2652, 2859, 2759). Some differences have been found indicating regional differences in age-0 red snapper between the eastern and western GOM (2781, 2859).

Growth Equations: Nelson and Manooch (2749) reported von Berta1anffy growth equations for fish from two areas in the GOM. They found that the von Bertalanffy growth curves for Louisiana, western Florida, eastern Florida, and the Carolinas differed statistically, as did the length-weight relations for fish from west Florida, east Florida, and the Carolinas. However, the differences in growth curves were small and the differences in length-weight curves had little if any biological significance. Parrack (2773) reported differences in growth curves between fish west of and fish east of the Mississippi Delta. This difference was inconclusive.

A number of studies have developed von Bertalanffy growth equations for red snapper populations respectively in the GOM and U.S. south Atlantic (2601, 2746, 2713, 2627, 2891, 2925, 2930, 2783, 2918, 2725, 2827). Most of the studies fitted models for the sexes combined. Wilson and Nieland (2925) and Fisher et al. (2627) developed separate models by sex of red snapper. Von Bertalanffy growth parameters for red snapper and other species of Lutjanidae were tabulated as part of a comparative study by Martinez-Andrade (2719).

Habitat varies greatly throughout the GOM and while numerous studies have aged red snapper, none have simultaneously compared the age and size structure and growth rates among standing and toppled oil and gas platforms with natural habitats (2827). The study examined the size and age structure and growth rates (using von Bertalanffy growth equations) of red snapper among three different habitats (shelf-edge banks, standing platforms, toppled platforms) and six recreational fishing regions of the GOM (South Texas, North Texas, Louisiana, Alabama, Northwest Florida, Central Florida). Across all of the habitats and regions, red snapper were small (mean TL = 526.84 mm, mean TW = 0.97 kg) and from younger age classes (mean age = 4.44 yr), representing the strong recruitments of 2004, 2005 and 2006, with few fish older than seven years (1.5%). Total length, weight and age frequencies, and growth models differed significantly among the habitats. Red snapper from the banks were significantly smaller at age and slower growing than red snapper from the artificial habitats. Also, shelf-edge banks appeared to support a higher predominance of older red snapper compared to the artificial habitats. Demographic differences in red snapper size and age frequencies and growth parameters were found across the GOM. Small, fast-growing individuals dominated the recreational catches of South Texas, Northwest Florida, and Central Florida, whereas larger, slower-growing red snapper constituted the majority of the Alabama and Louisiana catches. Also, both of the Florida regions’ catches were comprised of significantly younger red snapper than catches in the north-central and western regions. To prevent habitat- and region-specific overfishing and promote stock recovery, these differences should be weighed when evaluating future stock assessments and management decisions. It is also important for fisheries managers to note the absence of old red snapper in this study and its implications for the stock’s recovery status.

nodes.title: Commercial
nodes.body:
Gulf of Mexico

The red snapper is the most important fish in the GOM commercial snapper-grouper fishery between Cape San Blas, Florida, and the mouth of the Rio Grande (2546); 4.6 million lb were landed commercially at U.S. ports in the GOM in 1985 (2742, 2734).

From the 1880s to the 1950s, the red snapper fishery primarily operated out of Pensacola Florida (2602, 2570, 2857). Although the fishery began in the 1840s, red snapper was established as a major commercial product in the 1870s when the railroad system permitted the shipment of fishes from Pensacola to northern and inland markets. As early as 1883, it was evident that the number of red snapper was decreasing on the existing fishing grounds off Pensacola. Snapper fishermen had to go further east each year to obtain a profitable catch. Many fishing smacks sailed over 200 miles to the Florida Middle Ground. This area was also soon overfished. New red snapper grounds were discovered off the Dry Tortugas in 1885. From 1895 to 1929, the discovery of a large red snapper fishery on the Campeche Banks off Mexico brought the period of the highest production for Pensacola’s red snapper industry.

Snappers and groupers are often taken together in the snapper-grouper fishery. Various fishing methods for snappers and groupers have been used or tested over the years. Most commercial fishing is done with baited hooks and lines on e1ectric and hydraulic reels which were too expensive until recently (2734). These are all classified as handlines in National Marine Fisheries Service fishery statistics. From 2 to 40 hooks may be used with one reel (2546). Ladyfish and squid are the most effective bait (2592); red snapper select fish and squid equally often (2639). The industry has experimented with other fishing methods, but many were deficient; an otter trawl adapted for rough bottoms was effective (2861, 2591, 2745). An extensive bottom longline fishery that may take red snapper developed in the GOM since about 1980. The longline fishery in the eastern GOM has been directed primarily at yellowedge grouper (Epinephelus flavolimbatus) (2775).

Commercial fishing grounds for red snapper are well offshore in the GOM (2734). In 1955, the most important fishing grounds had 1ong been the Campeche Banks off the Yucatan Peninsula, Mexico, which were the principa1 grounds fished by the west Florida fleet (2585, 2687). Fishing there by American boats was curtailed, however, since the extension of Mexico's fishery conservation zone to the 200-mi limit. Red snapper 1andings from foreign waters have composed less than 13% of the total U.S. landings since 1973 (2657). Western Florida landings varied widely over the years (2585). They increased progressively as the fishery developed from 1880 to 1902, stabilized as the Campeche Banks were exploited during 1902-28, dropped with reduced effort during the Great Depression of 1929-35, increased again as the economy began to recover in 1936-39, declined markedly with reduced effort from 1939 to 1945 during World War II, and then began to recover again around 1946 (2585).

In the early 1960's, large numbers of commercia1 vesse1s were built to fish for snappers and groupers (2592). The average number of handline vessels in western Florida was 180 in 1957-60; increased to 290 in 1961-65; leveled off at 260 in 1966-70; and increased again to 320 in 1971-74. The average total number of handline fishermen in western Florida was 780 in 1957-60; increased to 1200 in 1961-65; and stabilized at 1030-1100 in 1967-74 (2630, 2657).

Porch et al. (2800) noted that statistics on commercial landings of red snapper have been recorded by the National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS) and its predecessors as far back as 1880. However, there are many gaps in the historical records. Censuses were conducted sporadically prior to 1949 and the water body were the catch was obtained was not recorded until 1963. Landings data obtained from several state and private agencies were used to supplement NMFS landings statistics. The data suggest a substantial red snapper fishery existed as early as 1872. The reconstructed landings are consistent with major events in the history of the fishery, but considerable uncertaintly remains over uncanvassed years between 1890 and the 1920s.

Landings for western Florida declined greatly during 1982-85 to the second-lowest level ever recorded. In 1983-85 catch per unit of effort (catch rate) was relatively high, but declined 26% during that period in the gulf east of the Mississippi River Delta for fish 3 years old and older in the bottom longline and the rod-and-reel fisheries (2775). Also, in 1983-85, a stock assessment showed that initial biomass (without recruits) declined 17% and recruitment biomass declined 98% in this area (2775).

The principal commercial fishing grounds used by fishermen from Alabama, Mississippi, Louisiana, and Texas are on the reefs offshore from those States. The average number of handline vessels in these four states was 150 in 1957-60 and 180 in 1961-65; declined to 90 in 1966-70; and leveled off at 80 in 1971-74. The average size of the vessels increased from 30 gross tons in 1957 to 61 gross tons in 1974 (2630, 2657). Landings peaked in the early 1960’s in Alabama and Texas, and in 1968 in Mississippi. Landings in Alabama, Texas, and Mississippi declined 73%-93% after these peaks in the 1960s, but Louisiana landings increased to a record high in 1984. A recent stock assessment showed that estimated initial biomass (without recruits) declined 45%, but estimated recruitment biomass increased 21%, for red snapper west of the Mississippi River Delta between 1980 and 1985 (2775).

An increase in the number of fishing boats and trips may cause competition among boats, because the number of boats that can make a good catch in the prime fishing areas is limited; competition among boats reduces the catch per unit of fishing effort. On the Campeche Banks, the catch rate declined from 1937 to 1940, when the number of fishing trips (and probably the competition) increased, and then greatly increased from 1941 to 1945 when competition probably declined because of reduced fishing effort during World War II. The catch rate declined from 1948 to 1951, but competition probably also declined (2585).

The commercial red snapper fishery in the GOM during the 1970s ranked eighth in total weight, seventh in total value, and sixth in price per pound (2743, 2734). The only species regularly exploited by offshore fisheries in the mid-1970s in the western gulf was the red snapper and the gulf menhaden, Brevoortia patronus (2686). The red snapper was the most important of about 17 species in the U.S. snapper fishery (2546). In the northern GOM, it made up about 86% of the total value of the catch by the large vessels (56-69 ft long) in the snapper-grouper fisher that could reach distant fishing grounds, and in the southeastern gulf, it made up about 37% of the total value of the catch of all vessels in the fishery (2593). At the time of their study, the Campeche Banks were not fished substantially by American boats for political reasons. Total profits were greater for the larger vessels in the northern GOM because the value per pound was higher for red snapper than for the other species that predominated in the southern GOM (2593).

nodes.title: South Atlantic
nodes.body:
As early as 1886, red snapper were fished commercially on the east coast of Florida (2603). Captain Latham fished on the east side of Florida, landing his catch chiefly at Savannah, Georgia. He generally fished for red snapper from off Cape Canaveral southwards to the Indian River, in 12 to 15 fathoms (24-30 m) of water.

Comparatively few snapper were caught north of Cape Canaveral. The benthic habitat fished was noted to differ from the west side of Florida. On the west coast, red snapper were generally caught in depressions of the sea bottom, commonly called “gullies”. On the east coast, the snapper were found most abundant on narrow coral ridges, which usually run parallel with the coast line, and are elevated 2 to 3 feet above the surrounding bottom. Some of these ridges were not more than 100 feet wide, while others may be 300 feet or more. Red snappers were not so abundant on the east coast as they were on the west coast, but they averaged larger in size. A vessel carrying a crew of seven men made a trip of about two weeks, and an average fare (catch) was about 6,000 pounds (lbs).

A small commercial fishery for red snapper along the Atlantic coast has existed at least since 1902 when 155,000 lbs were landed, primarily in Georgia (2832). The fishery continued at relatively low levels until after World War II. Landings jumped to approximately 250,000 lbs in 1945. By 1950, they had reached 363,000 lbs. Then, they fluctuated along a generally increasing trend through 1968, peaking at 974,000 lbs and declining to less than 100,000 lbs in 2006. Commercial landings of red snapper in the U.S. south Atlantic increased from 1950 through the 1960s, reaching a peak in 1968 of 1,043,000 lbs (454 mt) (2713, 2918). From 1975 through 1998, annual landings fell from 721,100 to 60,949 lbs (2918). Eastern Florida landings dominated the catch through the middle 1970s after which a precipitous decline occurred. During 1990-2001, 58% of the red snapper were landed in Florida (east coast), 6% in Georgia, 25% in South Carolina, and 11% in North Carolina.

nodes.title: Recreational
nodes.body:
Gulf of Mexico

The red snapper is one of the most desired species of sport fish in the GOM. Sport fishing grounds overlap commercial grounds (2734). In 1965 and 1970, the weight of the commercial catch was less than that of the sport fish catch (2738). Sport-fishing boats range from small 12-ft private boats to 85-ft party boats (head boats). The number of boats increased from 1956 to 1976 and probably partly displaced the inshore commercial fishery (2546, 2878).

Snappers are especially vulnerable to fishermen because, during cooler months the fish will remain in a fishing area (reef habitat) until it is overfished (2619), and sometimes rise to the surface and snap at bare hooks or whatever is offered-hence the name “snapper” (2872).

Between 1982 and 1985, the GOM sport fishery catch of red snapper declined by about 60% in Florida and 78% in Louisiana (2734). In western Florida, the commercial catch also declined sharply between 1982 and 1985. In Louisiana, the commercial fishery may have supplanted the recreational fishery over this period.

The largest annual sport catch for Louisiana from 1979 (when accurate statistics became available) to 1985 was about 2.7 million fish-the highest recorded for any gulf state for the same time period (2734). For that period, Alabama’s sport catch fluctuated with high catches about every other year; in years between 1979 and 1985, when the sport catch was higher (1979, 1981, and 1983), the commercial catch was also generally higher-except that the commercial catch peaked in 1982. A trend in the Texas catch could not be determined because too few data were available. Mississippi’s catch remained low, and the commercial catch in 1985 was the lowest in 17 years. Regulations in 1988 in the U.S. waters of the GOM allowed a maximum of 5 fish less than 12 inches in Florida per trip for headboats.

Moran (2734) tabulated the recreational catch of red snapper (thousands of fish) caught by the recreational fishery in the GOM from 1979-1985 in Alabama, Mississippi, Louisiana, and Texas. The total catch across all four states ranged from 1,746,000 fish taken in 1979 to 126,000 fish taken in 1984. The data were compiled from Current Fisheries Statistics reports of the National Marine Fisheries Service (2739, 2740, 2741, 2742, 2743).

In summary, the sport catch and commercial catch were sometimes positively correlated—possibly because both declined after heavy fishing pressure or because of a natural 30–month cycle in abundance (2585) – and sometimes negatively correlated, possibly because one fishery replaced the other (2546).

The red snapper ranked 19th in number of fish caught among groups of sport fish for which statistics wererecorded in the GOM in 1985; about 2 million red snapper were caught by sport fishermen in the GOM that year (2742).

nodes.title: South Atlantic
nodes.body:
The U.S. south Atlantic recreational fishery is comprised of the private sector and for-hire sector (2832). The private sector includes anglers fishing from shore (all land-based structures) and private/rental boats. The for-hire sector is composed of the charterboat and headboat (also called partyboat) sectors. Charterboats generally carry fewer passengers and charge a fee on an entire vessel basis, whereas headboats carry more passengers and payment is per person. The type of service, from a vessel- or passenger-size perspective, affects the flexibility to search different fishing locations during the course of a trip and target different species since larger concentrations of fish are required to satisfy larger groups of anglers.
In the U.S. south Atlantic, recreational landings peaked in 1985 at 619,000 lbs. In 2002, recreational fishermen landed 390,908 lbs of red snapper (2918). Recreational snapper grouper harvest in the south Atlantic has been variable during the period 2003-2008, averaging slightly above 11 million pounds (2832). On average, the private/shore mode of fishing accounted for the largest harvests at around 7.62 million pounds (MP). Well below this harvest level are those of the charter mode at 1.92 MP and headboat at 1.63 MP. Harvests in each state also fluctuated during the same period. On average, Florida accounted for most of the snapper grouper harvest in the U.S. south Atlantic at around 6.90 MP, followed by North Carolina at 2.21 MP, South Carolina at 1.51 MP, and lastly by Georgia at 0.62 MP.

Ecological Role: Red snapper is classified as a reef fish, and their reef association begins amost immediately after they leave the plankonic stage and settle to the bottom (2885, 2887, 2935, 2939).

 Species Stress: Based on 537 sectioned otoliths from red snapper collected in the southeast Atlantic from 1990-1996, Manooch and Potts (2711) found that red snapper length-at-age determinations were considerably smaller than the length-at-age estimates of red snapper determined from sectioned otoliths collected during 1974-1978 (2746). The reduction in length-at-age found by Manooch and Potts (2711) may have been due to variation in sample sizes, differences in interpretation of the sectioned otoliths by investigators, or sustained heavy fishing pressure that may have selectively removed, over many generations, the faster growing individuals of the populations.

Nieland et al. (2758) sampled 6,159 red snapper landed at a commercial dock in Cameron, Louisiana from October 1998 to May 2004 for morphometrics data and otoliths for age determination. The harvest was almost totally dominated by individuals of ages 2-6 years. Over the course of their sampling, they observed statistically significant decreases in mean total length (TL) of red snapper at ages 2-6 years. The decline in mean sizes at age might be attributed to density-dependence wherein as the population increased in numbers there was a decrease in resources (food, habitat etc.) per individual fish, which might be manifested in a compensatory decrease in growth rate. Thus declines in red snapper mean TL age may be an expression of recovery from an overfished condition. Conversely, the heavy commercial and recreational harvest of young (juvenile and adult) red snapper in the northern GOM, many of them at the minimum TL required for retention, may have resulted in an inadvertent selection for the survival of slow-growing individuals.


Jackson et al. (2695) noted that red snapper in the GOM are managed as a unit stock and the fishery management plan is based on minimal data regarding reproductive output, and the size and age at sexual maturation is not certain. Differences in size and age at sexual maturity of red snapper between the northeast and north-central GOM were evaluated to test whether the population conforms to the unit stock hypothesis. Red snapper were collected during the spawning season in 1999, 2000, and 2001 from the GOM off Alabama and Louisiana and were used to describe maturation schedules. Progression of oocyte maturation to vitellogenesis was used to define sexually mature females. Combined data showed the smallest mature red snapper was 267 mm FL and was two years old. The smallest with hydrated oocytes, indicative of imminent spawning, or postovulatory follicles, indicative of recent spawning, were 285 and 297 mm FL respectively, and both were two years old. Red snapper off Alabama reached maturation at smaller sizes and younger ages than those sampled off Louisiana. Growth rates did not differ between the regions. Such differences in maturation schedules may document an important stock response by red snapper in the GOM to reductions in population size. Jackson et al. (2695) stated that shifts in maturation schedules in red snapper may be attributable to genetic selection coincident with increased mortality.

Trippel (2895) reviewed fisheries literature worldwide and described situations where fish stock abundances have declined dramatically due to overfishing. Evidence indicates that stocks comprised of a broad range of sizes and ages are able to spawn more eggs over a longer period of time than eggs produced by stocks comprised primarily of young fish. He recommended that management should be pursued on the basis of reducing fishing pressure to levels that permit fish populations to reach older ages. The biological consequences of selective removal of large fish are now more clearly understood, and the excessive removal of fish can no longer be perceived as simply leading to a reduction in the number of eggs produced by the population. Important aspects of egg size and spawning time are also jeopardized by high levels of exploitation.

The truncated age structure and prevalence of faster growth rates of red snapper throughout the GOM are compensatory responses to overfishing that could severely hinder the population’s ability to recover (2827). Likewise, the temporal decrease in the length-at-age of red snapper and the precipitous decline in landings in the southeast Atlantic, and a low Spawning Potential Ratio (SPR) of 24-32% (2831) suggested that this species may have been overfished (2831, 2918). Fisheries managers should consider these maladaptive responses in the stock when evaluating future assessments and management options, as well as the potential stock responses associated with future management options.

Size limits are commonly used to manage commercial and recreational fisheries (2874). Minimum size limits, which are relatively easy to enforce, have been used to restrict total harvest, prevent growth overfishing, and allow individuals at least one spawning event before removal from the fishery. One widely acknowledged disadvantage of size limits is the mortality immediately at release for under-sized fish, but another emerging concern is that size-selective fisheries drive a phenotypic change in the life history traits of a population. Observed phenotypic changes can be driven by genetic and/or environmental influences. If the change is largely influenced by genetic changes, it may not be readily reversed. Recent studies have shown that high levels of fishing pressure can change the size at age, age at maturation, and size at maturation of fish species. Vermilion snapper (Rhomboplites aurorubens) and red porgy (Pagrus pagrus) were recently shown to exhibit these traits due to differential mortality (2874). The study found that the hook-and-line fishery targeted young, but large fish with a fast-growing phenotype. Their landed catch included many young, large fish, whereas discarded fish had a similar age range and mean ages, but smaller sizes at age than the landed fish. This indicated that the fisheries were altering the genetics of these species by selecting for the survival of slower-growing individuals. A similar shift to slower-growing red snapper populations has been documented in both the southeast Atlantic and the GOM (2711, 2758). Stephen et al. (2874) concluded that managers need to consider the life history characteristics of each species in light of its susceptibility to phenotypic shifts due to minimum size limits. They suggested that managers should consider adopting an ecosystem-based management plan that includes a multispecies quota system.

Status: Recent stock assessments conducted in both the GOM (2847, 2848) and southeast Atlantic (2849, 2850, 2852) indicate that red snapper have been subject to overfishing and are considered to be overfished.

Stock Status: Recent studies of red snapper population dynamics in the GOM are consistent with genetic studies	that indicated regional differences in population demographics. Patterson et al. (2783) reported no significant difference existed in growth rates between red snapper sampled off Alabama and fish sampled off Louisiana west of the mouth of the Mississippi River. Fisher et al. (2628) reported that growth was not significantly different between Alabama and Louisiana samples, but fish sampled off Texas were significantly smaller at age than fish from the other two regions. Further evidence of significant regional differences in population demographics was reported by Woods et al. (2932). They reported fish off Alabama reached sexual maturity at smaller sizes and younger ages than in the western GOM, where size specific fecundity was greater. The results reported by Woods et al. (2932), Fisher et al. (2628), and Jackson et al. (2695) indicate significant variability of GOM red snapper population dynamics and demographics exists among regions, despite the lack of genetic divergence in selectively neutral markers (2662, 2808, 2835). The main consequence of these studies demonstrating differences in age and growth and sexual maturity of red snapper populations between the eastern and western GOM, is that these differences have been incorporated into the catch-at-age model (CATCHEM); while still conducting the red snapper stock assessment Gulf-wide (2847, 2848).

Patterson et al. (2781) examined otolith microchemistry of age-0 red snapper in the northern GOM to determine if otolith elemental signatures could be employed as natural tags to estimate post-settlement connectivity. Fish (n=755) belonging to five successive year classes (1996-2000) were sampled from three GOM regions. Solution-based analysis of otolith chemistry was accomplished with sector field-induced coupled plasma-mass spectrometry (Ba, Mg, Mn, and Sr) and inductively coupled plasma-optical emissions spectrometry (Ca). Several regional trends observed for individual elements were consistent among year classes, yet elemental signatures were significantly different among years, as well as among regions (MANOVA, p<0.0001). Jackknifed classification accuracies from linear discriminant function analysis approached 80% (mean = 78.4%) in all years except 1998 (62.4%). Overall, these results indicate otolith elemental signatures may serve as effective region-specific natural tags of GOM red snapper.

Sluis (2859) investigated habitat-specific and region-specific otolith microchemistry of age-0 red snapper belonging to the 2005-2007 year classes. Year class-specific quadratic discriminant function analyses (QDFAs) distinguished nursery areas with 71-84% accuracy. Maximum likelihood analyses identified sources of sub-adult and adult red snapper sampled during the summer of 2006-2008 from the western Gulf and Mexico regions based on year-class specific otolith chemical core concentrations. Locally derived and Louisiana recruits were apparent among red snapper collected off Texas, but were inconclusive to estimate connectivity between the western Gulf and Mexico regions. Otoliths of red snapper collected from platforms and other habitats off Alabama, Louisiana, and Texas during the summer of 2007 and 2008 were analyzed to determine if platforms impart detectable signatures based on seventeen trace metals. Mean jackknifed classification accuracies from QDFAs indicated higher success from discriminating among regions (86%) than habitats (79%). Maximum likelihood estimate analyses estimated region and habitat origin of red snapper collected from natural habitats off Florida, Louisiana, and Texas during the summer of 2009. Platform signatures were evident in otoliths from red snapper collected off Florida, a region devoid of platforms, possibly reflecting a western Gulf contribution to the western Gulf sub-stock. The microchemical otolith signatures of western Gulf red snapper demonstrated discrete regional populations with some interpopulation mixing, further supporting the metapopulation structure. Sluis (2859) suggested that further study may show that GOM red snapper populations should be divided into four separate sub-stocks (TX, LA, AL/MS and FL), instead of the two-stock management approach currently established in the U.S. GOM.

No studies exist indicating differences in demographics between populations of red snapper in the U.S. south Atlantic that would justify treating them as separate stocks or sub-stocks (SEDAR15 2005, 2852).

nodes.title: Management Status
nodes.body:
Gulf of Mexico

The red snapper fishery in the GOM has been in existence since the mid-1800s (2691). Federal management of the fisheries in the GOM began in 1976 with the passage of the Magnusen-Stevens Fishery Conservation and Management Act and the establishment of the Gulf of Mexico Fishery Management Council (GMFMC). One of the first fishery management plans (FMP) developed by the GMFMC was the Reef Fish Fisheries Management Plan (2657). This FMP was implemented in November 1984 and established the first red snapper size and bag limits. In 1988, the stock was determined to be overfished (2669). Initially, the GOM red snapper fishery was managed based on stock assessments, updates, and working papers created by scientists at the NOAA/NMFS Southeast Fisheries Science Center (SEFSC) in Miami (2670, 2671, 2672, 2673, 2945, 2674, 2839, 2944, 2840, 2841, 2903, 2904, 2905). Subsequent, stock assessments have been conducted by teams of scientists through the Southeast Data, Assessment, and Review (SEDAR) process (2847, 2848). The GOM fishery has been managed to stay within total allowable catch levels in order to rebuild the stock. Management methods have included size limits, bag limits, seasonal closures, trip limits, and license limitation programs. The success of these methods has been limited in part due to high levels of juvenile red snapper mortality associated with shrimp trawling, high rates of discard mortality from the directed fishery, and socioeconomic requirements of the directed fisheries to maintain some minimal level of harvest.

Strelcheck and Hood (2949) outlined strategies being undertaken to help rebuild the red snapper population in the GOM. Since the GOM population was declared overfished in the late 1980s (2669), subsequent stock assessments (2674, 2670, 2841, 2761, 2847, 2798) have concluded the population was overfished and undergoing overfishing. The first rebuilding plan was established in 1989, setting a target of rebuilding the red snapper population by 2000 (2658). Changes in scientific advice and new information on red snapper biology resulted in revisions to this plan. The most recent revision was approved in 2004 and set a goal of rebuilding red snapper to maximum sustainable yield by 2032 (2659). Despite the recent implementation of this plan, a 2005 red snapper population assessment indicated additional management restrictions were necessary for this plan to be successful (2847). Managers are now confronted with several challenges to recover red snapper including addressing bycatch in the shrimp fishery and reducing discard and fishing mortality in the directed fishery. Social and economic considerations, competing conservation mandates, regulatory consistency, scientific uncertainty, political intentions, and the length of time allowed for recovery further complicate management and stock rebuilding. Managers will need to focus on short-term directions and periodically adjust management strategies to ensure adequate rebuilding progress is made. This will allow managers to incorporate new information and unanticipated developments when making adjustments to red snapper and shrimp regulations, should either insufficient progress or unexpected events occur.

Earlier in this review, huge bycatches of age-0 and age-1 red snapper were described associated with the shrimp trawl fisheries in the GOM (2575, 2642). There also are huge bycatches of undersized red snapper associated with the recreational headboat fishery and commercial hook-and-line fishery being discarded in both the GOM and the U.S. south Atlantic (2616, 2838, 2677, 2010, 2614, 2873). A broad-based public consensus has emerged that bycatch should be minimized to levels approaching insignificance (2609). Bycatches in their various forms can have significant consequences for populations, food webs, and ecosystems. The economic effects of bycatches can influence not only the levels of yields to fisheries, but also may have major effects on allocations among competing fisheries. The lack of comprehensive monitoring programs in most areas to assess bycatches and integrate them into population and multispecies models seriously impedes a full understanding of bycatch consequences and the efficacy of measures for their amelioration. Nevertheless, where evidence for significant bycatches exists, a risk-adverse and perhaps adaptive management philosophy is clearly warranted. Establishing the benefits and costs associated with bycatch management is a priority as managers attempt to define the practicality of bycatches approaching zero given the institutional, scientific, and industry resources necessary to accomplish the job.

The most recent red snapper stock assessment for the GOM suggested that red snapper in the western GOM were beginning to recover from overfishing (2848), and it is expected that as the stock rebuilds, there will be a shift to an older age structure (2847, 2549). While an increase in red snapper biomass has been observed in the fisheries, an age shift is not readily apparent (2827), as well as in the stock assessment, or with other recent studies (2847, 2549, 2755). Identification and protection of the strong year-classes is necessary in order to: 1) allow more red snapper to reach maximum spawning potential and ensure the success of future year-classes, and 2) repopulate the older age classes to eliminate the severely truncated age structure. It has been recommended that managers regularly review the red snapper rebuilding plan to include advances in scientific research and adapt the current policy in order to address the short-term directions while not losing site of the long-term goal (2949, 2848).

Smith et al. (2862) presented a case study concerning fisheries management of red snapper in the GOM.
