The paper noted that red snapper in the GOM is a major source of revenue resulting in a dichotomoy between maintaining the health of the fishery and meeting the demands of the local economies. In order to govern marine fisheries the Magnuson-Stevens Fishery Conservation and Management Act of 1976 was created. This act was used to establish a 200 mile exclusive economic zone (EEZ) around the United States coastline and 8 regional fisheries management councils were created whose roles are to develop fishery management plans. With the involvement of the fishers, the councils work to protect fishery resources while managing the fishery in such a way as to produce optimum benefits for society. Therefore, according to regulation, any change in the economic status of the Gulf Coast or the health of the red snapper fishery must result in a regulation change to uphold this balance. In an attempt to improve understanding of the complexity of managing the fishery, the case study illustrated the roles of various people involved in the extensive process of regulating the GOM red snapper fishery. The paper discussed the complications that arise in this process through the perspectives of biologists, policymakers, and fishers at each step along the way. By necessity, to introduce the process in a manageable way, various steps, people and complexities in the process are either reduced in importance or not introduced. All the people introduced in the case study were fictional, but they were based on actual individuals within the process. Basically, the paper summarized the management and regulatory processes that are presently being applied to many marine fisheries species through SEDAR.

Cowan (2606) compared and contrasted the stock assessments for red snapper that were recently conducted in the GOM (2847, 2848) and U.S. south Atlantic (2849, 2850). Cowan (2606) noted that assessments often rely on a wide array of biological and fisheries data of varying quantity and quality, making the assessment process data hungry, complex, and uncertain. Assessment scientists face the difficulty of estimating numbers of individuals (among other biological benchmarks) of a population of widely distributed, often mobile, fishes for which direct measurement of almost everything is impossible. Consequently, stock assessment scientists are forced to use tools designed to assemble a variety of indirect measures into a statistical model capable of producing predictions to inform fisheries management about stock status and the consequences of past, current, and future fishing practices. Despite large differences in estimates of the status of red snapper stocks in the U.S. GOM and U.S. south Atlantic, and the management conclusions drawn from these assessments, there are more similarities than differences in the basic data being used to inform assessment models, as well as in the model outcomes concerning the trends in biomass, catch-at-age and stock productivity. There are key differences in some of these data, and in how historical landings and uncertainty are handled in the assessment process, that result in large differences between the two management regions in beliefs about current and future productivity of red snapper stocks, and regulatory measures necessary for reaching management goals.

Cowan (2606) noted that both the GOM and the U.S. south Atlantic red snapper have recently been determined to be overfished relative to a risk-averse biomass benchmark and to be experiencing overfishing (Fs are too high to ensure stock recovery), except perhaps in the western GOM, where overfishing may no longer be occurring (2848). In contrast many fishers believe that numbers of red snapper in the GOM are high, perhaps historically so, and the stock is no longer overfished (2857). Fishermen in the U.S. south Atlantic also dispute the stock assessments, believing that red snapper have been increasing in abundance, as indicated by increasing catch rates (2684).

Differences in perception about the stock status of red snapper, is not new, and red snapper management has been controversial for more than 20 years (2606, 2608). The main factors in the assessments that are responsible for recent low recommended fishing levels are highly truncated age distributions in both the GOM and the U.S. south Atlantic and high fishing mortalities (Fs) on ages 2 through 8 by the directed fisheries (2608). These are problematic because long-lived red snapper do not reach full reproductive potential until ages 14-15, and high fishing mortalities earlier in life may not result in sufficient escapement to older ages to allow recovery of the spawning biomass.

nodes.title: South Atlantic
nodes.body:
The rapid decline of commercial and recreational landings of red snapper off the U.S. south Atlantic in the early 1980’s prompted the South Atlantic Fisheries Management Council to establish a minimum size of 12 inches and the bag limit of 10 red snapper per day in 1983 (2828). In 1991, with landings of red snapper still declining, the SAFMC increased the minimum size to 20 inches and the snapper bag limit was reduced from 10 fish to only two red snappers per day (2830).

The first formal assessment of red snapper in the U.S. south Atlantic was conducted by Manooch et al. (2712, 2713). In that assessment, two age-structured models were used: an un-calibrated separable VPA and FADAPT. The results from FADAPT were downplayed because the model was calibrated to an abundance index derived from MARMAP chevron trap data, which had very low sample sizes. Manooch et al. (2713) concluded that “the status is less than desirable, but does appear to be responsive to recent management actions.” They found that the fishing mortality rate (F) should be reduced by 33% to 68%, depending on the natural mortality rate and desired spawingin potential ratio (SPR). Prior to publication (2713), a report of that assessment was submitted to the SAFMC (2712). After publication, the results were revisited by Potts and Brennan (2803) in a trends report, also prepared for the SAFMC. Potts and Brennan (2803) repeated the findings of Manooch et al. (2713), but suggested a broader range of reduction in F, from 30% to 80%.

nodes.title: From Commercial Fisheries Value
nodes.body:
Commercial fishermen along the east coast of Florida dominated the commercial red snapper fishery in the U.S. south Atlantic until the mid-1970s (2832). By the late 1970s, the fishery had expanded into Georgia, South Carolina and North Carolina, and it declined in Florida. In 1993-2007, logbook-reported commercial landings of red snapper ranged from 202,000 pounds (whole weight) worth approximately $544,000 in current year dollars in 2001 to 81,000 pounds worth $263,000 in 2006. Dockside revenue and pounds landed fluctuate in the same direction, which suggests that ex-vessel demand is price elastic. The policy implication is that regulations that reduce industry landings in the short-term are expected to reduce dockside revenue in the short-term. Conversely, dockside revenue is expected to increase over time if regulations successfully increase biomass and landings. Average annual dockside prices for red snapper increased steadily in current year dollars. However, prices in 2007 dollars declined through 2002 before increasing in 2006 and 2007.

According to the NMFS logbook database, on average in 2003-2007, 1,385 trips a year landed 121,000 pounds of red snapper worth $388,000 in 2007 dollars, and 2.0 million pounds of other species worth $4.5 million on trips with at least one pound of red snapper (2832). Clearly, red snapper was not the primary revenue species on most of these trips. Boat revenue for all species and trips came to $9.8 million, with 4% for red snapper. Among the 220 boats that landed at least one pound of red snapper, 102 boats landed less than 100 pounds of red snapper per year, 84 boats landed 101-1000 pounds, and 34 boats landed more than 1000 pounds.

Red snapper was the primary source of trip revenue on an average of 163 trips per year, 12% of the trips on which it was landed (2832). These trips accounted for approximately 31% ofthe total commercial harvest, with an annual average of 38,000 pounds of red snapper worth $125,000 in 2007 dollars, and 49,000 pounds of other species worth $103,000. On the 1,222 trips wherein red snapper was a lesser source of trip revenue, it accounted for an annual average of 82,000 pounds of red snapper ($263,000 in 2007 dollars) and 1.9 million pounds of other species ($4.4 million in 2007 dollars). Red snapper is part of the mid-shelf snapper grouper complex that includes scamp, gag, vermilion snapper, red porgy, gray triggerfish, and red grouper, among other species. Red snapper is most commonly caught on trips with vermilion snapper, gag or scamp as the primary revenue species on the trip. Red snapper is landed mostly in South Carolina, Georgia and northeast Florida, and central-southeast Florida and it is caught mostly with vertical lines.

nodes.title: From Recreational Value
nodes.body:
Gillig et al. (2653) stated they had estimated the recreational value of red snapper fishing in the Gulf of Mexico. The paper discusses the statistical approaches taken, but no quantitative estimates for the fishery were presented. A second study by Gillig et al (2956) extended the joint estimation of revealed and stated preference data literature by accounting for truncation in the revealed preference data. The analytical model and estimation procedure was used to estimate the value of recreational red snapper fishing in the GOM. Employing the contigent valuation method (CVM) and the truncated travel cost method (TCM) individually, the joint CVM and truncated TCM model was also adapted. The three different model specifications yielded a wide range of welfare estimates. The CVM yielded the highest willingness-to-pay (WTP) of $85.70 per fish, whereas the truncated TCM yielded the lowest WTP ($9.85). The WTP of the joint model fell in between ($14.50).

Estimates of the economic value of a day of saltwater recreational fishing in the U.S. south Atlantic indicate that the mean value of access per marine recreational fishing trip is $109.31 for the South Atlantic (2680). While this estimate is not specific to snapper grouper fishing trips, it may shed light on the magnitude of an angler’s willingness to pay for this type of recreational experience.

Willingness to pay for an incremental increase in catch and keep rates per trip was also estimated to be $3.01 for bottom fish species by Haab et al. (2680). Whitehead and Haab (2951) estimated the marginal willingness to pay to avoid a one fish red snapper bag limit decrease to be $1.06 to $2.20. Finally, Haab et al. (2680) provided a compensating variation (the amount of money a person would have to receive to be no worse off after a reduction of the bag limit) estimate of $2.49 per fish when calculated across all private boat anglers that targeted snapper grouper species in the South Atlantic.

In their study of the North Carolina for-hire fishery, Dumas et al. (2621) estimated several measures of consumer surplus (CS) for anglers fishing through the for-hire mode. Anglers were distinguished as to whether fishing was their primary or secondary purpose for taking the trip to the coasts. An additional snapper-grouper caught and kept would generate consumer surplus of $93.51 per trip, for primary purpose anglers, and $60.79 per trip for secondary purpose anglers. Consumer surplus per site per trip for primary purpose anglers ranged from $4.88 to $27.03 in charter trips taken in Federal waters, or from $0.35 to $9.55 in charter trips taken in state waters. The corresponding range of values for secondary purpose anglers were $0.24 to $16.62 for charter trips in Federal waters, or $0.12 to $16.54 for charter trips in state waters. On headboat trips in both state and Federal waters, consumer surplus per site per trip ranged from $0.59 to $4.12 for primary purpose anglers, and from $0.48 to $4.76 for secondary purpose anglers. Consumer surplus trip for the opportunity to take a for-hire fishing trip was estimated at $624.02 per angler per trip on charterboats and $101.64 per anger per trip on headboats.

In addition to the above economic values, there are estimates of the economic value of a red snapper and a red snapper trip in the GOM provided by NMFS (2764). Although these values are derived for the GOM recreational fishery, they can be used as proxy values for the South Atlantic fishery. It is noted, however, that red snapper is a significantly more important recreational target fishery in the GOM than in the South Atlantic. As a result, the estimates of economic value may overstate the true values for the south Atlantic. The estimated CS to a recreational angler of one red snapper is $6.04, while the estimated CS of a red snapper fishing trip is $53.53. These values were used to estimate the impacts of the red snapper interim rule in the South Atlantic (2832). Extrapolations were made to estimate the respective values of the various recreational fisheries from North Carolina to Florida. While the total value for the snapper-grouper fisheries is in the millions of dollars, the value of the recreational fisheries for red snapper was not presented; since it was not separated from the other species of reef fish.

nodes.title: STOCK ENHANCEMENT
nodes.body:
Induced Breeding: Red snapper were spawned in captivity when held at temperatures and photoperiods which approximated conditions in the Texas Gulf of Mexico region (2553). Multiple spawns were observed in May and June 1978. Minton et al (2728) induced red snapper to ovulate following injections of human chorionic gonadotropin (HCG). Females were injected initially with 1.1 IU/g body weight. When subsequent injections were necessary, 0.55 IU/g of body weight was used. Ovulation occurred between 42 and 56 hr following injection. Eggs were wet stripped and fertilized simultaneously with sperm from two males. Initial mitosis was detected 30 min post fertilization. Hatching occurred in 20 hr at 27oC. Further details concerning induced spawning are given by Collins et al. (2601) and Bourque (2573).

Phelps et al. (2791) provides a good review and new information concerning spawning of red snapper in response to hormonal induction in a hatchery setting. When, female red snapper collected from off Alabama in the GOM were injected with HCG, 56% of the females ovulated. Fecundity (ovulated floating eggs) was noted to vary; for 60 spawns it averaged 197,212 eggs/kg female. Percentage hatch averaged 42.1%. Wild-caught and adult red snapper can be held in confinement and natural spawning obtained when temperature and photoperiod are controlled. Adult red snapper held in tanks (8-10 fish per tank), where temperature and photoperiod were adjusted, spawned naturally 63 times over a 105-day period, with a mean egg production per tank of 4.2 million eggs. Mean fertilization rate, hatch rate, and survival at 36-40 hours post-hatching were 90.5%, 83%, and 49%. Natural spawns produce better quality seed, but the occurrence of fertilized spawns was unpredictable. Hormone-induced spawns are easier to schedule but egg quality can be variable. Further information on induced spawning of red snapper can be found in theses by Bootes (2568), Bourque (2571), Bueno (2578), and Papanikos (2768), and from meeting abstracts (2792, 2572, 2701, 2790).

Rearing: The diet of juvenile red snapper in the wild has been fairly well documented (2585, 2574, 2639, 2734, Lee 1998) and consists of prey items with high levels of protein and moderate levels of lipids. Nutritional data regarding levels of crude protein and lipid necessary to promote growth in Lutjanidae are sparse (2727). Some information exists for red snapper with the publications by Wakeman et al. (2899) and Marnell (2715).

Many marine fish can be held in captivity and will spawn naturally when given a proper environment and an appropriate diet. Papanikos et al. (2769) compared egg and larval quality of red snapper from natural spawns of domesticated brooders with hormone-induced spawns of wild fish. Eggs and larvae from natural spawns were more viable in terms of fertilization, hatching, and survival rate. Also, eggs from natural spawns were larger, and eggs and recently hatched larvae had large oil-globules. The findings indicated that natural spawning of red snapper can be a sustainable and reliable source of good quality eggs.

Papanikos et al. (2770) conducted two experiments to evaluate the spontaneous spawning of red snapper under controlled temperature and photoperiods in association with broodstock diets supplemented with oils rich in polyunsaturated fatty acids. In experiment 1, broodstock were fed a standard diet (ST1) and one enriched with menhaden oil (ER1) over a 355-d period. ER1-influenced egg fatty acid profile, however, it did not positively influence egg production. Both diets produced highly viable eggs and larvae but results varied with treatments. In Experiment 2, broodfish were fed either with a standard diet (ST2) or one supplemented with oils (ER 2) rich in docosahexaenoic and arachidonic acid using a 203-d cycle. Both treatments produced eggs but fertilization rates ranged from 0-10%. There was no clear influence of the diets on egg fatty acid profiles. These results indicate that red snapper can spawn spontaneously in tanks under controlled environmental conditions and produce viable eggs and larvae when fed diets based on squid, shrimp, and fish. The fatty acid composition of the diets was reflected in the eggs to some degree, but the oil enrichments did not further enhance the reproductive performance of egg quality under the conditions of this study.

The challenge with red snapper aquaculture has centered around meeting the food requirements for larvae at the time of exogenous feeding (2623). Snapper larvae demand sufficient quantities of small prey organisms at the onset of first-feeding (2702, 2762, 2706, 2816). Copepod nauplii have proved to be an appropriate prey for red snapper larvae (2764, 2705, 2763).

Chigbu et al. (2595) evaluated the relationship between copepod nauplii available per fish on the day of first feeding and survival of larval red snapper. Additionally, they assessed the suitability of various types of containers, from 10 L black plastic containers through 20 L polycarbonate containers filled with 100 liters (L) of seawater, for rearing red snapper larvae. There was a significant positive correlation between prey number per fish on the day of first feeding and survival of red snapper Similarly, larval survival was positively correlated with the number of copepod nauplii.

Rearing studies using 10 L and 20 L black plastic containers resulted in 100% mortality of larvae by day 7 post-hatch (2592). Experiments carried out using polycarbonate containers and 200 L black tubs containing 50 L or 100 L of brown seawater resulted in 0 to 34% larval survival. The number of larvae that survived was significantly higher in polycarbonate containers than in black tubes with 50 or 100 L of water. Differences in larval survival in the culture containers probably resulted from interactions between the amount of light present in the containers and container color that, presumably, affected prey visibility to, and therefore consumption by larval snapper.

In 2004 experiments were conducted to formulate red snapper culture methods using marine primary nursery ponds (2623). Twenty 0.1 ha ponds were prepared with either 250 or 500 kg/ha rice bran organic fertilizer. Two day-old red snapper larvae were stocked in ponds at either 5, 7, or 10 days post-filling (dpf). At the end of 30 d the ponds were harvested. Zooplankton results showed high densities of copepod nauplii (averaging 774.65 ± 962.9 org/L) during the first 5 days following larval stocking in ponds receiving the 250 kg/ha fertilizer rate. These low rate ponds experienced significantly higher densities of nauplii than the 500 kg/ha ponds (p=0.021). A high degree of variation in nauplii abundance was observed between and within ponds during the study period. Average red snapper survival also varied greatly between treatments, ranging from nearly 0% survival in treatment 2 (250 kg/ha and stocked 7 dpf) to 1.07 % in treatment 5 (500 kg/ha, stocked 10 dpf, and continuous aeration). The treatment receiving 250 kg/ha of rice bran and stocked 10 days post-filling resulted in higher snapper survival when compared to the remaining low fertilizer treatments. Following these results recommendations for future research might suggest incorporating continuous aeration with the low rate fertilizer treatment and stocking larvae at 10 dpf. In addition to the pond study a computer model was constructed to predict the best day to stock red snapper determined by copepod nauplii density. The model used a forecasting method incorporating 29 pond parameters and resulted in an adjusted R² of 0.6954. The model was inconsistent at predicting nauplii abundance for 3 out-of-sample pond nauplii counts and therefore was not recommended as an appropriate management design. Alternatively, an empirical approach was evaluated to determine the number of ponds that would be needed to satisfy stocking requirements under conditions of uncertainty. This approach yielded more manageable results.

Williams et al. (2952) described the development of yolk-sac larvae of red snapper from endogenous utilization of nutrient sources to the development of feeding ability. Larvae from several spawns were reared at a salinity of 31 g/L and a temperature of 28oC. Yolk utilization rate, changes in body parameters and the development of morphological characters were observed. Maximum standard length (SL) and body depth were observed concurrently with yolk-sac exhaustion at 56 hours post-fertilization (hpf). A decrease in SL, body width and body depth was observed following yolk-sac exhaustion. Orbit pigmentation, followed by jaw articulation, were observed at 65 hpf. Substantial cranial and body cavity development occurred in the absence of visibly yolk-sac material and less than 2% of the oil globule volume at hatching were observed at the time of development of feeding ability. This indicates an absence of a transitional feeding period and the critical nature of first-feeding in this species within controlled environments.

Ogle and Lotz (2765) developed an experimental-scale rearing system for larval red snapper that combined extensive outdoor production of live-feed zooplankton with intensive larval fish rearing. The salient features of the system are (1) use of size graded copepods as life feed; (2) culture in clear water; (3) three-phase water management consisting of an initial static water phase followed by a volume doubling phase in which water is gradually added and, finally, a recirculation-biofiltration phase; (4) a lowered salinity of 25 g/L water; and (5) an indoor location at constant temperature under artificial light. A total of 19,835 juvenile red snapper were produced from 12 larval rearing tanks in three separate batches with an overall survival of 16.5%. Survival varied from 1% to 31% in individual larval rearing tanks. Water quality variables (oxygen, temperature, salinity, total and un-ionized ammonia, nitrite, nitrate, pH, and alkalinity) were not significantly correlated with larval fish survival. A mean number of 5.36 copepods/mL was added daily to larval tanks during the culture period, with a range of 0.57-23.48 copepods/mL. There was no correlation between mean feed rates and survival in individual tanks. The mean residual copepods per milliliter averaged 2.24, with a range of from 0 to 15.86. There was a significant negative correlation between residual copepod density and survival.

Larval mortality at first feeding remains a fundamental challenge for the culture and artificial propagation of red snapper (Williams et al. 2004). Red snapper show evidence of starvation within hours of the appearance of functional mouth parts. The observed reductions in larval body parameters may be symptomatic of tissue reabsorption, and suggest that red snapper larvae may be more sensitive to starvation than commonly cultured fish species. Further advances in larval rearing protocols are likely to come from an improved understanding of the reproductive life history and the energetic dynamics of the prefeeding stages.

Diet: Miller et al. (2727) formulated twelve diets to contain varying levels of protein and lipid to evaluate their effects on growth and body condition of juvenile and sub-adult red snapper. In trial 1, juvenile red snapper (initial weight 5.9 g) were offered diets with graded levels of dietary protein (32%, 36%, 40%, and 46%) and practical protein to energy ratios. In trial 2, juvenile red snapper (initial weight 8.64 g) were offered isonitrogenous diets (44% protein) containing graded levels of dietary lipid (8%, 10%, 12%, 14%). Sub-adult fish (initial mean weight 151.5 g) were used in trial 3 and maintained on diets similar to trail 1 (32-44% protein). Sub-adult fish (initial mean weight 178.3 g) in trial 4 were offered isonitrogenous diets containing 32% dietary protein and graded levels of dietary lipid (6%, 8%, 10%, 12%). There were no significant differences in growth, feed conversion ratio (FER), or survival of juvenile fish. Juvenile fish offered 32% dietary protein exhibited a significantly greater (P=0.0497) protein conversion efficiency (PCE) than fish offered a diet of 44% dietary protein. Juvenile fish in trial 2 also had significantly higher (P=0.005) intraperitoneal fat ratios (IPFRs) at 14% dietary lipid than fish offered diets containing 8-10 % lipid, and displayed trends towards greater protein as a percent of whole-body composition at 8-10% dietary lipid. Sub-adult snapper in trials 3 and 4 showed no significant differences in growth, FER or survival. However, in trial 4 there was a general trend towards increasing % weight gain (P=0.0615), FER (P=0.0601) and final mean weight (P = 0.0596) with increasing dietary levels of lipid. Fish in trial 4 offered 6% dietary lipid also had significantly lower (P= 0.03439) IPFR and PCE (P= 0.0188) than fish offered 12% dietary lipid. Based on data obtained in these trials, inclusion of dietary protein at levels of 32-36% appears sufficient to support growth. For this level of protein, dietary lipid should be ~ 10% in order to meet the energetic demands of the fish and to spare dietary protein growth.

 Stocking: Pruder et al. (2807) described the U.S. Gulf of Mexico Stock Enhancement five-year program: 1999-2004. They noted that many fisheries in the United States are under stress from overexploitation and/or habitat degradation. In response, Congress mandated the restoration of depleted fisheries, within a given time period. Preliminary estimates indicate that conventional restrictive management protocols alone cannot satisfy these congressional mandates. The tools and options of fishery management need to be expanded to include proactive actions and activities. One such potentially proactive option is stock enhancement. A decision was made to fund a research stock enhancement program to better evaluate its potential value. The U.S. Gulf of Mexico Marine Stock Enhancement Program (USGMSEP) is a multi-institutional, multi-year and multi-million dollar integrated science effort to develop and demonstrate sound and broad-based stock enhancement methods to augment conventional management strategies. The authors identified and characterized the critical components of an integrated, scientifically sound investigation of a highly complex stock enhancement system. It initiates use of a computerized management approach which enhances planning, review, and evaluation of efforts by identifying and tracking critical activities, institutional assignments and responsibilities, developing time line and completion projections, and managing resource allocation.

Blaylock et al. (2566) described the components of the USGMSEP. The program investigated the use of aquaculture technology as an additional tool for the restoration of marine stocks, particularly the red snapper. Molecular genetics, feed production technology, and larval production technology were used to address three critical stock enhancement issues: 1) understanding the nature of the system to be enhanced, 2) producing robust, compatible individuals for release, and 3) critically evaluating the effects of releases. The program developed: 1) microsatellite and mitochondrial DNA markers that allow population analysis, broodstock analysis, and offspring analysis; 2) a method of copepod culture that allows mass production of red snapper; and 3) a manageable repeatable procedure for larval rearing of large numbers of red snapper, a species which heretofore could not be cultured in large numbers.

Stock enhancement has been proposed to facilitate stock recovery for GOM red snapper (2652). While recent advances in red snapper culture have made stock enhancement more feasible (Williams et al. 2004, 2765, 2816, 2791), there are other concerns that need to be addressed. Among these are the potential effects of stocking on genetic diversity of red snapper populations, some of which already may be showing signs of being genetically compromised due to overfishing (2835, 2663). Another concern is whether large-scale stocking efforts are likely to have a measurable positive effect on red snapper Spawning Stock Biomass (SSB) (2733). Clearly, if stock enhancement is pursued further for GOM red snapper, then development of a method to estimate the effect of stocking on red snapper population size will be essential.

Gibson et al. (2652) evaluated otolith chemical signatures as natural tags to distinguish wild from hatchery-produced juvenile red snapper. Otoliths were sampled from 59 hatchery-reared fish and 146 wild fish collected over the continental shelf from northwest Florida to Texas. One sagitta from each fish was cleaned, dissolved in ultrapure nitric acid, and analyzed with a sector field inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry to test for differences in otolith element: Ca ratios (Ba:Ca, Li:Ca, Mg:Ca, Mn:Ca, and Sr:Ca) between wild and hatchery fish. The second sagitta was cleaned, ground to fine powder, and analyzed with stable isotope ratio mass spectrometry to test for differences in delta (δ) values of the stable isotopes 13C and 18O. Significant differences were found in otolith chemical signatures between hatchery and wild juveniles. Jackknifed classification accuracies from linear discriminant function analysis indicated that hatchery fish could be distinguished from wild fish with 100% accuracy based on otolith chemical signatures. Overall results suggest that otolith chemical signatures may be employed as effective natural tags for mass marking of future stockings of red snapper or other marine fishes to estimate the hatchery contribution to wild populations.

A critical component to any stock enhancement program is assessing the effect of stocking on spawning stock biomass (SSB) or fisheries yield. Gibson et al. (2652) concluded that a relatively simple approach to marking hatchery-reared fish could be manipulation of hatchery water chemistry or feeds such that unique chemical signatures are imparted onto otoliths of hatchery-reared fish. In the case of δ13C values, this could be accomplished simply by including terrestrial plant material, with its lower δ13C values, in hatchery feeds.

Disease Control: Huff and Burns (2692) described hypersaline and chemical control methods to treat the marine parasite Cryptocaryon irritans infecting red snapper under culture conditions. Masson et al. (2716) studied the susceptibility of juvenile spotted seatrout (Cynoscion nebulosus) and juvenile red snapper to the parasitic dinoflagellate Amyloodinium ocellatum, which infects warm-water marine and estuarine fishes and causes mortality in aquaculture. There was no significant difference in dinospore infecton rates or dinospore lethal doses between spotted seatrout and red snapper; however trophonts of Amyloodinium remained attached longer and attained a larger size in red snapper than in spotted seatrout.

nodes.title: Stock Assessments
nodes.body:
Some definitions of acronyms being used associated with Magnuson-Stevens Act (MSRA) provisions, Annual Catch Limits, and National Standard Guidelines are herein presented (2613). The biological reference points are based on Maximum Sustainable Yield (MSY). The MSY fishing mortality rate (Fmsy) is the fishing mortality rate, that if applied in the long term, would result in MSY. The MSY stock size (Bmsy) means the long-term average size of the stock or stock complex, measured in terms of spawning biomass or other appropriate measure of the stock’s reproductive potential that would be achieved by fishing at Fmsy. Status determination criteria (SDC) mean the quantifiable factors, maximum fishing mortality threshold (MFMT), overfishing limit (OFL), and minimum stock size threshold (MSST), or their proxies that are used to determine if overfishing has occurred, or if the stock complex is overfished. The Magnusen-Stevens Act (section 3(34)) defines “overfishing” and “overfished” to mean a rate or level of fishing mortality that jeopardizes the capacity of a fishery to produce the MSY on a continuing basis. To avoid confusion, “overfished” relates to a biomass of a stock or a stock complex, and “overfishing” pertains to a rate or level of removal of fish from a stock or a stock complex.

Maximum fishing mortality threshold means the level of fishing mortality (F), on an annual basis above which overfishing is occurring (2613). The MFMT or a reasonable proxy may be expressed as a single number (a fishing mortality rate or F value), or as a function of spawning biomass or other measure of reproductive potential. Overfishing limit means the annual amount of catch that corresponds to the estimate of MFMT applied to a stock or stock complex’s abundance and is expressed in terms of numbers or weight of fish. The OFL is an estimate of the catch level above with overfishing is occurring. A stock or stock complex is considered “overfished” when its biomass has declined below a level that jeopardizes the capacity of the stock or stock complex to produce MSY on a continuing basis. Minimum stock size threshold means the level of biomass below which the stock or stock complex is considered to be overfished.

The F/Fmsy or SSB/SSBmsy ratios were used in SEDAR15 (2849) and SEDAR24 (2852) to simplify the presentation for council members and are believed to be more robust than the actual numbers (2953). If the F/Fmsy is greater than 1.0 then the fishery is overfishing, and similarly, if SSB/SSBmsy is less than MSST (usually 1- M) then the stock is overfished. Since, these ratios are new, they were not used for SEDAR7 (2847).

Assessment: SEDAR7
The first SEDAR stock assessment for red snapper in the GOM was conducted using the CATCHEM catch-at-age model (2847). A total of 18,859 age determinations from otloliths were used for creation of von Bertalanaffy growth equations. Briefly, the CATCHEM algorithm was applied to information on red snapper populations in U.S.waters during the years from 1872 to 2008. Five fisheries were designated for each of two regions (east and west of the Mississippi River): handline, longline, recreational, closed season discards and shrimp bycatch. Three four-month seasons were modeled, starting in January. Spawning was assumed to occur during the second season. Spawning and recruitment were modeled separately for each region, essentially assuming that the eastern and western populations are relatively independent. Thirty one age classes were modeled starting with age 0, with the number of age 0 fish being computed as lognormal (bias-corrected) deviations from a Beverton and Holt function of the spawn produced during that year.

The minimum size limits for red snapper in the GOM have varied over time between 13 and 18 inches (2691). The current minimimun size limits are recreational = 16 inches and commercial = 13 inches (effective 2/28/08). Lower size limits in the GOM in comparison to the South Atlantic have allowed the fisheries to retain more fish and minimize discarding.

Age-specific vulnerability coefficients were estimated for each fleet, but were assumed to be relatively unchanged through time. However, the truncating effect of minimum size limits on the size distribution of the landings was modeled directly based on the growth parameters used in SEDAR 7. Moreover, the relative effort of each fleet was allowed to vary by year essentially as a free parameter. Hence, the effective selectivity across the mix of fleets (i.e. the fishery as a whole) varied noticeably through the years. The vulnerability coefficients for the fishery independent video surveys were fixed to 0 for ages 0-1 and 1.0 for ages 2 and older. The larval indices were taken as indicators of spawner abundance, so fecundity at age vector was used in place of vulnerability coefficients.

A benchmark assessment SEDAR7 Update was conducted in 2009 (2848). Most of the input criteria were kept the same as the original SEDAR7 (2947) but additional landings and catch rates were updated to 2008. The benchmark criteria listed below were taken from the SEDAR7 Update (2848).

The GOM red snapper spawning stock biomass (SSB) currently is estimated to be only a fraction of historical levels, but recruitment is predicted to have increased in recent years, though historical data prior to the mid-1980’s are sparse especially before the 1950s (2848, 2606). Higher recruitment since 1971 has caused some to speculate that productivity of red snapper in the GOM is increasing. Reduction in biomass in the GOM is believed to be due to overexploitation. One additional factor promoting the assumption that productivity and stock size of red snapper in the GOM have increased in recent years is that red snapper are reappearing in the eastern GOM in places from which they had been extirpated by overexploitation before and during the late 1980s and early 1990s (2606). But an increase in range does not necessarily indicate an increase in productivity of the stock. Assessment outcomes (2848) still show that fishing mortality in the eastern GOM is high and likely not sustainable, and SSB there is still low.

In the GOM, strong year-classes of red snapper were produced in 1989, 1996, 1999, and most recently the period 2004-2006 (2606). The correlation between age-0 and age-1 red snapper is relatively poor, a result long thought attributable to high vulnerability of age-1 red snapper to capture by shrimp trawlers as bycatch. However, shrimp fishing effort has declined steadily since 2002. The reduction in bycatch has made it feasible to separate mortality due to shrimp bycatch from other sources of mortality such as predation, and empirical estimates of natural mortality rates (M) are high (0.54 to >2.0 per year; 2916, 2939, 2848). These empirical estimates of non-bycatch-related mortality rates of age-0 and age-1 red snapper imply that shrimp trawl bycatch may not have been played as large a role in red snapper population regulation as once thought and that high and variable natural mortality rates of age-0s may be responsible for the lack of correlation (2608).

The selectivity relationship with age for red snapper from all fisheries in the GOM when averaged over all gears and sectors, is a dome-shaped function (2848). Age-0 and age-1 fish are vulnerable mostly as bycatch in the shrimp fishery. Ages 2 to 8 are fully vulnerable to the directed fisheries (2606). Older red snapper (10 years and older) are less than fully (50% or less) vulnerable to the fishery in the CATCHEM fishery model because of their tendency in nature to move off structured habitat. The decrease in selectivity (vulnerability) of larger, older females in the GOM assessment model affects estimates of stock productivity because of the large contribution that older females make to SSB and egg production.

Required SFA and MSRA evaluations for Gulf of Mexico red snapper were presented. Mortality rate criteria are reported relative to Fcurrent (i.e., geometric mean F for 2006-2008). Biomass criteria are reported in terms of relative spawning potential (millions). Yields are reported in millions of pounds whole weight. Reported values come from AS3 run with shrimp effort rebuild scenario, which was accepted by the Statistical Science Committee (SSC) for Overfishing Limit (OFL) determination.

The spawning stock estimates, S, are not the actual number of eggs produced by the population, but should be interpreted as the effective number of fully-productive spawners, i.e. the number of eggs produced by the spawning population relative to the number that would have been produced if all of the spawners were 30 years old.

Assessment: SEDAR15
The SEDAR15 stock assessment for red snapper in the U.S. south Atlantic applied a statistical catch-age model (BAM) using data from 1945 to 2006 (2849, 2850).
The 2008 assessment relied on fishermen’s logbooks for records of what was caught at various depths (2849). The logbook entries were not uniform or consistent, leaving stock assessment scientists to conclude that the commercial fishermen were fishing in deeper waters (2789). The deeper red snapper are caught, the more likely they will die from internal injuries due to the pressure change or hook injuries.

Because the spawner-recruit parameter of steepness was not estimable (hit its upper bound), the SEDAR review panel recommended using proxies for Maximum Sustainable Yield (MSY) related benchmarks based on 40% Spawning Potential Ratio (SPR). Relative to those benchmarks, the assessment found that since the 1960s, overfishing had been occurring and the stock had been overfished. In the terminal year, the assessment estimated the fishing mortality ratio F2006/F40%=7.7 and the Spawning Stock Biomass ratio SSB2006/SSBF40%=0.03. Although quantitative results varied, these qualitative results of overfishing a depleted stock were consistent across all catch-age model configurations examined during and after the assessment process (~40 sensitivity runs), as well as with an alternative model formulation (surplus-production model). Uncertainty was evaluated with a Monte Carlo Bootstrap approach (MCB) applied to the model inputs.

The stock assessment found that red snapper in the south Atlantic was overfished and undergoing overfishing (2849). The catch-at-age of red snapper was highly truncated, with fewer fish of age 8 to 10 and older being captured than in past years. The mean selectivity function makes almost all ages of red snapper after age-3 equally vulnerable to fishing (flat-topped selectivity at age), with no significant decrease on assessment outcomes for red snapper older than age 10 (Figure 9, 2606). This difference with the GOM assessment (2848) has a big impact on assessment outcomes because of obvious implications concerning reproductive potential and SSB in the south Atlantic (2606). The shape of this function in the south Atlantic implies that banning the longline fishery in 1992 did not result in similar protection for older fishes. It is evident that catches at size and age are different in the GOM and south Atlantic. One can only speculate about the reasons for that difference. What is clear, however, is that the current biomass-at-age of south Atlantic red snapper is more truncated compared to the GOM, and that this difference is one of the most important factors driving the call for closure of the south Atlantic to fishing for red snapper and, by association, other species of reef fishes because of the potential for red snapper bycatch in other fisheries.
Because longline catches from the south Atlantic were not used in the SEDAR15 (2849) assessment, it is impossible to speculate about the impacts these data would have on assessment outcomes (2606). Fishers contend that older, larger red snapper do escape to deeper, difficult to fish waters on the Blake Plateau of the south Atlantic. But, a recently conducted fishery-independent survey conducted by NOAA Fisheries failed to locate a large cryptic biomass of red snapper in the region.

The relative lack of management, and its consequences, in the U.S. south Atlantic became very evident in the assessment (2849), because the red snapper had previously been assessed only once (2713) prior to 2008 (2606). When long time periods pass between management actions without assessment of the effects, surprises can and do occur. This was abundantly clear in SEDAR15 and the update documents. During the assessment workshop phase, the panel was provided with a new set of historical landings from 1945 to 1980 collected by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS) that were deemed to be trustworthy by NOAA Fisheries and the SEDAR workshop panel. After much discourse, the panel concluded that the decline was real and more likely attributable to high fishing mortalities (Fs) prior to and after 1965, rather than to a significant reduction in stock productivity and recruitment. Matching the high rate of decline after 1965 caused the model to generate the selectivity pattern and worrisome biological benchmarks that are reflected in the SEDAR15 findings. Simply put, the model assumed that the trends in catches were real and then tried to determine the most parsimonious explanation for changes in trends. The decision to include the old landings data collected by the USFWS is without question, the most controversial issue surrounding SEDAR15-these data drastically changed the historical perspective of the south Atlantic red snapper stock along with current estimates of stock status, which now must be considered relative to the Magnuson-Stevens Reauthorization Act (MSRA) passed by the U.S. Congress in 2006. This decision, and all that it entails, is the issue that has driven the call for closure by fisheries management and governance (2606).

A fisheries scientist representing the Southeastern Fisheries Association contested the SEDAR15 stock assessment findings (2684). Hester noted that the Recreational Working Group had dismissed landings estimates taken from USFWS Salt-Water Angling reports as being unreliable, but that the SEDAR15 Assessment Panel decided to use them. Therefore, recreational landings were interpolated between zero in 1946 to 1981 with intermediate landings estimates used for 1960, 1965, and 1970. This created a set of landings data from 1946 to 1981 when data were actually only available for three years. Deciding to use the USFWS data caused a major problem. The total weight was apportioned into catch in number using the recreational selectivity graph. Hester noted that there was a discrepancy in mean weights derived from the flat-topped selectivity graph and mean weights computed in a USFWS report. In 1965 and 1970, the average weights for red snapper were a bit over three pounds. Given the small size of the fish, the large number caught and the disproportionate size of the recreational take versus commercial landings, one expects catch-at-age to heavily favor fish younger than three years old. In reality, the distribution from the catch-age-age model appears to include a disproportionate number of older fish. This is the result of the selectivity pattern, which, for recreational catch, is flat. Hester stated that in order to have the average age of the fish to be about 3 lb and still have a large, lightly exploited biomass, as was likely in the early years at least, the selectivity graph should be dome-shaped. The result is that the model was fooled into assigning a high rate of fishing mortality on the older fish in these early years when in reality the USFWS low average weights were evidence that the higher catch rates were on young fish, and the spectacular decline in biomass from nearly 30,000 MT in 1945 to the low levels estimate after 1980 may be the result of using an incorrect selectivity at age (partial recruitment) curve.

Hester (2684) suggested that one change in regulations that might improve the economics of the fisheries, and perhaps improve the stock status, would be to remove all size restrictions and require that every red snapper that is caught be retained. This would stop the odious practice of regulatory discards and move the discard mortality into the fishing mortality column where at least the yield would be utilizable in sales or personal consumption and recreational experience.

Assessment: SEDAR24
A more recent stock assessment for the south Atlantic was conducted to address some of the issues generated by SEDAR15 (2852). The BAM catch-at-age model was run forward from 1955 to 2009. The model used 13,000 otoliths to fit a von Bertalannffy growth curve. This included 4,000 more otoliths than used in the SEDAR15 Update (2850). By using the von Bertalanffy growth equation and filling in length frequencies collected in more recent years, the model created frequencies at age and landings at age for the years lacking monitoring data back to 1955. The age studies included red snapper from deeper water (2789).

In SEDAR24 (2852), the commercial fishermen were able to show that they were fishing in shallower water (2685). This agreed with observer data collected on commercial vessels associated with the hook-and-line fishery (2677, 2010). Consequently, the discard mortality for the commercial fishery used in the BAM model was reduced from 90% used with SEDAR15 to 48% used in the SEDAR24 assessment. Recreational discard mortality stayed about the same (40% in SEDAR 15 and 39% in SEDAR24).

The fishermen had complained that red snapper recreational catch numbers before 1976 were unreliable and inflated, making the historical population seem larger and the declines today seem even worse (2789). To come up with a more accurate estimate, the stock assessment scientists agreed to adjust the amount of red snapper caught by recreational fishermen before 1976 to a proportion of the amount of fish caught at that time by commercial fishermen (2852). Historic records of commercial red snapper catch are more extensive and uniform. Whereas, previously the model predicted a precipitous decline in the population abundance of red snapper in the early years (2850); a more gradual decline was predicted from 1955 to 1984 in SEDAR24 (2852).

The estimated time series of the red snapper stock status (SSB/MSST) in the U.S. south Atlantic shows decline until the late 1980s, and then some increase since the mid-1990s (2852). The increase in stock status appears to have been initiated by the 1992 management regulations, and then perhaps reinforced by strong recruitment events. Base-run estimates of spawning biomass have remained below MSST throughout most of the time series. Current stock status was estimated in the base run to be SSB2009/MSST = 0.09. Uncertainty from the MCB analysis suggests that the estimate of overfished status (i.e., SSB < MSST) is robust. The age structure estimated by the base run shows fewer older fish than the (equilibrium) age structure expected at MSY. However, in the terminal year (2009), ages 3 and 4 approach the MSY age structure as a result of recent strong year classes. The estimated time series of F /FMSY suggests that overfishing has been occurring throughout most of the assessment period. Current fishery status in the terminal year, with current F represented by the geometric mean from 2007–2009, is estimated by the base run to be F2007−2009/FMSY = 4.12. This estimate indicates current overfishing and appears robust across Monte Carlo Based trials. It might, however, be subject to some retrospective error.

Surplus Production model (ASPIC)

Surplus production models (ASPIC) were developed for both SEDAR 15 and SEDAR 24. These are simpler models because they only use annual catches and either effort or indices. The F/Fmsy values from ASPIC were at a lower scale compared to BAM, indicating a lower level of over-fishing. The values of B/Bmsy from ASPIC were below 1.0 over the entire assessment time frame (1955-2009), whereas BAM indicated biomass above Bmsy prior to 1970. BAM also indicated that current (2009) biomass is much less than Bmsy (i.e., 10%), whereas ASPIC is somewhat more optimistic (B2009/Bmsy = 0.39; B2010/Bmsy = 0.25). ASPIC is run from January 1, so the 2009 and 2010 biomass ratios bracket the BAM estimate, which is computed at the time of peak spawning (mid-year). The differences between BAM and ASPIC results are partially related to differences in the catch and effort time-series used by ASPIC, and the catch age time series inferred by BAM. ASPIC is a more limited stand-alone assessment model for red snapper because it does not use available age and length data.

nodes.title: Management Regulations
nodes.body:
Assessments conducted in 1988 and in1990, in the U.S. south Atlantic, indicated red snapper was experiencing overfishing (2955, 2954). In 1990, scientists recommended size limits for red snapper to achieve reductions necessary to end overfishing. In response, the Council developed Amendment 4 to the Fishery Management Plan for the Snapper Grouper Fishery of the South Atlantic Region. In January 1992, new regulations for red snapper established a 20 inch total length minimum size limit and an aggregate bag limit of 10 snapper (excluding vermilion snapper) with no more than 2 red snapper included in the aggregate bag limit. These regulations were determined to be sufficient to end overfishing based on the science available at the time.

In 1997, a new red snapper stock assessment was conducted by the NOAA Fisheries Service using landings data from 1986 to 1996 (2712). The assessment estimated red snapper reached a maximum age of 25 and noted that few fish over the age of 12 were landed. The assessment concluded that the red snapper stock was in a “transitional” condition. “The status of the stock is less than desirable, but does appear to be responding for the better to something, possibly management, in the most recent years.” The Council did not implement any changes to red snapper management at the time based on the assessment conclusions.

The SEDAR15 stock assessment for red snapper in the U.S. south Atlantic found that the stock was overfished and undergoing overfishing (2850). Likewise with SEDAR24, despite changes and the addition of more up-to-date data, assessment scientists still concluded that red snapper in the U.S south Atlantic were seriously overfished and undergoing overfishing (2852). The red snapper fishery in the south Atlantic was closed January 4, 2010. Members of the SAFMC, in a 9-4 vote, approved Amendment 17A to the Snapper Grouper Fishery Management Plan to end overfishing of red snapper and rebuild the South Atlantic stock of red snapper during its June 2010 meeting in Orlando (2832). The amendment was designed to meet the Congressional mandates of the MSRA.

Management measures that were considered by the SAFMC through Amendment 17A included: 1) a continuation of the closure of the red snapper fishery; 2) a new area closure off of northeastern Florida and southern Georgia, where fishing for all snapper grouper species in water depths of 98-240 feet would be prohibited (with the exception of spearfishing and use of black sea bass pots); 3) a requirement for the use non-stainless steel circle hooks when fishing for snapper grouper species north of 28 degrees N. latitude; and 4) the development of a fishery-independent monitoring program to help track the rebuilding and recovery of red snapper (2832).

In addition to the red snapper closure, the area closure was considered to be necessary to reduce harvest of red snapper by 76%, including the estimated number of fish that die even when released (2832). The area closure was a highly controversial issue, and the Council discussed its size and configuration in an effort to meet the mandates of the Act and minimize negative economic and social impacts. The Council reduced the size of the area, eliminating more than 1200 square miles off the coast of Georgia, after modifying the biological parameters and considering other variables such as enforcement compliance and effort shifts in the fishery. Eventually, the SAFMC decided to drop the area closure but decided to retain the closure of the red snapper fishery.
During a June 2012 meeting in Orlando, the SAFMC requested an emergency rule to provide recreational and commercial fishermen with the opportunity to harvest a limited number of red snapper during the fall of 2012 (SAFMC News Release June 18, 2012). The Council determined that 13,067 red snapper could be harvested after reviewing the latest estimates of total removals of red snapper (dead discards). The emergency rule recommended allows a total of 9,399 fish to be caught by recreational fishermen during three-day weekend openings, and 3,668 fish or 20,818 pounds (gutted weight) to be landed by the commercial fishery. The commercial fishery would open in seven-day “mini-season” increments subject to the quota, with a limit of 50 pounds per trip and no size limits. The current allocation for the red snapper fishery is 72% recreational and 28% commercial.

nodes.title: ECOLOGICAL INTERACTIONS
nodes.body:
Competition: The grey snapper (Lutjanus griseus) probably competitively excludes juvenile red snapper from inshore waters in some localities (2860).

Predation: Sharks sometimes strike at fish being brought up by hook and line (2574).

Parasites/Diseases: Parasitic leeches have been found attached to the gills of red snapper (2922).

Perturbations No information found.

Climate- No information found.

nodes.title: HUMAN IMPACTS
nodes.body:
Oil Spills: Red snapper in an offshore oilfield were not contaminated with petroleum hydrocarbons, although 13 other species of fish were contaminated (2726). No evidence of toxic effects was found in testes of five red snapper from oilfields in the Gulf (2843).

Contaminants: Concentrations of chlorinated hydrocarbons were lower in flesh samples of red snapper than in samples of species with a natural oil content (3% of oil), though contaminant levels in this group were low (2875). Wet snapper fillets had an average of 0.039 ppm of DDT and metabolites; the U.S. legal maximum is 5 ppm (2875). The same fillets had 0.121 ppm of PCB’s; the U.S. legal limit is 3 ppm. Only one of nine samples of red snapper had detectable levels of the pesticides dieldrinand endrin.

nodes.title: Entrainment/Impingement/Eutrophication
nodes.body: Pollutant Toxicity: 2916 studied the effects of trawling and habitat on mercury concentration in juvenile snapper from the northern GOM. They evaluated mercury (Hg) contamination in juvenile snapper (<250 mm TL) as an indicator of mercury pollution on the northern GOM continental shelf. The examined the effects of fish size, commercial shrimp trawling, and habitat type on total Hg concentrations and nitrogen isotope ratios (δ15N; a proxy for trophic position) in red snapper. Red snapper Hg concentrations and δ15N values were positively and significantly correlated with fish size. In addition, red snapper collected over trawled habitats had significantly higher Hg concentrations and δ15N values than did red snapper collected from similar, non-trawled habitats. Red snapper also exhibited habitat-specific differences in Hg concentrations and δ15N values, but differences were size depedent and generally small. The study suggests that the Hg concentrations of juvenile red snapper in the northern GOM are elevated in areas where commercial shrimp trawling occurs, possibly due to increases in both red snapper trophic position and bioavailable Hg in trawled areas. Additional studies are needed to determine whether Hg concentrations are elevated in fish from trawled areas in other marine ecosystems.

sections.heading: HEADER
sections.content:
Title: Species Profile Red Snapper (Lutjanus campechanus)
Revisions and Updates
8-28-2012. Peter J. Rubec; Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission, Fish and Wildlife Research Institute
Ecospecies Code: 168853

sections.heading: Summary/Abstract
sections.content:
To further enhance the information needed to support Essential Fish Habitat (EFH) and the Fisheries Ecosystem Plan (FEP), the SAFMC contracted the Florida Fish and Wildlife Research Institute (FWC-FWRI) in 2012 to create a database called Ecospecies (2948, 2940). Ecospecies builds on an earlier database created by the FWC-FWRI called the Florida Estuarine Living Marine Resources (FLELMR) system (2947). FLELMR was created in collaboration with the NOAA/NOS Strategic Environmental Assessments Division as a statewide application of NOAA’s Estuarine Living Marine Resources (ELMR) system. FLELMR has comprehensive species life history (SLH) profiles that summarize information from both primary and secondary (gray) literature. In addition to fish-habitat information, it includes information about population status and stock assessments for species that were not part of the ELMR SLH profiles (2946). FWC-FWRI has created a web-enabled Ecospecies database that includes SLH profiles organized by the FLELMR SLH outline.

Major components of the Red Snapper (Lutjanus campechanus) species life history (SLH) include the following: Taxonomy, Geographic Range, Benthic Habitat, Water Column Habitat, Artificial Reefs, Shrimp Trawl Bycatch, Food Habits, Reproduction, Growth, Value and Status, Stock Enhancement, Population, Management Regulations, Ecological Interactions, and Human Impacts. Citations and references are available for each entry in the Ecospecies database. Almost everything published concerning red snapper is reviewed in the present SLH profile.

Fishermen will be interested in sections that indicate where fish might be located, both for fishing and for nursery areas. Scientists can use the basic information and the citations to locate more in-depth data in a particular area. Managers can have rapid access to concise summaries, as well as the ability to correlate proposed actions with species likely to be affected by those actions. Short summary and overview information is provided for more casual readers.

sections.heading: TAXONOMY
sections.content:
Scientific Name: Lutjanus campechanus (2794)
Subspecific names: None
Synonyms: Mesoprion campechanus (2794), Lutjanus campechianus (2796), Lutjanus blackfordii (2668), Lutianus blackfordii (2688).
 Common Name: Red Snapper
Other Common Names: Sow snapper, rat snapper, (northwest coast of Florida), mule snapper, chicken snapper (northeast coast of Florida), gulf red snapper, American red snapper, northern red snapper, caribbean red snapper, pensacola red snapper, mexican redsnapper, mutton snapper, and bream. Other common names are acara aya (Spanish), boca negra (Papiamento), chillo (Spanish), cora (Papiamento), huachinango del golfo (Spanish), luciano-do-golfo (Portuguese), pargre fine (French), pargo (Papiamento), pargo colorado (Spanish), pargo del golfo (Spanish), pargo guachinango (Spanish), parge real (Spanish), roodvis (Dutch), sarde rouge (French), vermelho (Portuguese), vivaneau campeche (French), vivanot jolle-bleu (French).

sections.heading: Family- Lutjanidae
sections.content:
Taxonomic Characteristics:	 The following descriptions are taken from Rivas (2818), Anderson (2552), and Vergara (2896, 2897). Anderson‘s description includes fish that are Caribbean red snapper, L. purpureus which he considered to be conspecific with L. campechanus. He suggested the name Lutjanus aya for the composite species. However, Rivas (2818) noted that the species name aya (2567) does not apply to a snapper, and that campechanus (2794) is the oldest species name available for the Gulf red snapper. Reviews by Hildebrand and Ginsburg (2688) and Ginsburg (2654) applied the species name campechanus to the Caribbean red snapper. The information presented by Rivas (2818), however, indicates that the name campechanus refers to the Gulf red snapper and that the frequently accepted name blackfordii is synonymous with it. While there are some differences in scale counts above and below the lateral line (2818), it is not clear whether or not the Caribbean red snapper, L. purpureus (2795) is synonymous with the Gulf red snapper (Lutjanus campechanus). Rivas (2818) recognized the Caribbean red snapper as a distinct species (Lutjanus purpureus). Allen (2547) likewise treated L. purpureus and L. campechanus as separate species.

Egg/Parturition: Red snapper eggs average 0.82 mm in diameter (range: 0.77-0.85 mm). The egg is pelagic, spherical, unpigmented, and transparent, and has a single oil globule (2809).

Larva: Newly hatched larvae in the laboratory averaged 2.2 mm in standard length (SL) (2809). Lutjanid larvae collected in the field could be identified only to family by Collins et al. (2599), who also reported that the head was proportionately large and head length was about equal to body depth for red snapper larvae and juveniles 4-22 mm SL.

Identification and description of larval red snapper, Lutjanus campechanus, were based upon the general morphology, meristic characters, head spination, and pigmentation of specimens, ranging from 4.0-7.3 mm SL (2599). These specimens were selected from a total of 226 larval and juvenile L. campechanus which were collected mainly along the Texas coast from 1975 to 1977. Lutjanids <4.0 mm lacked recognizable characters, that are diagnostic at the species level. The smallest larva had not yet developed pelvic fin soft rays but had developed the pelvic spine. The pelvic spine was smooth on the anterior margin on 4.0 and 4.7 mm specimens. Between 4.7 and 4.8 mm this spine developed 30 fine serrations along its anterior margin. All larvae and juveniles 4.8-12.4 mm had these serrations. The number of serrations generally increased with specimen size between 4.8 and 12.4mm. The key to the development of the series was a unique meristic count. A brief comparison was made between L. campechanus and other lutjanid larvae and juveniles.

Bootes (2568) and Drass et al. (2618) described the development of red snapper from hatchery-reared larvae (2568) and specimens collected from the GOM. The larvae were characterized by the following features: a deep body; moderately short gut, 24 myomeres; and elongated dorsal and pelvic fins that form early in development. Specimens (1.9 to 26.1 mm) also showed the presence of weak serrations on pelvic-fin spines, absence of serrations on preopercular or dorsal spines, early forming pigment in dorsal and pelvic fins, and notochord flexion between 3.6 and 5.5 mm. Species-specific differences in number, spacing, and size of melanophores in the posterior ventral series are evident in the youngest larvae of species from the GOM whose development has been described (Ocyurus chrysurus, L. analis, L synagris, L. griseas, L. campechanus, and Rhomboplites aurorubens). Among lutjanid larvae, body depth, pelvic-ray length and serrations on the angle spine of the preopercle can be used in combination with pigmentation to identify larvae to species. Key morphological characters used to identify red snapper larvae are given in Lindeman et al. (2708) and Lyczkowski-Shultz and Hanisko (2710).

Young of Year- Identification and description of young-of-year red snapper were based upon the general morphology, meristic characters, head spination, and pigmentation of specimens ranging in length from 9.5-22.4 mm SL (2599). The specimens were collected mainly along the Texas coast from 1975 to 1977. The 12.4 mm specimen had ~ 60 fine serrations on the anterior margin of each of its pelvic spines. Between 12.4 and 22.4 mm these serrations were lost.

Juvenile- Age-1 red snapper have not been taxonomically described. Juveniles (12.4-22.4 mm SL) described by Collins et al. (2599) were most probably young-of-year (age-0) red snapper.
Presumably, juvenile (age-1) red snapper are similar in appearance to adult red snapper.

Adult: Dorsal fin IX – X spines, usually X, 13-15 soft rays, usually 14; anal fin l11-IV, usually 111, 8-10, usually 9; pectoral fin rays 15-18, usually 17; scales on lateral 1ine usually 45-47; gill rakers on lower limb of anterior arch 9 (excluding rudiments) (2734). Head large; lower jaw projecting slightly beyond upper; snout somewhat pointed; eyes small, contained more than 6.5 times in head length; interorbital region convex in the transverse plane; anchor-shaped patch of strong teeth on roof of mouth, a posterior median extension of the patch moderately developed. Pectoral fins long, reaching to anus when pressed against body; anal fin angulate in specimens longer than 50 mm; margin of caudal fin deeply notched.

Potthoff et al. (2801) described osteological development of red snapper from 129 specimens representing larvae, juvenile, and adult life stages using cleared and stained material. Emphasis was placed upon development of the vertebral column, ribs, fins and their supports, hyoid arch, branchial skeleton, mandibular arch, and opercular series.

Similar Species; Lutjanus vivanus (silk snapper), Lutjanus analis (mutton snapper), Lutjanus purpureus (Caribbean red snapper), Pristipomoides aquilonaris (wenchman), Rhomboplites aurorubens (vermilion snapper).

There is a remarkable similarity in morphology between L. campechanus and L. purpureus, starting by their same red color pattern, and coupled with completely identical (hard and soft dorsal and anal fin rays) and overlapping (hard and soft pectoral fin rays, scale on lateral line, and gillrakers) meristic characters. Based on these characters, Cervigón (2597) raised the hypothesis of the existence of a single species of red snapper for the western Atlantic Ocean distributed as far south as Brazil.

Evolutionary Relationships-Based on morphology, Rivas (2818) and Vergara (2897) hypothesized three phenetic groups within western Atlantic Lutjanus: the griseus group (L. griseus, L. apodus, L. jocu, and L. cyanopterus); the syangris or mahogoni group (L. mahogoni and L. synagis); and the analis or vivanus group (L. analis, L. campechanus, L. purpureus, and L. vivanus). Vegara and Rivas disagreed on the placement of L. buccanella. Vegara placed it in the mahogoni group, whereas Rivas placed it in the analis group. Based on isozyme and morphological data Chow and Walsh (2596) suggested there were only two well-defined groups, griseus and analis, with a third group (syangris) that had affinities to both well-defined groups.

Sarver et al. (2837) studied phylogenetic relationships of western Atlantic red snappers (Family Lutjanidae) based on mitochondrial DNA sequences Two gene regions of the mitochondrial genome were amplified: a 359 bp region of the cyt b gene and a 450 bp region of the 12S gene. The 318 base pairs of the 12S gene contained 47 informative sites. Combined 12S and cyt b sequences resulted in 640 base pairs, 112 of which were informative phylogenetically. Parsimony analysis generated three equally parsimonious trees of 282 steps. The relationship L. griseus (L. jocu, L. apodus) was supported by both bootstrap and decay indices. Moderate support was also indicated for a sister relationship between L. vivanus and L. campechanus, and for L. cyanopterus as the sister group for all other snapper species examined. In addition to analysis of the combined 12S and cyt b sequence, they also analyzed the 12S and cyt b data separately. When analyzed separately, both the 12S and cyt b sequence data indicated the occurrence of a clade containing L. jocu, L. apodus, and L. griseus and a clade containing L. vivanus and L. campechanus. On the other hand, separate analysis of 12S and cyt b differed in the placement of L. cyanopterus and E. oculatus. The authors concluded that additional sequence data will be needed to better resolve relationships among western Atlantic snappers.

A genetics study by Gomez et al. (2667) investigated the degree of similarity and the genetic structure between L. campechanus and L. purpureus. They constructed a common database of D-loop mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) sequences obtained from four populations of L. purpureus from Brazil and L. campechanus from the Atlantic coast of the USA (Florida, Louisiana, and Mississippi). Phylogenetic and population genetic analyses depicted high similarity between L. campechanus and L. purpureus, compatible with the hypothesis of a single species of red snapper for the Western Atlantic Ocean.

Gold et al. (2665) conducted phylogenetic analyses of 20 nominal species of tropical lutjanine snappers (12 from the western Atlantic, one from the eastern Pacific, and seven from the Indo-Pacific). They noted that phylogenetic relationships among western Atlantic lutjanines are not well established, in part because of morphological and behavioral similarities with the group, and in part because of the occurrence of both interspecific and intergeneric hybrids. Unfortunately, they did not include specimens believed to be Lutjanus purpureus. Neither did Sarver et al. (2837). Gold et al. (2665) stated that Gomez et al. (2667) had presented convincing evidence that there is only a single widespread species of red snapper in the western Atlantic (i.e., that L. purpureus is synonymous with L. campechanus). However, they also noted that taxonomic revision of western Atlantic lutjanines appears warrented, and they recommended that the genera Ocyurus and Rhomboplites be subsumed within Lutjanus. Until a taxonomic revision is published, it may be premature to consider L. purpureus as being synonymous with L. campechanus.

Studies to examine genetic population structure within the species Lutjanus campechanus have shown that variation in selectively-neutral genetic markers such as mtDNA and nuclear DNA satellites is low. Thus significant differences among geographic regions in haplotype frequencies have not been found (2590, 2664, 2662, 2660, 1998, 2835, 2836, 2833, 2649, 2663). However, Pruett et al. (2808) reported evidence of evolutionarily recent isolation by distance was apparent in mtDNA haplotype frequencies and Saillant and Gold (2006) reported significant differences in red snapper effective population size among northern Gulf of Mexico (GOM) regions. Therefore, although some selection pressure may exist to maintain mover phenotypes in red snapper population (2637), competing pressures must also exist, else selection likely would have driven red snapper populations to display even greater movement than what has been observed (2778).
The mtDA control regions of red snapper from the GOM (N =140) and Atlantic coast of Florida was sequenced (2649). Intra-sample haplotype and nucleotide diversities ranged from 0.94 to 1.00 and 1.8% to 2.5%, respectively. All population analyses were consistent with the hypothesis that red snapper constitute a single, panmictic population over the sampled range. A ubiquitous, predominant haplotype , shared by 23% of the specimens, appeared to be evolutionarily recent, in contrast to previous findings based on restriction fragment length polymorphism data. Tajima’s D values were suggestive of a recent bottleneck. Mismatch distributions from Gulf samples were smooth and unimodal, characteristic of recent population expansion. However, the Atlantic sample exhibited a comparatively broader, possibly multimodal distribution, suggestive of a more stable population history. Additional control region data may clarify potentially disparate histories of Gulf and Atlantic red snapper.

Saillant et al. (2834) examined temporal and spatial variations of 18 nuclear encoded microsatellites in age-0 red snapper sampled from 2004 and 2005 cohorts in each of five regions in the northern GOM and a mixed-age group off northwest Florida. A significant, positive spatial autocorrelation of microsatellite genotypes among fish sampled within the geographic range 20-100 km was detected. The results demonstrate that spatial genetic structuring among young-of-the-year red snapper occurs at small geographic scales and is consistent with a metapopulation stock-structured model of partially connected populations. This accentuates the importance of maintaining healthy local populations of red snapper in all regions across the northern GOM.

sections.heading: GEOGRAPHIC RANGE
sections.content:
Overall: The Gulf of Mexico including the Campeche area of Yucatan, and the Atlantic Coast as far north as Cape Hatteras, North Carolina; not reported in the Caribbean Sea (2818, 1970; 2083). SEDAR24 (2852) listed the range of L. campechanus as also extending through the Caribbean to Brazil. A similar species (L. purpureus) occurs in the Caribbean with a range as far south as Brazil (2818, 2547).

By State: North Carolina to Texas, less frequently as far north as Massachusetts (2819).
By Stock: Growth rates and size-at-age information have been used to evaluate the stock structure of GOM red snapper. Fisher et al. (2627, 2628) modeled growth of red snapper from Alabama, Louisiana, and Texas with weighted mean fork length (FL) at age and weighted mean total weight (TW) at age using the von Bertalanffy growth model. Additionally, the authors compared growth of red snapper aged 1-10 years for each state by comparing linear regressions of mean FL and mean TW at age. The von Bertalanffy models predicted significantly smaller estimates for both maximum length and maximum theoretical weight for Texas red snapper compared with those from Alabama and Louisiana. Additionally, Texas red snapper were shown to differ significantly in regressions of mean weight at age. This led the authors to conclude that Texas red snapper were significantly smaller in mass (TW) at age and reach smaller maximum sizes than red snapper from Alabama and Louisiana. Fisher et al. (2628) suggested that this demographic variation in growth rates may indicate the existence of separate management units of red snapper in the GOM.
By Estuary: While red snapper are not commonly found in estuaries, Franks et al. (2928) found red snapper associated with a small artificial reef structure in Mississippi Sound. Age estimates from some specimens (N=36, 326-713 mm TL) ranged from 2-5 years. Histological examination of the gonads of 13 fish collected during late summer and fall found sexually mature males (N=5) and females with regressed (N=5) or immature ovaries (N=2). However, one female collected during July contained oocytes in the final stage of maturation. Tag recaptures were from the tag-release site and extended from 1-373 days-at-large indicative of site fidelity.
Adult red snapper sometimes move closer to shore in summer; they were collected in trawls in the lower parts of St. Andrews Bay system, Florida, in summer and fall but not in winter and spring (2766).

sections.heading: Life Mode
sections.content:
Egg/Parturition- Red snapper spawn mainly during June through August in the northern GOM (2812). The early life history comprises a planktonic egg stage of 18-27 h (2809; 2728).
Larva-A larval stage occurs with a duration of 25-47 d (2704). Lyczkowski-Shultz and Hanisko (2710) analyzed Southeast Area Monitoring and Assessment Program (SEAMAP) larval survey data from the U.S. GOM. Red snapper larvae were captured throughout the survey area on the middle to outer continental shelf from Florida to Texas, but were consistently observed in greatest abundance on the mid-continental shelf west of the Mississippi River, especially off western Louisiana and central Texas.
